papers.title: Mesons, Confinement, and Complexity: A Krylov Space Perspective on the Long-Range Ising Chain
papers.abstract: We investigate the interplay between confinement and Krylov complexity in the long-range transverse-field Ising chain, where power-law interactions $\sim 1/r^{\alpha}$ generate an effective confining potential between domain walls without an explicit symmetry-breaking field. Using the time-averaged Krylov state complexity after a quench as a diagnostic, we find that the complexity is strongly suppressed and only weakly system size-dependent at small $\alpha$ and small transverse field $h_x$, where confinement is strongest, and crosses over to rapid growth at larger $\alpha$, where it increases with system size. Within the confined regime, the oscillation frequencies of the complexity agree with the meson masses of an effective two-kink model, with the dominant frequency growing linearly with the lightest meson mass and the time-averaged complexity decreasing approximately as its inverse square. We further study operator Krylov complexity at finite temperature using the Wightman inner product. At low temperature, it exhibits bounded oscillations that directly encode the meson spectrum, whereas this structure is progressively washed out as the temperature increases. These results identify Krylov complexity as a spectroscopic probe of interaction-induced confinement and reproduce, in a microscopic lattice model, the hallmarks of Krylov complexity identified in confining field theories.

papers.title: Magnons in {\alpha}-Fe2O3 microdisks: from thermal to coherent excitation
papers.abstract: Hematite is a prototypical antiferromagnetic insulator for spintronic and magnonic applications, yet controlled studies of coherent magnons in thin films remain challenging due to strain sensitivity and spatial inhomogeneity. Here, we investigate magnon excitations in lithographically patterned hematite microdisks, and obtain reproducible magnon spectra from multiple individual microdisks. Brillouin light scattering reveals bulk-like field-dependent thermal magnon resonances with an ultralow effective damping parameter on the order of ~10-5. Coherent magnons are further excited using a stripline antenna adjacent to the microdisk, revealing a power-dependent frequency blue shift accompanied by a nonlinear evolution of the coherent response under strong microwave driving. Field-dependent analysis indicates a power-dependent increase of the effective magnetic anisotropy field, suggesting a tunable nonlinear response of antiferromagnetic magnons in laterally confined microdisks. These results establish patterned hematite thin films as a platform for exploring coherent and nonlinear antiferromagnetic magnon dynamics.

papers.title: Understanding the limits of latent world models
papers.abstract: World models are widely proposed as core components for enabling agents to reason over long temporal and spatial horizons. Yet current evaluations often emphasize task performance while providing limited insight into whether learned world models acquire predictive latent dynamics that reflect the underlying structure of the environment. Here we introduce the concept of faithful latent world models as an equivariance condition between the environment's transition map and the learned latent dynamics. We propose latent rollout consistency (LRC) as a metric to evaluate action-conditioned latent prediction. Strikingly, we find that across the studied state of the art latent world models, none solves the task by actually faithfully modeling the dynamics of the environment.

We call a latent world model faithful when its representation preserves the environment state and its latent dynamics evolve consistently with the true dynamics under the same actions. We measure this with latent rollout consistency (LRC) and post-hoc state decoding. Our results make two main points. First, task reward alone does not reveal whether a world model learns accurate latent dynamics or preserves the underlying physical state. LRC and state decoding expose these failures directly. Second, these diagnostics reveal two recurring failure modes under pixel observations: inaccurate velocity estimation and difficulty learning dynamics through nonlinear observation mappings. Together, these results suggest that improving both learned representations and latent dynamics is central to building more faithful world models.

papers.title: Geometric priors for single-patch neural Calabi--Yau metrics on the quintic: a conservative fixed-$\psi$ Ablation study
papers.abstract: We investigate how geometric priors shape neural approximations of the complex Monge--Amp`ere equation on the quintic Calabi--Yau threefold. This fixed-$\psi$ diagnostic compares four single-patch ans"atze: a coordinate SIREN potential model, a direct-metric Cholesky baseline, an algebraic section ansatz, and a section-plus-neural hybrid. In a 96-run learning-rate and frequency archive, section-based models reach validation $\sigma=4.14$--$4.16%$, whereas SIREN and Cholesky remain at $41.29%$ and $44.27%$. Multi-seed controls use a shared affine-$\eta$ evaluator and five fresh validation clouds. Stable section settings give $3.84$--$4.77%$, compared with $28.46$--$30.59%$ for Cholesky and $34.73$--$38.13%$ for SIREN. Hybrid projective features do not improve best-case accuracy, but they stabilise the stressed regime. They limit $\sigma$ to $4.26$--$4.41%$, versus $4.45$--$205.45%$ for raw coordinates. Within this protocol, section-based geometric structure is the main driver of accuracy; coordinate-only models plateau at substantially higher error, and raw hybrid flexibility can amplify instability. We provide a projective-scaling derivation, document protocol asymmetries, and identify projectively consistent hybrid corrections as the next step.

This gap between existence and explicit computation has persisted for nearly five decades. It motivates both classical balanced-metric algorithms and, more recently, neural approximations to Calabi–Yau metrics. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), neural operators, and related scientific machine-learning models have become practical tools for approximating nonlinear partial differential equations and expensive numerical solvers [5–7]. Their success, however, is rarely a consequence of raw network capacity alone. Across recent scientific-ML work, performance depends strongly on how the architecture represents the underlying geometry and how physical constraints enter the loss [8–11]. These issues become sharper for geometric PDEs, where the learned object is not a scalar field but a metric, and downstream quantities depend on its determinant, inverse, and derivatives.

This paper studies these issues in a controlled setting: the complex Monge–Ampère equation for Ricci-flat Kähler metrics on the quintic Calabi–Yau threefold. The aim is diagnostic rather than competitive. We do not claim a new state-of-the-art Calabi–Yau metric approximation, a complete phenomenological pipeline, or a universal limitation of neural solvers. Instead, we ask a narrower question: when persistent plateaus appear in a fixed single-patch protocol, are they better explained by hyperparameter tuning, raw model capacity, geometric constraint enforcement, or the representation built into the ansatz?

Neural approaches offer a complementary route. Early work trained networks on Donaldson-generated data [21]; holomorphic-network methods showed the value of section-aware architectures [22]; and later work trained directly from Monge–Ampère or related residuals, incorporated moduli dependence, and developed packages such as cymetric, CYJAX, and cymyc [23–27]. Recent symmetry-aware, symbolic, and section-based methods further show that explicit geometric structure can improve accuracy, stability, or interpretability [28–30]. In particular, Grassmannian learning keeps Donaldson’s section framework but uses optimisation to select efficient section subspaces and Hermitian data [30]. The present paper is positioned inside this line of work, but it isolates a smaller question than those full pipelines address.

papers.title: The SIRMOS mission concept: a space-based near-IR spectroscopic survey of 100 million galaxies in the Euclid Wide Survey footprint
papers.abstract:
SIRMOS is a mission concept for a future NASA Astrophysics Explorer opportunity that aims to revolutionize our understanding of the universe by mapping the large-scale structure of galaxies in unprecedented breadth and detail to explore cosmic origins and evolution. Specifically, the primary science goals of SIRMOS are to discover how cosmic inflation seeded large-scale structure, reveal the nature of the accelerating expansion of the universe, and measure the sum of neutrino masses to exceptionally high precision. Its secondary science goals include determining how environment shapes galaxy evolution at cosmic noon and beyond, and probing the Milky Way's dust-enshrouded regions, reaching the far side of our Galaxy.
  To accomplish its transformative science goals, SIRMOS executes a 3-year cosmology survey over the Euclid footprint of ~14,000 deg$^2$, obtaining slit spectra for ~100 million galaxies at 1<z<4. SIRMOS is the first space mission designed specifically to leverage Euclid's wide near-infrared (IR) imaging survey for target selection and employs a digital micro-mirror device (DMD) to acquire up to 4,000 simultaneous spectra over a wide 0.9 deg$^2$ field of view. The instrument's excellent spectral resolution of $R=1300$ and continuous wavelength coverage from 1.25--2.5 $\mu$m capture the redshifts of distant galaxies with no gaps, reducing systematic biases to achieve ground-breaking science.

papers.intro:
A generation ago, the emergence of dedicated, highly-multiplexed spectroscopic instruments on 8–10 m class telescopes enabled a golden age of mapping the large-scale three-dimensional distribution of galaxies. Wide-field surveys like 2dFGS covered large areas of the sky to a moderate depth while “pencil beam” surveys like DEEP and DEEP2 on Keck probed far deeper but over more restricted areas of the sky, ultimately delivering new insights into both cosmology and galaxy evolution.[7, 39, 6] More recently, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) on the KPNO 4-m telescope has gathered redshifts of over 10 million galaxies and a million quasars, demonstrating that a highly-efficient multi-object spectrograph (MOS) can generate rich datasets even when coupled with telescopes of relatively modest aperture.[18, 11]

We can achieve more powerful probes of key cosmological parameters by observing more distant galaxies at redshifts out to z≈4z\approx 4, but those key spectral features shift out of the visible and into the near-infrared. While infrared multi-object spectrographs have now been deployed on major telescopes like Keck (MOSFIRE[19]) and VLT (KMOS[34]), the quality of data gathered by these instruments is limited by the blurring effect of the Earth’s atmosphere, the opacity of the atmosphere at wavelengths where water and other species absorb significant light, and the high background generated by thermal and telluric emission — OH airglow lines in particular — that contribute substantial noise and limit the ability to observe faint targets. The opacity gaps due to water vapor also produce broad gaps in redshift coverage for key spectral lines in the galaxy spectra. Ultimately this leads to redshift-dependent biases in the data which are challenging to model. These redshift-dependent selection effects contribute uncertainty to the derived cosmological parameters.

Putting an IR MOS into orbit confers important advantages over similar instruments on the ground. The absence of atmospheric absorption and emission lines and the cooler instrument temperatures achievable in space both reduce the noise resulting from the IR night sky and telescope emission and eliminate the problematic gaps in redshift coverage, reducing bias in measurements of the galaxy distribution. Observing above the atmosphere also reduces time-varying atmospheric blur typical of ground-based telescopes that contributes to source confusion and degrades the signal-to-noise ratio (S/NS/N). The NIRSpec instrument on JWST is one such MOS instrument that can exploit these advantages of observing from space. However, the scarcity of JWST observing time, the relatively low multiplexing capability of NIRSpec, the relatively small field of view (FoV), and the long slew and settle time for JWST all conspire to limit the effectiveness of JWST as a survey instrument on large scales. An IR space telescope of more modest aperture but large field of view coupled with a highly capable IR MOS is well positioned to make major strides in mapping the Universe in the critical redshift range 1<z<41<z<4 beyond the grasp of its ground-based counterparts.

However, the scarcity of JWST observing time, the relatively low multiplexing capability of NIRSpec, the relatively small field of view (FoV), and the long slew and settle time for JWST all conspire to limit the effectiveness of JWST as a survey instrument on large scales. An IR space telescope of more modest aperture but large field of view coupled with a highly capable IR MOS is well positioned to make major strides in mapping the Universe in the critical redshift range 1<z<41<z<4 beyond the grasp of its ground-based counterparts.

This paper describes our concept for such a mission: the Satellite for Infrared Multi-Object Spectroscopy (SIRMOS). This mission concept draws from earlier incarnations in the form of the ATLAS Probe mission [38, 9] and was previously conceived as a “small explorer” (SMEX) mission [8] before being recast as a more capable spacecraft planned for submission to the next NASA astrophysics “medium explorer” (MIDEX) opportunity.

SIRMOS features superior multi-spectral capabilities compared to other facilities in orbit. The pending Roman and operational Euclid spacecraft have smaller apertures but much wider fields of view compared to JWST, enabling surveys of vast portions of the sky to capture broadband colors and slitless spectra of modest resolution for tens of millions of galaxies. The resulting spectra posess sufficient nominal spectral resolution to measure moderately accurate galaxy redshifts, but because they observe in slitless mode the resulting data are subject to confusion from closely spaced galaxies and reduced spectral resolution due to the finite spatial extent of galaxies. SIRMOS achieves similar spectral resolving power but its slitmask-based design reduces source confusion and produces consistent spectral resolution from target to target, yielding superior redshift accuracy.

papers.title: Machine learning enabled design of sustainable alloys considering real world constraints
papers.abstract: Designing sustainable alloys must reconcile high performance with real-world constraints, including feedstock scarcity and variability, processing and energy requirements, regulatory thresholds, and economic limitations. Addressing these constraints reaches far beyond today's conventional performance-focused frameworks. It needs to consider not only complex property-processing-performance trade-offs but also sustainable production pathways. Here, we propose a physics-informed ensemble (PIE) learning framework that integrates fundamental structure-property relationships with processing routes and sustainability criteria for mechanism-based alloy design. It predicts properties from composition-microstructure relationships and infers processing routes under sustainability constraints, establishing an interdisciplinary approach to identifying sustainable alloy solutions. We validate the approach for Mg alloys, a lightweight yet energy-intensive metallic material class, considering performance, cost, and carbon emissions. Trained on a benchmark dataset, the PIE model systematically explores plausible alloy compositions and microstructures to construct a digital library of millions of candidate alloys. From this space, we identify two sustainable Mg alloy solutions that overcome the conventional performance-cost-emission trade-off: a rare-earth-containing alloy increases yield and tensile strength by 72.8 percent and 61.1 percent, respectively, over alloys from the same family at comparable cost and emissions; and a rare-earth-free alloy reduces cost and carbon emissions by 40.4 percent and 88.9 percent, respectively, relative to its primary-feedstock counterpart, without compromising mechanical performance. This work introduces a general, physics-informed, and quantifiable framework for designing sustainable alloys under real-world constraints.

papers.title: Generation and Verification: Human-Agent Collaboration for Safety-Critical Automotive Software Engineering
papers.abstract: Research on coding agents mainly focuses on generation quality. Yet, safety-critical automotive software makes two additional demands. It prioritizes verification, since every change is reviewed, traced to a requirement, and checked against industry standards such as MISRA and AUTOSAR before it can be committed. It is also a narrow domain, written against layered architectures, embedded resource constraints, and organization-specific interface conventions that are scarce in the data general-purpose LLMs are trained on. We present a coding assistant for automotive C/C++ that addresses both demands. First, it exposes three tools to the user over the Model Context Protocol (generate, edit, and verify), allowing developers to run verify on any code on demand rather than relying on the agent to check its own output. Second, rather than using a general-purpose model, we customize the underlying LLM for the automotive domain through prompt engineering and fine-tuning. We construct a dataset from automotive production code of AUMOVIO, where each function is paired with the requirement texts and Unified Modeling Language (UML) behavior it must satisfy. In a two-week pilot on active production projects, developers report verify as the most-used tool and confirm using it on their own code and not only on generated output. Comparing model customization strategies, 75% prefer the faster prompt-engineered configuration. MISRA- and AUTOSAR-inspired pattern checkers indicate that prompt engineering achieves a lower number of violations on C, while fine-tuning shows better conformance with architecture patterns for C++.
papers.intro:
Research on AI coding assistants is organized largely around generation quality (Jiang et al., 2024), asking whether a model produces code that compiles, passes tests, and resembles a reference implementation (Paul et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025). Automotive software development is adopting these assistants as car makers seek productivity gains (Hepp et al., 2025). Yet, they fall short of safety-critical requirements such as AUTOSAR (AUTOSAR, 2017) and MISRA-C (Association, 2013), which establish strict rules for reliability in automotive systems. Recent studies show that popular LLMs struggle to produce MISRA-compliant code by default (Umer, 2025), while hallucinations pose tangible safety risks (Pavel et al., 2025). This places two additional demands on coding assistants for automotive software.

The first demand is verification. In safety-critical settings, developers cannot accept LLM output blindly, since every change is reviewed, traced to a requirement, and checked against coding standards before it can be committed. The practical question is therefore not only whether the model can write compliant code, but how the agent should collaborate with the developer so that compliance can be verified, audited, and trusted.

A general-purpose model fits this setting poorly, since the conventions it must follow are underrepresented in its training data (Cassano et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023).

This paper introduces an agentic assistant for automotive software, built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) (Anthropic, 2024), that addresses both demands. We address the first demand by exposing verification as a separate tool. Rather than providing a single code generation mode, the system exposes three tools: generate, edit, and verify. The first two generate and revise function bodies from a signature, documentation, and context such as imported functions and UML diagrams. This task is central to automotive workflows, where interfaces are specified upfront and implementations must follow established patterns. The third tool lets developers run the same automotive rule checks the agent uses internally, on demand and independently of generation. Most coding agents treat checking as an internal step that the agent itself decides to invoke. We argue that in safety-critical settings the developer must be able to trigger evaluation directly, because a check the agent can skip is not a reliable check.

We address the second demand by customizing the model to the domain. We build a dataset from an AUMOVIO’s production automotive code in which each function is paired with the context needed to implement it compliantly, including requirement texts resolved from AUMOVIO’s requirements-management system and the UML behavior the function must realize. On this dataset we compare the two customization strategies most used for code models (Shin et al., 2025; Freire et al., 2026): prompt engineering (PE) with general-purpose API models and domain-specific fine-tuning (FT) (Zirak and Hemmati, 2024), both scored against custom rule sets inspired by established automotive standards. PE here involves supplying the assembled context and the rule sets in full at inference time, rather than tuning instruction wording, so the two strategies differ in when the domain information reaches the model and not in what it contains. Because those rule sets are pattern matchers, we treat their output as pattern conformance rather than compliance, and report how that changes what the numbers support.

The main contributions are the following. First, we present an MCP-based architecture in which verification is exposed as a tool the developer can invoke directly, on any code and at any time, and articulate the corresponding division of labor between human and agent in safety-critical review. Second, we implement a context engineering pipeline that assembles requirement texts, UML behavior, and API context into training and inference examples, which lets us compare PE against FT on the same domain information, differing in whether it arrives during training or at inference. We analyze how the two methods perform in terms of architecture and coding pattern violations and generation latency. Finally, we report results from a two-week pilot with nine developers from AUMOVIO and show how the three tools are taken up in a real-world production workflow.

papers.title: Derivation of OH sum rules without Rayleigh--Jeans approximation: a powerful tool for measuring the variation of fundamental physical constants
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that the optical depths of any OH $\Lambda$-doublet quartet obey one exact linear relation in every velocity channel. No approximation is needed. The only exception is the $^{2}\Pi_{1/2}$ $J{=}1/2$ level, which has three transitions only, because its $F{=}0{\leftrightarrow}0$ line is strictly forbidden. The relation is $\tau_{S_1}(v)/\mu_{S_1}^{2}+\tau_{S_2}(v)/\mu_{S_2}^{2}=\tau_{M_1}(v)/(a\mu_{M_1}^{2})+\tau_{M_2}(v)/(b\mu_{M_2}^{2})$, where $a=2J^{2}+J-1$, $b=2J^{2}+3J$, and the $\mu_i^{2}$ are reduced transition dipole moments derived from the catalogued Einstein $A$ coefficients. It holds equally for gas in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE), for non-LTE gas, for masers and for conjugate gas. We suggest that it is a powerful tool for measuring the variation of fundamental physical constants.

papers.intro:
The hydroxyl radical OH was the first molecule detected in the interstellar medium at radio wavelengths (Weinreb et al. 1963), and it remains one of the most useful molecules in radio astronomy. The coupling between the electronic orbital angular momentum and the molecular rotation splits every rotational level into a pair of parity states, the well-known Λ\Lambda-doubling (Dousmanis et al. 1955). The proton spin I=1/2I{=}1/2 splits each parity state further into hyperfine sublevels. The lowest rotational state, Π3/22{}^{2}\Pi_{3/2} J=3/2J{=}3/2, therefore has four sublevels, connected by four radio lines near 18 cm (Fig. 1). These lines have been seen in emission from diffuse interstellar gas, in absorption toward bright continuum sources, and as masers around evolved stars and in star-forming regions (Robinson and McGee 1967; Elitzur 1992; Lo 2005; Dawson et al. 2022, e.g.).

papers.title: Closed-Loop Aware Planning via Imitation-Free Speed Scoring for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has predominantly relied on open-loop imitation learning for training, which presents two limitations. First, expert demonstrations show only one behavior per scenario, so the model cannot learn alternative valid behaviors and, in turn, cannot adapt to user-specified preferences at test time. Second, noise or ambiguity in these demonstrations can produce inconsistent, unreliable supervision for the end-to-end models. Driving is inherently multi-modal: multiple different behaviors can be valid responses to the same scene, and this diversity arises largely from speed rather than path. We introduce a planning paradigm that learns the path through imitation while scoring a set of candidate speeds across multiple criteria with a learned function supervised by physically grounded safety constraints. We realize this paradigm as Closed-Loop Aware Planning for Autonomous Driving (CLAP-AD), a plug-in planning head that integrates with existing end-to-end driving models and, to our knowledge, is the first to enable explicit test-time control over their speed selection without speed-conditioned training. On Bench2Drive-Speed, CLAP-AD sets a new state of the art Speed-Adherence Score of 82.53, topping TFv6, the strongest baseline on this metric, by 12.9 points while retaining strong closed-loop driving performance. On Bench2Drive, it improves driving score by +28.5 and +32.7 over UniAD and VAD, and on NAVSIM v2, built on real-world driving data, EPDMS by +6.1 over its backbone. Project page: https://clap-ad.github.io

To improve closed-loop performance, one line of work disentangles path from speed, observing that a shared temporal-waypoint representation entangles a largely deterministic, lane-constrained path with a genuinely multi-modal speed [12]. Follow-up methods retain this separation but still imitate a single speed value or profile per class [33, 43, 47], leaving the multi-modality of driving speed unresolved. A separate line of work scores a fixed trajectory vocabulary against several driving criteria alongside an imitation score [26, 27, 40], yet the evidence for a benefit from these criteria over imitation alone in fully reactive closed-loop settings is mixed at best (Sec. 2). Across both lines, path and speed remain optimized under the same objective and architecture, overlooking their fundamentally different nature, and neither offers any support for user test-time controllability over the model’s decisions.

Motivated by this, we argue that path and speed should be learned under different objectives, retaining imitation learning for path prediction while replacing expert speed imitation with a multi-criteria scoring mechanism over a set of diverse speed classes. This formulation brings two key advantages. First, evaluating multiple candidate speeds along the predicted path yields a range of safe speed profiles, enabling explicit deployment-time customization of driving speed, a capability largely unexplored in existing E2E driving models. Second, since each criterion is supervised directly from physically grounded constraints rather than a single noisy expert trace, the model learns genuinely safe behavior per criterion, and the resulting scores are directly interpretable, letting us attribute driving failures to particular failures in speed score prediction. To realize this framework, we propose CLAP-AD, a plug-in planning head that integrates into existing E2E driving models: given upstream perception features, it first predicts a driving path, then scores candidate speed classes along it via dedicated, criterion-specific heads. As shown in Fig. 1, this design lets CLAP-AD substantially improve how faithfully each backbone follows a user-specified speed while retaining strong closed-loop driving performance.

This controllability comes at little to no cost in driving quality: CLAP-AD improves UniAD by +28.5 DS and VAD by +32.7 DS on Bench2Drive and LTFv6 by +6.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, while on TFv6 it retains driving performance within a few points of the baseline.

papers.title: Protostellar Outflows at the EarliesT Stages (POETS) X. Preliminary statistics of 6.7 GHz masers near POETS sources
papers.abstract: So far, the POETS survey has focused on studying at high angular resolution the properties of both 22.2 GHz H2O masers and the radio continuum emission near young stellar objects (YSOs). Now, we want to add the information coming from another star formation tracer, the Class II 6.7 GHz CH3OH (methanol) maser, towards the same POETS targets. We seek to probe the existence of 6.7 GHz maser emission near POETS sources with high sensitivity observations and study their kinematic properties with respect to local radio continuum and 22.2 GHz maser emission at high angular and spectral resolutions. Within the POETS survey, we used the Very Large Array (VLA) in the A configuration, operating at high spectral resolution (0.1 km/s) and achieving a sensitivity of a few mJy/beam per channel map, in order to (i) probe the emission from methanol gas in the 6.7 GHz maser transition and (ii) trace its absolute spatial distribution and local standard of rest velocity. We present a preliminary analysis of 6.7 GHz CH3OH maser emission toward a subsample of the POETS survey (22 fields observed so far), 60 % of which show detection above a brightness temperature threshold of 10^7 K. Five sources among this subsample are new detections. We draw a 6.7 GHz maser brightness function by studying the distribution of the intrinsic luminosity of the maser population and predict that more than 30 % of the whole population is undetected at typical interferometric sensitivities of a few 10 mJy/beam. We confirm that 6.7 GHz masers arise close to the young star they are associated with and quantify that, on average, 90 % of them are distributed within radii of 3000 au only. Furthermore, we find a tight correlation between the 6.7 GHz maser luminosity coming from a given source and the local free-free emission, suggesting that the radio continuum provides the dominant source of seed photons amplified by the methanol gas.

papers.intro:
In the early `​90`90s, Karl Martin Menten reported about the first detection of a widespread and bright maser emission in the 6668.5 MHz 51−605_{1}-6_{0} A+ transition of interstellar methanol (CH3OH), coming from luminous star forming regions in the Galaxy (Menten, 1991b). Its maser action was ever since identified as a Class II type methanol maser whose population inversion is triggered by a radiative pumping mechanism, as opposed to the collisional pumping of Class I type (Menten, 1987; Batrla et al., 1987; Menten, 1991a, e.g.,). The mid-to-far infrared (IR) continuum field of dust grains, warmed at an equilibrium temperature around 100–200 K, is the cause of the radiative pumping. The Planck spectrum of dust grains, peaking at wavelengths around 25​μ\rm 25\,\mum, preferentially excites methanol molecules into the first two torsional states. This excitation ultimately produces the population inversion of the lower-energy levels responsible for the maser action (e.g., Cragg et al. 2005 and references therein).

Heating of dust grains ignites maser emission twice: while serving as pumping mechanism, it does release methanol molecules in the gas phase by sublimation from the grains’ ice mantles. Enhancing methanol abundance with respect to molecular hydrogen (H2\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}) to values near 10−610^{-6} (and above), it is a strict requirement for reproducing the observed maser brightness temperatures, largely exceeding 10910^{9} K typically (Sobolev et al., 1997; Sanna et al., 2015a, e.g.,). Notably, having methanol-rich dust grains heated to a few hundreds kelvin are conditions met in the envelopes of intermediate- to high-mass young stars preferentially. Furthermore, modelling of Class II methanol maser excitation predicts two major constraints locally, where: (i) the dust temperature should be systematically higher than the gas kinetic temperature and (ii) the hydrogen volume density should not exceed values of 10810^{8} cm-3, above which the maser emission is promptly quenched (Cragg and others, 1992; Cragg et al., 2002; Cragg et al., 2005, e.g.,). These physical conditions can be qualitatively explained to sustain both a steady population inversion while preventing thermalization of the energy levels for very high particle densities.

Observationally, in the last thirty years the appearance of 6.7 GHz maser emission at milli-arcsecond (mas) resolution has been studied in detail. At this angular resolution, unblended spectral features with typical linewidths 0.3 km s-1 wide are resolved in spatially contiguous compact spots each of a few au in size, for source distances up to a few kilo-parsecs (Menten et al., 1992). These observations have allowed to assess a number of 6.7 GHz maser properties as follows. Firstly, individual maser spots are made up of a compact bright core coincident with the observed size of the emission; this emission is surrounded by a fainter halo up to an order of magnitude larger that best shows up in plots of intensity versus spatial frequency (Minier et al., 2002, their Figs. A). Secondly, these maser spots are spatially grouped in regular filamentary structures that persist over several years, showing Local Standard of Rest (LSR) velocity gradients of the order of 0.1 km s-1 au-1 (Sanna et al., 2010a, their Fig. 6). These properties also make 6.7 GHz masers preferred astrometric tools (Reid et al., 2017). Thirdly, each association of spots, grouped within a single cloudlet as large as 10 au typically, moves on the plane of the sky at slow velocities of 10 km s-1 and less, comparable to the total spread of maser LSR velocities (Sanna et al., 2010b, their Fig. 6). Fourthly, there is a clear correlation between the proper motion vector of a cloudlet and its internal LSR gradient that statistically trace the same orientation (Moscadelli et al., 2011b, their Figs. 5 and 6). Notably, a strong correlation holds between proper motion vectors and the maser polarization vectors too (Sanna et al., 2015b, their Fig. 3a), with the latter following an orientation statistically consistent with the outflow direction (Surcis et al., 2013). Altogether, these results suggest that the kinematic properties of methanol masers at 6.7 GHz are representative of the overall environment where they are excited.

Further information about the 6.7 GHz maser environment can be inferred from the maser proper motions taken as an ensemble. To date, by including all regions where 6.7 GHz masers were observed at milli-arcsecond resolution over (at least) 3 epochs, proper motions trace expansion from a local common center (paired with rotation typically) in all regions but two (Sanna et al., 2010a; Sanna et al., 2010b; Moscadelli et al., 2011a; Moscadelli et al., 2013; Bartkiewicz et al., 2020; Bartkiewicz et al., 2024, e.g.,). In these sources, the radial distribution of methanol masers extends up to projected distances of 3000 au approximately. At variance with this (most) common phenomenology, in two sources 6.7 GHz masers were also observed to trace proper motions that converge towards a common center, at comparable radial distances (Goddi, C. et al., 2011; Sugiyama et al., 2014; Sanna et al., 2017). Whether or not this latter phenomenology catches a stage of stellar evolution different from the former, and how frequently it can be observed, it has to be further investigated in the future. Nevertheless, these kinematic properties overall suggest that 6.7 GHz CH3OH masers trace circumstellar gas influenced by the young star directly, although the upper limit in density imposed by the maser quenching requires that these masers cannot be found too close to the star.

papers.title: Any3R: Feedforward 3D Reconstruction from Any Camera Type
papers.abstract: Geometry foundation models recover camera poses and dense geometry from a set of images with a feed-forward network, but they expect pinhole images. That assumption is inside the backbone too: the positional encoding and the training loss both bind an image position to a direction in space, and both depend on the lens. We condition both on the dense ray field, the unit direction through every pixel, which describes any central camera without a lens type, distortion coefficients or a bound on field of view. Angular coordinates give the rotary encoding the measured ray angle of each patch, evaluated per view, and solid-angle weighting scales the point loss by the area each pixel covers on the sphere, so neither the encoding nor the supervision depends on the lens. Any3R is therefore a feed-forward model that takes any central camera, and is robust to mixing many camera types per scene, with no retraining per lens. On a benchmark of thirteen central cameras across three datasets, where every method reconstructs with its own predicted camera poses, it is the most consistently accurate method. Any3R enables scalable 3D reconstruction from heterogeneous crowdsourced and archival imagery collections sourced across diverse camera types. Project page: https://jingong-chen.github.io/Any3R/

papers.intro:
Recovering the 3D structure of a scene from a set of images is a fundamental problem in computer vision. Geometry foundation models such as VGGT [57], π3\pi^{3} [61], MapAnything [25], VGGT-Ω\Omega [58] and Depth Anything 3 [34] now solve it with a feed-forward network [60, 29, 13, 4, 56, 59, 65, 75]. A regular camera sees only a narrow part of a scene in each view, so covering a whole room or street takes many views captured densely and carefully.

Recovering the 3D structure of a scene from a set of images is a fundamental problem in computer vision. Geometry foundation models such as VGGT [57], π3\pi^{3} [61], MapAnything [25], VGGT-Ω\Omega [58] and Depth Anything 3 [34] now solve it with a feed-forward network [60, 29, 13, 4, 56, 59, 65, 75]. A regular camera sees only a narrow part of a scene in each view, so covering a whole room or street takes many views captured densely and carefully.

The direct way to cover more of a scene per view is a wider lens, and wide-angle and panoramic cameras are already common in autonomous driving [72, 33] and indoor scanning [5, 1]. Feed-forward models cannot use such images as they are, because they read every frame as a pinhole image. Recent work adapts them to particular lenses, with a discrete token for the camera model, an adapter around a frozen backbone, a pairwise alignment stage, a conversion of the input to a cubemap, or retraining on equirectangular images [22, 12, 19, 3, 18, 31], but each supports only a fixed list of camera models, so an unseen camera needs retraining or a new conversion step. Mixing cameras of different types in one reconstruction, such as a pinhole view, a fisheye frame and a panorama of one scene as in Fig. 1, is harder still. Wid3R [22] and Fisheye3R [12] mix only the camera types they support, CAM3R [19] reconstructs two views at a time and aligns them afterwards, and the panoramic models accept panoramas alone. MapAnything [25] and OmniVGGT [39] take the intrinsics of each view as input and could mix cameras in principle, but a pinhole intrinsic matrix cannot describe a field of view of 180∘180^{\circ} or more, the range of many fisheye lenses and every panorama.

Both limits trace back to the backbone’s positional encoding, which none of these methods changes: it locates each patch by its pixel index [49]. On a pinhole camera, the index tells the backbone roughly where the patch looks; on a fisheye, each pixel covers a wider angle, so the same index points somewhere else (Fig. 2(ii)). The training loss has a similar problem: it weights every pixel equally, but a fisheye pixel near the edge sees a different amount of the scene than one at the center (Fig. 2(i)).

We present Any3R, which removes the pinhole assumption by giving the ray direction of every pixel to both the encoding and the loss (Fig. 2(iii)). In pinhole, fisheye and panoramic cameras, all rays pass through one point. Such central cameras are fully described by the ray direction of each pixel, whatever the lens. Angular coordinates position a patch by the angle of its ray instead of its index, so one unit of position means the same angle on every camera. Solid-angle weighting scales the loss by how much of the scene each pixel sees, so every part of the scene counts equally whatever the lens. Because each view carries its own ray field, Any3R reconstructs from any central camera without rectification, and views from different cameras can be processed together, in any number. On three public datasets imaged through thirteen camera models, where every method reconstructs with its own predicted camera poses, Any3R gives the most accurate reconstruction and camera poses on wide-angle and panoramic lenses and is on par with the strongest pinhole baseline at 90∘90^{\circ}. It also outperforms the methods built for wide-angle or panoramic lenses on every lens they take, and its pose estimates on real pinhole photographs are competitive with the strongest pinhole baselines. Its margin over the pinhole models is smallest at 90∘90^{\circ} and much larger on the wider lenses.

papers.title: Unveiling the nonthermal environments of NGC 3411 and NGC 5903 through new MeerKAT observations
papers.abstract: Galaxy groups are key laboratories for investigating the interplay between active galactic nucleus (AGN) outbursts and the dynamical processes of the intra-group medium. We aim to characterize the morphology, spectral properties, and magnetic field structure of the diffuse nonthermal radio emission in two peculiar galaxy groups, NGC 3411 and NGC 5903, selected from an originally larger sample, in order to constrain its origin and its connection with the dynamics of the intra-group medium. We present new MeerKAT UHF- and L-band observations of the two groups, complemented by archival Chandra and XMM-Newton data already analyzed in previous works. In NGC 3411, we detect extended radio emission surrounding the central AGN over scales of ~70 kpc, and resolve previously undetected arc-shaped substructures on scales of ~20-30 kpc. This extended component exhibits a relatively uniform steep spectrum ($\alpha$ ~ -1.7). We discuss possible scenarios for its origin, including mini-halos, aged AGN plasma, weak shocks, and the possibility of a radio galaxy observed along the line of sight. In NGC 5903, MeerKAT reveals a complex filamentary morphology, including a previously unknown ring-like structure surrounding the central AGN. Spectral-index mapping shows localized flattening ($\alpha$ ~ -0.9) along the north arc, while polarization data reveal ordered magnetic fields and a patchy rotation measure distribution across the source. Together with the disturbed X-ray morphology, these results support a scenario in which fossil AGN plasma has been redistributed and locally reenergized by group-scale dynamical processes such as turbulence, shear, and weak compression. Our results demonstrate that galaxy groups can host a rich variety of nonthermal phenomena, whose properties can only be fully revealed through the combination of sensitive, high-resolution, and multifrequency radio observations.

papers.intro:
Galaxy groups represent the most common environment for galaxies in the local Universe, containing more than half of the total galaxy population (Eke et al. 2004; Tully 2015, e.g.,). As an intermediate step in the hierarchical formation of structures that bridge the gap between individual galaxies and massive clusters, they play a crucial role in driving galaxy evolution. The majority of baryons in these systems reside in the hot, X-ray-emitting intra-group medium (IGrM), the thermodynamic state of which is determined by the interplay between gravitational processes, radiative cooling, and nongravitational heating (see Sun 2012; Lovisari and Ettori 2021; Bahar et al. 2024, for a review).

Galaxy groups represent the most common environment for galaxies in the local Universe, containing more than half of the total galaxy population (Eke et al. 2004; Tully 2015, e.g.,). As an intermediate step in the hierarchical formation of structures that bridge the gap between individual galaxies and massive clusters, they play a crucial role in driving galaxy evolution. The majority of baryons in these systems reside in the hot, X-ray-emitting intra-group medium (IGrM), the thermodynamic state of which is determined by the interplay between gravitational processes, radiative cooling, and nongravitational heating (see Sun 2012; Lovisari and Ettori 2021; Bahar et al. 2024, for a review).

Of the nongravitational processes, feedback from active galactic nuclei (AGNs) is widely accepted as the primary mechanism preventing catastrophic cooling of the hot gas in the centers of groups and clusters (McNamara and Nulsen 2007; Fabian 2012). In the standard "radio mode" feedback scenario, the central supermassive black hole launches relativistic jets that inflate cavities in the surrounding medium. The energy deposited through these bubbles balances radiative losses, maintaining the global thermal equilibrium. While this cycle is well studied in massive galaxy clusters, AGN feedback is expected to be even more impactful in the shallower gravitational potentials of galaxy groups (Giodini et al. 2010; Oppenheimer et al. 2010), where the energy output of the AGN can be comparable to the binding energy of the gas. Evidence of this impact is provided by the reduced gas fractions observed in galaxy groups (Eckert et al. 2021; Siegel et al. 2026, e.g.,).

While this cycle is well studied in massive galaxy clusters, AGN feedback is expected to be even more impactful in the shallower gravitational potentials of galaxy groups (Giodini et al. 2010; Oppenheimer et al. 2010), where the energy output of the AGN can be comparable to the binding energy of the gas. Evidence of this impact is provided by the reduced gas fractions observed in galaxy groups (Eckert et al. 2021; Siegel et al. 2026, e.g.,).

A key, yet often elusive, component of the feedback cycle is the generation of shocks, which can be driven by powerful AGN outbursts propagating through the intra-cluster medium (ICM), as observed, for example, in systems like M87 (Forman et al. 2005), Hydra A (Nulsen et al. 2005), and MS 0735.6+7421 (McNamara et al. 2005). These shocks are efficient at converting kinetic energy into thermal energy, thereby reheating the cooling gas (Fabian et al. 2006). However, detecting such features in galaxy groups has historically been challenging due to the lower surface brightness of the IGrM and the typically smaller physical scales involved compared to those in massive clusters. Consequently, the precise contribution of shock heating to the thermodynamic budget of galaxy groups remains an open question (Osmond and Ponman 2004; Panagoulia et al. 2014).

These shocks are efficient at converting kinetic energy into thermal energy, thereby reheating the cooling gas (Fabian et al. 2006). However, detecting such features in galaxy groups has historically been challenging due to the lower surface brightness of the IGrM and the typically smaller physical scales involved compared to those in massive clusters. Consequently, the precise contribution of shock heating to the thermodynamic budget of galaxy groups remains an open question (Osmond and Ponman 2004; Panagoulia et al. 2014).

The nonthermal component of the IGrM, as revealed through radio emission, offers a unique window into the history of galaxy groups (Pasini et al. 2021, e.g.,). Relativistic plasma displaced by subsonic motions (e.g., turbulence, uplift, and shear) and by magnetic draping can be gently compressed, stretched, and reenergized, producing filamentary morphologies and regions of locally flatter radio spectra without the need for strong shocks. For this reason, deep radio observations provide a complementary probe of the AGN heating cycle, mixing and transport processes, and the long-term duty cycle of central engines (Brienza et al. 2021; Brienza et al. 2022, e.g.,). Models that include multiphase condensation and chaotic cold accretion predict intermittent, multidirectional outbursts regulated by the competition between cooling and turbulent eddy-turnover times (Gaspari et al. 2013; Gaspari et al. 2018, e.g.,). In this picture, radio emission is not only a tracer of current jet activity or strong shocks but also a long-lived record of fossil plasma. This plasma can be redistributed, compressed, and magnetically draped by the evolving IGrM, which produces sharp filaments and locally flatter spectra without requiring strong shocks through the thermal gas (Gaspari et al. 2012; Yang et al. 2019; Wittor and Gaspari 2020). Recent improvements in low-surface-brightness sensitivity, provided by instruments such as MeerKAT and the LOw Frequency ARray (van Haarlem et al. 2013), have unveiled new classes of diffuse radio sources, including odd radio circles (ORCs; Norris et al. 2021). While the nature of ORCs remains uncertain, proposed scenarios range from spherical shock waves generated by powerful events to old AGN lobes reenergized by group-scale disturbances (Norris et al. 2021; Shabala et al. 2024; Kumari and Pal 2024, e.g.,). Although only a handful of ORCs are currently known, several new candidates have been identified in recent surveys (Norris et al. 2021; Gupta et al. 2022; Koribalski et al. 2024; Bulbul et al. 2024b; Gupta et al. 2025), including those carried out by LOFAR (De Gasperin et al. 2026).

The nonthermal component of the IGrM, as revealed through radio emission, offers a unique window into the history of galaxy groups (Pasini et al. 2021, e.g.,). Relativistic plasma displaced by subsonic motions (e.g., turbulence, uplift, and shear) and by magnetic draping can be gently compressed, stretched, and reenergized, producing filamentary morphologies and regions of locally flatter radio spectra without the need for strong shocks. For this reason, deep radio observations provide a complementary probe of the AGN heating cycle, mixing and transport processes, and the long-term duty cycle of central engines (Brienza et al. 2021; Brienza et al. 2022, e.g.,). Models that include multiphase condensation and chaotic cold accretion predict intermittent, multidirectional outbursts regulated by the competition between cooling and turbulent eddy-turnover times (Gaspari et al. 2013; Gaspari et al. 2018, e.g.,). In this picture, radio emission is not only a tracer of current jet activity or strong shocks but also a long-lived record of fossil plasma. This plasma can be redistributed, compressed, and magnetically draped by the evolving IGrM, which produces sharp filaments and locally flatter spectra without requiring strong shocks through the thermal gas (Gaspari et al. 2012; Yang et al. 2019; Wittor and Gaspari 2020). Recent improvements in low-surface-brightness sensitivity, provided by instruments such as MeerKAT and the LOw Frequency ARray (van Haarlem et al. 2013), have unveiled new classes of diffuse radio sources, including odd radio circles (ORCs; Norris et al. 2021). While the nature of ORCs remains uncertain, proposed scenarios range from spherical shock waves generated by powerful events to old AGN lobes reenergized by group-scale disturbances (Norris et al. 2021; Shabala et al. 2024; Kumari and Pal 2024, e.g.,). Although only a handful of ORCs are currently known, several new candidates have been identified in recent surveys (Norris et al. 2021; Gupta et al. 2022; Koribalski et al. 2024; Bulbul et al. 2024b; Gupta et al. 2025), including those carried out by LOFAR (De Gasperin et al. 2026).

In this work, we present new MeerKAT observations of two galaxy groups, NGC 3411 and NGC 5903. These systems were selected from a larger sample of groups originally used to investigate the coupling and interactions between AGN outbursts and the thermal phase of the IGrM. According to previous observations, both targets exhibit peculiar, multiphase environments and complex radio morphologies that challenge standard feedback models. NGC 3411 appears relaxed in X-rays but hosts a puzzling temperature structure with a "cool shell" (O’Sullivan et al. 2007, hereafter OS07). Conversely, NGC 5903 displays a complex interaction between neutral hydrogen (HI) filaments, hot gas, and steep-spectrum radio emission (O’Sullivan et al. 2018, hereafter OS18), suggesting a history of interactions and mixing. By combining our new MeerKAT data with archival X-ray and optical observations, performing a spectral analysis, and examining polarization, we aim to disentangle the origin of the nonthermal emission and explain the peculiar environments observed in these two systems.

papers.title: NOCTURNE. VI. Hour-timescale radio variability in early-stage active galactic nucleus SDSS J122844.81+501751.2
papers.abstract: Recently, a sample of radio-weak active galactic nuclei (AGN) was discovered to exhibit extreme Jy-level radio flares at 37~GHz. The origin of these extraordinary flares remains unknown. All sources host low-mass supermassive black holes, and most of them can be classified as narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. We employed multiwavelength observations to investigate one of these sources, SDSS J122844.81+501751.2, during a period of high 37~GHz activity. Our data include radio observations from Mets\"ahovi Radio Observatory (MRO) at 37~GHz, OVRO at 15~GHz, and JVLA at 15, 22, and 33~GHz, as well as optical, UV, and X-ray observations from \textit{Swift}/XRT and UVOT. We studied the variability of the multiwavelength light curves (LC) using statistical tests, as well as derived the $e$-folding timescales of the flares. Utilising the timescales and the observed flare properties, we estimated the variability brightness temperatures and Doppler factors associated with the flares. Most individual LCs do not show statistically significant variability, which is likely due to the low number of measurements. The shortest timescale we estimated is only 1.1~hours, measured between MRO 37~GHz and JVLA 33~GHz detections. This is the fastest intrinsic radio variability reported in an AGN so far. This yielded an extreme variability brightness temperature of $T_\mathrm{B}$ = 4.20 $~\times$ 10$^{18}$~K and a variability Doppler factor of 438. We discuss magnetic eruptions near the black hole as a possible explanation for the extreme radio flares, and show that both incoherent and coherent processes can produce flares at these timescales. These flares challenge our current understanding of AGN radio variability. Whereas magnetic eruptions offer a viable explanation for the flares, more observations, preferably broadband and including polarisation, will be required to confirm their origin. (abridged)

papers.intro:
Approximately 10% of active galactic nuclei (AGN) can launch and sustain powerful relativistic jets (Padovani, 2017), which are often highly variable yet persistently detectable at radio frequencies. Due to their strong radio emission, jetted AGN have often been identified using the radio loudness parameter, RR11 1 Radio loudness parameter, ​R\emph{R}, is defined as the ratio between 5 GHz flux density and optical BB band flux density. Sources with ​R>\emph{R}> 10 are considered radio-loud, ​R<\emph{R}< 10 radio-quiet (Kellermann et al., 1989).. Whereas it is still able to pick out the radio-brightest sources, this parameter fails to represent the true diversity of the jet phenomenon in AGN, spanning from powerful relativistic jets to non-collimated outflows and everything in between (Padovani, 2017; Lähteenmäki et al., 2017; Panessa et al., 2019; Järvelä et al., 2022). Moreover, the RR parameter often fails to identify even jetted AGN if they are misaligned or low-power. Alternatively, non-jetted AGN whose hosts exhibit strong star formation can be classified as radio-loud (Caccianiga et al., 2015; Järvelä et al., 2022; Vietri et al., 2022).

Radio-loudness faced another hurdle with the discovery of a small sample of extremely variable radio AGN (Lähteenmäki et al., 2018). Most of these sources are narrow-line Seyfert 1 (NLS1) galaxies (Crepaldi et al., 2025). The NLS1 identification is based on their optical spectrum: the full-width at half maximum (FWHM) of their broad Hβ\beta emission line is <<2000 km s-1, and their [O III] emission is weak compared to the broad Hβ\beta: SS([O III])/SS(Hβ\beta)<<3 (Osterbrock and Pogge, 1985; Goodrich, 1989). A large fraction of them also exhibit strong Fe II emission, confirming the unobstructed view of the central engine. The narrowness of the broad lines can be attributed to the low rotational velocity of the broad-line region (BLR) gas around an intermediate-to-low-mass supermassive black hole (106–10M⊙8{}^{8}M_{\odot}, Peterson, 2011; Komossa et al., 2018). This interpretation is supported by several lines of evidence, such as reverberation mapping studies (Wang et al., 2016; Du et al., 2018), predominantly turbulence-dominated Lorentzian emission line profiles (Kollatschny and Zetzl, 2011; Goad et al., 2012; Sulentic et al., 2000; Marziani et al., 2003; Cracco et al., 2016; Berton et al., 2020a), the detection of tidal disruption events in NLS1s (Blanchard et al., 2017; Katebi, 2020; Frederick et al., 2021), and the prevalence of disk-like host galaxies with pseudo-bulges (Orban de Xivry et al., 2011; Järvelä et al., 2017; Olguín-Iglesias et al., 2020; Varglund et al., 2022; Varglund et al., 2023, e.g.,). On average, NLS1s accrete at very high rates (average L/LEdd∼L/L_{\mathrm{Edd}}\sim 0.3), often exceeding the Eddington limit (Boroson and Green, 1992), as also indicated by their strong Fe II emission in comparison to the broad Hβ\beta (R4570 or RFe​IIR_{\mathrm{Fe\penalty\ II}}), known to correlate with the Eddington ratio (Marziani et al., 2025). These properties suggest that NLS1s are fast-growing AGN in an early evolutionary stage (Mathur, 2000).

The sample of NLS1s showing extreme variability properties was discovered as part of the Metsähovi Radio Observatory (MRO, Finland) AGN monitoring programme at 37 GHz (Lähteenmäki et al., 2017), and later all of them have also been detected at 15 GHz by the Owens Valley Radio Observatory (OVRO, USA) (Berton et al., 2020b; Järvelä et al., 2024). These sources are intriguing because they are often undetectable, but during flares they can reach Jy-level flux densities. NLS1s were found to host relativistic jets in the late 2000’s (Komossa et al., 2006; Yuan et al., 2008; Abdo et al., 2009), so the initial hypothesis was that these sources host such jets. One of them was even identified as a gamma-ray emitter and was observed to brighten in X-rays soon after an MRO-detected flare (Romano et al., 2023), supporting the jet hypothesis. However, subsequent medium- and high-resolution radio observations using the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA) and the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) did not find any hints of jets (Berton et al., 2020b; Järvelä et al., 2021; Järvelä et al., 2024). In VLBA observations at 15 GHz (rms∼60​μ\sim 60\penalty\ \muJy), none of the sources was detected, ruling out high brightness temperature radio cores seen in other jetted NLS1s, and blazars in general. Multifrequency radio data, including JVLA data from LL- to QQ-band, complemented by archival observations down to 144 MHz, revealed that all sources exhibit steep broadband spectra, with several sources undetected at higher frequencies (Järvelä et al., 2024, see Fig. 1 in). Only one source, J122844.81+501751.2 (J1228+5017 hereafter), also the focus of this study, showed a flattening of the spectrum at high frequencies, possibly indicating a flat core or a coronal component. (2024) report blazar-like variability brightness temperatures (TB≈T_{\mathrm{B}}\approx1013-1015 K) and variability Doppler factors (δ≈\delta\approx10-30) for one of these sources, which had enough data to perform these estimates. papers.title: Learning Multi-Phase Robot Loco-Manipulation via Phase-Conditioned Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Complex whole-body loco-manipulation requires executing diverse maneuvers, such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion, within a single long-horizon task. While performing simple pick-and-place behaviors is well-established, scaling to complex, long-horizon tasks remains difficult. Currently, this challenge is addressed by relying on human motion data and correspondingly humanoid platforms, which limits platform independence and introduces substantial data processing overhead. Instead, we extend proximal policy optimization (PPO) to train a single policy for multi-phase tasks across diverse robotic hardware, leveraging prior task structure to shape behavior. Our method adapts PPO using a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated reward functions, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to guide exploration. To support varied hardware, we employ a decoupled hierarchical control architecture that separates lower-level balancing dynamics from high-level phase execution. We demonstrate multi-stage loco-manipulation skills on hardware on both the Unitree G1 and a Boston Dynamics Spot equipped with a manipulator arm, and validate our design choices through ablations. Our approach enables the acquisition of complex loco-manipulation behaviors purely through environment interaction while directly incorporating high-level task structure into policy learning.

Loco-manipulation is an essential capability for deploying mobile robots in real-world environments, where they must navigate, interact with, and reconfigure their surroundings. Although reinforcement learning (RL) methods have been increasingly employed with success in short-horizon pick-and-place tasks [1, 2], they usually struggle in long-horizon settings due to the large exploration space and complex contact mechanics [3, 4].

Loco-manipulation is an essential capability for deploying mobile robots in real-world environments, where they must navigate, interact with, and reconfigure their surroundings. Although reinforcement learning (RL) methods have been increasingly employed with success in short-horizon pick-and-place tasks [1, 2], they usually struggle in long-horizon settings due to the large exploration space and complex contact mechanics [3, 4].

Additionally, complex loco-manipulation tasks, such as lifting and carrying a box, mandate coordinating distinct physical modes (walking, crouching, rising) within a unified policy. This poses a major challenge for standard reward tuning, which might cause training to collapse into unwanted local minima, such as learning to kick or drag a box instead of lifting and carrying it. To bridge this gap, recent work increasingly relies on human motion datasets [5] and demonstrations, driving the widespread adoption of humanoid platforms in research. While effective, this paradigm requires substantial data processing overhead and results in platform-specific methods that fail to generalize to diverse robotic hardware. More recent approaches have successfully solved humanoid loco-manipulation tasks by learning through autonomous environment interaction, without human guidance [6, 7, 8]. However, they only focus on simple table-to-table object transportation, ignoring the distinct physical transitions, such as low crouching and rising, required to pick up or deposit an object directly from the ground.

Crucially, long-horizon tasks are inherently compositional and naturally break down into a sequence of distinct behavioral stages, each demanding specialized local control. For example, a box-lifting policy can be split into approaching, crouching and lifting phases. Exploiting this inherent multi-phase structure provides a promising route to tackle the exploration challenge without demonstration data. While traditional methods often rely on finite state machines to chain independently trained sub-policies sequentially—a strategy previously applied also to humanoid box-lifting [9]—managing transitions across highly dynamic regimes can be problematic. In contrast, consolidating these stages into a single policy natively manages inter-phase transitions and eliminates external orchestration. To this end, we introduce a variant of the popular PPO [10] algorithm that incorporates the sequential nature of the task. A state machine segments the task into manageable behavior windows and masks MDP terms. The actor is forced to internalize task progression by predicting the current phase, and the critic is conditioned on the active phase to better capture local value changes. We evaluate our framework across two distinct platforms and multiple tasks, including a Spot quadruped maneuvering a tire and a Unitree G1 humanoid carrying a box. For the latter, we also resolve several sim-to-real issues to enable stable, prolonged grasping. Finally, through targeted ablations, we validate the impact of our core algorithmic choices.

papers.title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.

Persistent memory lets an agent carry preferences, task state, and factual updates across sessions. A deployed system must therefore solve at least two distinct problems: retrieving the relevant information, and selecting the currently valid version when memory contains both an old fact and a later correction. End-to-end accuracy hides this distinction. The retriever may return the newest fact, yet the language model can still answer with the older one.

Persistent memory lets an agent carry preferences, task state, and factual updates across sessions. A deployed system must therefore solve at least two distinct problems: retrieving the relevant information, and selecting the currently valid version when memory contains both an old fact and a later correction. End-to-end accuracy hides this distinction. The retriever may return the newest fact, yet the language model can still answer with the older one.

We ask the following question: when the correct update is retrieved, how do evidence budget, unrelated distractors, and an older competing fact affect whether an LLM uses it? We study this question using the MemoryAgentBench’s FactConsolidation task (Hu et al., 2026). In this task, numbered statements are chronological and higher numbers replace lower conflicting statements. The facts are synthetic and can therefore contradict ordinary world knowledge. For example, the memory may first state that the author of The Marriage of Figaro is Pierre Beaumarchais and later state that it is Thomas Kyd. Under the benchmark’s chronology, Thomas Kyd is then the correct answer.

Under the benchmark’s chronology, Thomas Kyd is then the correct answer.

We address the question in three parts: RQ1 asks how the evidence budget affects the use of a retrieved update; RQ2 asks whether failures are concentrated on questions for which an obsolete value is also retrieved; and RQ3 asks whether an obsolete competing fact is more harmful than unrelated evidence of the same size.

We extend their pipeline-level finding with a controlled intervention. It isolates evidence composition while holding reader, prompt, latest fact, and four-statement size fixed.

papers.title: Calculation of distant retrograde orbits and their use in space weather forecasting
papers.abstract: There is current renewed interest in using Sun-Earth distant retrograde orbits (DROs) for a space weather forecasting mission, which would temporarily place spacecraft at a position near the Sun-Earth line, but closer to the Sun than the L1 point (such as the ESA HENON mission and ESA SHIELD concept). With in situ observations of the magnetic field on a DRO, the southward ($B_z < 0$) magnetic field of interplanetary coronal mass ejections (ICMEs), which is not routinely accessible remotely, could be measured several hours in advance. This $B_z < 0$ field is a decisive factor for forecasting geomagnetic storm intensity. We present an analysis of DROs at different sub-L1 distances for their efficacy for a space weather forecasting mission. An open-source numerical framework to generate DRO trajectories is presented. Our pre-calculated orbits in Heliocentric Earth Ecliptic coordinates can be introduced into numerical or empirical simulations of the ambient solar wind and ICMEs. We then analyze the corresponding forecast lead times, the resulting observational gaps depending on the number of spacecraft and distance of a DRO, and the "cone of acceptance" of the maximum longitudinal separation of a spacecraft to the Sun-Earth line. We define different domains regarding radial evolution and longitudinal CME structure, and show the historical coverage of sub-L1 ICME observations with our ICMECAT catalog. An optimal mission configuration can be selected based on the characteristics of DROs presented here, depending on the requirements of such a mission deemed acceptable with respect to results on CME evolution and coherence.

papers.intro:
Distant retrograde orbits [14, DROs,] are a family of heliocentric orbits that have recently come into focus for their potential use in space weather forecasting and for multipoint heliospheric solar wind observations. Spacecraft on a Sun–Earth DRO, during the portion of their orbit when they are positioned near the Sun–Earth line upstream of Earth, can measure parameters of a solar coronal mass ejection (CME) in situ, in particular their magnetic field orientation, and transmit the data to Earth in real time. This would allow the magnitude of the resulting geomagnetic storm to be forecast with a much improved lead time compared to data from the Sun–Earth L1 point.

The advantages of DROs are that they are easier to reach than Venus-like heliocentric orbits [40] and that they are stable over long periods [14, 7, 36, 6]. Although in principle it is possible to extend their minimal distance along the Sun–Earth line to quite close to the Sun [14], Venus at about 0.72 au poses a problem in the Solar System as it will perturb the orbits of spacecraft at any given DRO that crosses the distance of Venus’s orbit at some point. However, the closer one places the DRO spacecraft to the Sun, the longer the potential warning lead time for a CME will be, at the cost of the orbit also becoming wider in longitude [14]. This means that there is a trade-off between forecasting lead time and correlation of the observations at the sub-L1 point and near Earth that needs to be studied for the optimal scientific and operational return of a space weather DRO mission.

The understanding of the 3D structure of CMEs and space weather forecasts could be greatly improved if several spacecraft were available at separations of up to 10–20∘ in heliospheric longitude and temporarily closer to the Sun–Earth line. These are known as sub-L1 monitors, and mostly case studies have so far revealed that this concept should be feasible for improved forecasts [21, 43, 17, 18, 24, 46, 10, see]. The reason why sub-L1 monitoring should be possible is that CMEs consist of large-scale magnetic obstacles that propagate away from the Sun [4, 20, 3, 32, 1, e.g.]. While they undergo interactions with other structures and expand during propagation [28, 27, 44, e.g.], the magnetic flux ropes that form the core parts of CMEs tend to be stable enough over time and distance to be first measured somewhere closer to the Sun and later found with sufficient coherence in the near-Earth solar wind [13, e.g.]. Large-scale magnetic flux ropes are thus the key property that make sub-L1 monitoring a viable method for CME forecasting, given the pivotal role of internal magnetic fields in regulating the space weather response at Earth.

A major open question concerns how far away from Earth the sub-L1 monitor can be positioned, radially and longitudinally, to achieve the needed consistency in the observations with those at L1 for reliable space weather forecasts, and how large the gaps can be in between the spacecraft. Recent studies on multipoint CME observation have been made possible since 2020 with the current fleet of spacecraft including Solar Orbiter, Parker Solar Probe, BepiColombo, and STEREO-A in addition to L1 probes [31, 39, 2, 34, e.g.]. Power laws derived from ICME catalogs are highly useful as a general description of the ICME magnetic field and plasma properties evolution and expansion with heliocentric distance [19, 9, 42, 29, e.g.]. Nevertheless, [1] recently summarized the overall picture of CME flux ropes that has emerged from four decades of observations: a highly complex and irregular structure characterized by e.g. a kinked axis, a non-uniform cross-section, mixed open and closed magnetic field lines, and several “bumps and lumps”. This raises the question of how far a sub-L1 monitor can be separated from the Sun–Earth line while still measuring structures that remain coherent with those later observed at L1, particularly given that individual features may be highly localized. [33] provided a theoretical basis for a limit of around 10∘ at 1 au, beyond which information may no longer propagate between two spatially separated observers. Consistent with this, [2] showed that the probability of jointly detecting a CME in situ at two spacecraft decreases below 50% when their longitudinal separation exceeds 15∘. However, when both spacecraft do detect the same CME, the average magnetic field and plasma properties measured at the two locations remain comparable, indicating that a degree of coherence is retained even at these separations.

[35] provided a historical summary of works that have employed serendipitous sub-L1 observations to predict CME magnetic fields and/or plasma quantities at 1 au in a hindcast fashion. The authors also found a potential longitudinal asymmetry, with greater (smaller) gains in lead time when STEREO-A was east (west) of the Sun–Earth line.

papers.title: SpeeDiff: Scalable Pixel-Anchored End-to-End Latent Diffusion Model
papers.abstract: We present Scalable Pixel-anchored End-to-end Diffusion (SpeeDiff), a latent diffusion method that jointly trains the VAE and the diffusion model from scratch. In principle, joint training allows the diffusion loss gradient to directly guide the VAE encoder, encouraging the formation of a generation-friendly latent space and potentially yielding faster convergence than the conventional two-stage approach with a pretrained frozen VAE. However, a naive end-to-end implementation severely degrades performance, as unrestricted backpropagation of the diffusion loss leads to latent space collapse. Our main technical contribution is a simple yet effective Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction (TPR) loss, which provides additional pixel-level feedback by decoding a predicted clean latent from an intermediate noisy state using Tweedie's formula, thereby alleviating collapse. Furthermore, our method enables jointly scaling a fully transformer-based architecture and enhances representation alignment within the end-to-end framework. Our SpeeDiff-XL model achieves over 140x and 61x faster training compared to Vanilla SiT and REPA, respectively, while attaining an FID of 1.50 without guidance on ImageNet 256x256 generation. With a more efficient 32x compressed VAE, our model further reaches an FID of 1.53 without guidance on ImageNet 512x512 generation.

Latent diffusion models (LDMs) [54, 46, 41] have emerged as a dominant paradigm for visual synthesis. These models perform the diffusion process in a compact latent space produced by a visual tokenizer, typically a variational autoencoder (VAE) [28]. In the standard two-stage training pipeline, the visual tokenizer is first trained to encode raw visual data into a compressed latent space, after which a diffusion model is learned to operate within that latent domain while keeping the pretrained visual tokenizer frozen.

Recent advances in LDMs have largely focused on enhancing the VAEs by leveraging vision foundation models (VFMs) [40, 50, 45, 61, 18]. Despite their success, VAEs trained with reconstruction objectives primarily capture low-level pixel statistics, resulting in latent spaces that do not directly associate with sufficient semantic knowledge, posing challenges for the diffusion model to learn efficiently. Motivated by semantically rich representations from self-supervise pretrained VFMs, recent works either incorporate representation alignment to a VFM [58, 33] or directly replace the VAE encoder with a VFM [63, 49, 3, 5]. These approaches have achieved remarkable improvements in training efficiency and generative quality.

These approaches have achieved remarkable improvements in training efficiency and generative quality.

In contrast to improving the visual tokenizer through VFMs, much less attention has been given to enhancing it via end-to-end optimization with direct feedback from the diffusion model training. This idea can in fact be traced back to LSGM [54], where the VAE and diffusion model were jointly trained. However, vanilla end-to-end training was found to degrade overall performance, a phenomenon that has also been revisited in recent studies [33]. We believe that enabling truly end-to-end optimization holds the potential to further push the performance limits of LDMs, yet existing approaches still lack effective mechanisms to support that.
