In this paper, we focus on the core idea of enhancing the VAE through end-to-end direct gradient feedback from diffusion training, and show that allowing the latent space to evolve under generative supervision further improves both training efficiency and synthesis quality. After carefully analyzing the vanilla end-to-end training, we find that the diffusion loss tends to collapse the latent space into a degenerate representation. Specifically, we observe that the latent statistics exhibit severely suppressed per-channel variances and large per-channel biass (see Fig. 3). Extensive experiments show that this additional pixel-level feedback anchors the VAE and prevents latent degeneracy, resulting in robust and well-converged end-to-end training.

papers.title: Three-flavor neutrino Boltzmann transport and flavor instabilities in long-lived neutron-star merger remnants
papers.abstract: Binary neutron-star (BNS) mergers are multimessenger sources whose kilonova emission and nucleosynthesis depend sensitively on neutrino microphysics and flavor conversion. Most BNS merger simulations assume $\mu$-$\tau$ neutrino degeneracy in a two-flavor treatment. We investigate the fast flavor instability (FFI) and the collisional flavor instability (CFI) in long-lived BNS merger remnants using axisymmetric general-relativistic three-flavor Boltzmann neutrino transport with a comprehensive treatment of muons and muonic interactions, following a handoff from 3D grey moment-based simulations. Our simulations largely reproduce the parent 3D simulations, recovering trapped weak equilibrium in the core, muonic non-equilibrium in the semitransparent outer disk due to prolonged demuonization, and cold weak equilibrium in transparent regions. Linear stability analysis reveals strong and widespread CFI in all three flavor sectors, including narrow resonance-like structures. Muonic interactions reshape the FFI distribution, shifting the $e\tau$-sector instability toward denser disk regions compared with the extended FFI outside the disk in the two-flavor model, while disk demuonization produces a strong $\nu_\mu$ excess and one-sided muon-lepton-number angular distributions that suppress FFI in the $e\mu$ and $\mu\tau$ sectors. Local three-flavor quantum kinetic equation (QKE) calculations reveal nonlinear coupling among flavor sectors that excites coherence even in an initially stable sector. Diagonal collisional repopulation is decisive for the nonlinear evolution and asymptotic flavor populations, and neglecting it overestimates flavor equilibration. We establish the necessity of three-flavor transport from both classical and quantum perspectives, and underscore the importance of consistently coupling flavor conversion with diagonal collisional repopulation in future CFI subgrid models.

papers.intro:
Binary neutron-star (BNS) mergers are among the most important multi-messenger sources in the Universe [68, 26, 78], producing signals such as gravitational waves [8, 14, 103], short gamma-ray bursts [105, 107, 62], and kilonovae caused by the production of heavy elements via rr-process nucleosynthesis [52, 58, 79]. The first multi-messenger observation of a BNS merger, GW170817/GRB170817A/AT2017gfo, provided a new avenue for probing and constraining a broad range of physics [2, 122, 29]. BNS mergers involve physics across widely separated scales, thus requiring numerical-relativity simulations for quantitative modeling (see, e.g., the reviews in Refs. [8, 112]).

Binary neutron-star (BNS) mergers are among the most important multi-messenger sources in the Universe [68, 26, 78], producing signals such as gravitational waves [8, 14, 103], short gamma-ray bursts [105, 107, 62], and kilonovae caused by the production of heavy elements via rr-process nucleosynthesis [52, 58, 79]. The first multi-messenger observation of a BNS merger, GW170817/GRB170817A/AT2017gfo, provided a new avenue for probing and constraining a broad range of physics [2, 122, 29]. BNS mergers involve physics across widely separated scales, thus requiring numerical-relativity simulations for quantitative modeling (see, e.g., the reviews in Refs. [8, 112]).

Among the major uncertainties in BNS merger modeling, neutrinos play one of the most important roles. Neutrinos carry away thermal energy and lepton number from the hot remnant and disk, and they also regulate cooling and heating. Neutrino microphysics plays a decisive role in determining the electron fraction of the disk and ejecta, largely affecting rr-process nucleosynthesis, lanthanide production, and electromagnetic counterparts, particularly kilonova light curves [36, 137, 121, 100]. Modeling these effects requires solving neutrino transport together with the hydrodynamics and a large set of sophisticated weak interactions. Considerable progress has been made in recent years using moment-based, Monte Carlo, lattice-Boltzmann, and Boltzmann-transport methods, together with increasingly complete neutrino microphysics [101, 82, 118, 128, 102, 36, 21, 85, 61, 93, 6, 35, 104]. Nevertheless, these approaches describe neutrino transport only within a classical picture.

A crucial missing piece of neutrino physics is the quantum-kinetic behavior of neutrinos, in particular their quantum flavor coherence. In addition to vacuum oscillations, neutrino–neutrino self-interactions and collisions in a dense neutrino gas can trigger collective flavor instabilities. Depending on the flavor and momentum distributions of neutrinos and the collisional environment, the quantum kinetic equations (QKEs) can have flavor instabilities in which small flavor coherence grows exponentially, initiating these flavor conversion processes [97, 113, 24, 106, 120].

In addition to vacuum oscillations, neutrino–neutrino self-interactions and collisions in a dense neutrino gas can trigger collective flavor instabilities. Depending on the flavor and momentum distributions of neutrinos and the collisional environment, the quantum kinetic equations (QKEs) can have flavor instabilities in which small flavor coherence grows exponentially, initiating these flavor conversion processes [97, 113, 24, 106, 120].

This self-coupled quantum evolution can give rise to several classes of flavor instabilities, including fast flavor instability (FFI) driven by neutrino self-interactions as a refractive effect [134, 25, 31, 32, 125, 54, 133, 135, 81], collisional flavor instability (CFI) arising from the interplay between self-interactions and collisions [56, 55, 70, 132, 59, 73, 119], many-body effects [64, 67], and slower flavor modes involving the vacuum scale [9, 95]. These phenomena can operate on extremely small length and time scales, far shorter than those of the global astrophysical system, making their self-consistent coupling to neutrino radiation hydrodynamics computationally prohibitive [109, 18, 1, 106, 86].

These phenomena can operate on extremely small length and time scales, far shorter than those of the global astrophysical system, making their self-consistent coupling to neutrino radiation hydrodynamics computationally prohibitive [109, 18, 1, 106, 86].

BNS mergers are favorable environments for the flavor conversion processes because of the high neutrino number densities, complex geometries, anisotropic radiation fields, and extended semitransparent disks. As resolving the quantum-kinetic scales in a global BNS simulation remains prohibitively expensive, different studies have employed local QKE calculations [106, 44, 124], applied linear stability analysis (LSA) [129, 40, 38, 63, 37], or incorporated approximate flavor-conversion treatments [69, 57, 30, 99, 100, 77], showing significant impacts on the dynamics, composition, nucleosynthesis, and neutrino signatures. However, one important ingredient remains unexplored: the muon degree of freedom. Most of these studies employ two-flavor calculations, assuming only neutrons, protons, and electrons in matter, i.e., n​p​enpe-matter, where muon- and tau-flavor (anti)neutrinos participate in identical weak interactions. Although some works [111, 124] have considered three-flavor QKE calculations, they have not consistently incorporated muons and muonic interactions in the matter background. Recent studies have shown in either core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) or BNS simulations that matter with sufficiently high temperature and density contains an appreciable fraction of muons owing to their charged-current reactions from the large reservoir of νμ\nu_{\mu} and ν¯μ\bar{\nu}_{\mu} generated by pair processes [10, 33, 42, 91, 96, 41] (see also related works [76, 49]). In this work, we investigate three-flavor neutrino flavor instabilities in long-lived BNS merger remnants using general-relativistic Boltzmann neutrino transport with three flavors, following a handoff from 3D merger simulations employing a grey moment-based transport scheme. The paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we introduce the framework of QKEs, the LSA for FFI and CFI, and the classical Boltzmann transport and weak-interaction physics. In Sec. III, we describe the numerical methods and setup, including the handoff procedure, the treatment of muonic interactions, and the implicit coupling between neutrino radiation and matter composition. In Sec. IV, we present the global simulation results and compare the occurrence and properties of FFI and CFI between two- and three-flavor treatments, highlighting the widespread CFI in all three flavor sectors and the substantial changes in FFI morphology induced by muonic interactions. In Sec. V, we perform local, isotropic, multi-energy three-flavor QKE calculations to investigate the nonlinear evolution of CFI, focusing on the coupling among flavor sectors and comparing the effects of including or omitting diagonal collision terms on the flavor evolution, asymptotic states, and relaxation timescales. We find that a full collision operator in QKE calculations is necessary to achieve the accurate asymptotic states. Finally, in Sec. VI, we summarize our findings and conclusions.

papers.title: ASKAP Discovery of a Giant Odd Radio Circle at $z=0.15$
papers.abstract: Odd radio circles (ORCs) are a recently recognized class of faint, roughly circular diffuse radio sources, typically a few hundred kiloparsecs across, whose origin is still debated. We report the serendipitous discovery of a giant ORC, ORC~J1928$-$5056, in 856~MHz continuum data from the ASKAP observations. The emission forms a single, mildly elliptical structure $4^{\prime}$ across, corresponding to $0.63$~Mpc at the redshift $z=0.1507$ of the central galaxy LEDA~140850, the brightest cluster galaxy of Abell~3639, which makes it one of the largest single ORCs known. After subtracting the radio nucleus associated with the host galaxy, the ORC has a flux density of 73~mJy integrated within an area of $\sim 12$~arcmin$^2$, i.e.\ a mean surface brightness of only $1.7$~$\mu$Jy~arcsec$^{-2}$, and a rest-frame luminosity of $L_{1.4}=2\times10^{24}$~W~Hz$^{-1}$, comparable to those of the most luminous ORCs. Including its nucleus, the system reaches $L_{1.4}=6.6\times10^{24}$~W~Hz$^{-1}$, higher than that of any other ORC reported so far. The host is a massive ($M_{\ast}\sim10^{11}\,M_{\odot}$), passive elliptical galaxy with negligible star formation. It contains an AGN jet with a power-law spectrum of index $\alpha=-0.877\pm0.089$ between 856 and 1656~MHz. Finally, we discuss the implications for ORC formation models and the observations needed to establish the nature of this system.

papers.intro:
Odd radio circles (ORCs) are faint, roughly circular patches of diffuse radio emission discovered serendipitously in continuum images from the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) pilot survey [41]; two further examples were identified, in archival Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope data [41] and in ASKAP imaging [31]. The sample has since grown thanks to deep MeerKAT observations [42, e.g.] and searches of the EMU data, both automated and visual [20, 16, 50, e.g.]. Related shell systems have been identified around interacting early-type galaxies and in merging groups [8, 32, 30, 33]; similar rings have been reported at other radio frequencies [34, 22]. Most confirmed ORCs are hosted by massive elliptical galaxies and span ∼\sim100–500 kpc, with integrated flux densities of only a few mJy at GHz frequencies [40, 45]; their edges are usually brighter than their interiors.

The physical origin of ORCs remains unknown. Proposed mechanisms include spherical blast waves powered by cataclysmic events such as supernova or tidal disruption event in the host galaxy [43, 44], termination shocks of powerful starburst winds [36, 9, 18], AGN jet-inflated bubbles viewed in projection [35], faded radio-galaxy lobes re-energized by a passing shock (“phoenixes”; 47), virial shocks around massive halos [54], and merger-driven shocks in galaxy groups and clusters [13, 26, 8]. Distinguishing among these scenarios requires accurate sizes, luminosities, spectra, polarization properties, and host-galaxy properties.

papers.title: SetGRPO: Calibrating Grader-Induced Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning uses fine-grained grader feedback to train large language models on open-ended tasks, but grader randomness can alter GRPO updates in ways that score discrepancies alone cannot characterize. Because GRPO jointly normalizes rewards within each response group and combines the resulting training coefficients with response-level gradients, a scoring discrepancy can shift the coefficients of the entire group and induce policy-dependent update changes. Selective execution further affects the direction-reversal risk of retained updates. To address this, we propose Set-Valued Group Relative Policy Optimization (SetGRPO). It comprises three modules: (a) Joint Reward Set Calibration constructs a joint uncertainty set for the training coefficients; (b) Geometry-Guided Safe Recovery maps candidate coefficients into the current policy's local update geometry and determines the largest safe recovery ratio for each response group; and (c) Selective Risk-Gated Optimization selects a global threshold through independent risk calibration to control the conditional direction-reversal risk of accepted updates while preserving the original GRPO objective. Under exchangeability, SetGRPO provides finite-sample marginal coverage for the joint coefficient set and simultaneous risk control across candidate thresholds. On ten open-ended benchmarks spanning three domains, SetGRPO achieves the highest macro average among all compared training methods on both Qwen3.5 and Llama3.2 model families.

Nowadays, Rubric-based Reinforcement Learning (Rubric-based RL) has emerged as an important training paradigm for improving the performance of large language models on open-ended generation tasks (Li et al., 2026a; Zhou et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024). It uses fine-grained rubrics and LLM judges to evaluate open-ended responses across dimensions such as relevance, completeness, factuality, and style (Li et al., 2026a; Zhou et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023). These dimension-level scores are aggregated into response-level rewards that serve as training signals for reinforcement learning (Ouyang et al., 2022; Stiennon et al., 2020), thereby accommodating grader’s score discrepancies during training and enabling optimization of open-ended generation tasks. Related work has also explored multimodal fusion, video-language adaptation, and parameter-efficient training for large models (Li et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b).

Recent reinforcement-learning studies have also explored how to improve the utility of sampled trajectories through reflection, trajectory reuse, and rollout transformation (Bi et al., 2026a; Bi et al., 2026b). Other work examines selection and self-evaluation mechanisms in multimodal or embodied settings (Aniri et al., 2026a; Bi et al., 2025a; Bi et al., 2025b). Specifically, for a given response group, GRPO derives the training coefficients from the shared mean and scale of the group rewards and combines them with the response-level gradients of each response under the current policy to form a local policy update. We therefore conjecture that a change in a single reward alters multiple training coefficients within the group through the shared statistics, and that different policy snapshots induce different update outcomes.

To verify this conjecture, we score fixed response groups twice with the same grader and compare the two scoring results pairwise (detailed in Section 3). As shown in Figure 1(a), we first compare score discrepancies with the coefficient residuals obtained after within-group normalization, testing whether shared statistics propagate score discrepancies to the entire group of coefficients. As shown in Figure 1(b), we further compare the local updates of the same response group under different policy snapshots, testing whether the effect of coefficient discrepancies depends on the gradient geometry of the current policy. The results show that shared normalization propagates score discrepancies to multiple coefficients within a group, whereas similar coefficient shifts can induce different update directions under different policy geometries, thereby changing which groups are retained by selective execution. These findings support our conjecture and motivate the following question: how can we characterize the effect of the training coefficients used by the optimizer on the current policy update while preserving effective training progress and avoiding directional deviation?

papers.title: Advancing global crop simulations with differentiable modelling
papers.abstract: Global gridded crop models (GGCMs) are crucial for assessing the performance of food producing systems, for example under climate change or their contribution to environmental challenges. However, systematic calibration of their parameters remains a long-standing challenge. Persisting uncertainties in these parameters propagate into future crop projections, thereby affecting and potentially biasing food security assessments. Here we present a fully process-based differentiable GGCM implementation that offers a fundamentally new approach to parameter calibration, uncertainty quantification, yield loss attribution, and management optimization. Using automatic differentiation, we optimize selected model parameters against site-scale carbon and water flux observations, reducing normalized root-mean-square errors at held-out sites by 24.8-36.2% compared to the default state-of-the-art model. Without calibration against yield data, the optimized model better captures detrended yield anomalies across 61.2-64.3% of global crop area and reduces low-yield errors by 3.4-43.5% for wheat, rice, maize and soybean. It also ranks among the best performers in comparison with GGCMI Phase 3 models. Future simulations show that calibration reduces the projected end-of-century rice production increase from 55.1% to 22.1% under SSP5-8.5. Parameter ensembles further reveal that parameterizations with comparable historical skill can produce markedly different future production responses. Beyond calibration, differentiability enables the attribution of crop losses under extreme events and supports the design of adaptive crop management strategies. For the 2018 European drought, we identify spring heat and water limitation as major contributors to wheat yield losses and develop more effective irrigation strategies for mitigating simulated regional yield losses.

papers.intro:
Climate change increasingly threatens global food production, with impacts varying among crops and regions Jägermeyr et al. (2021); Hultgren et al. (2025); Heikonen et al. (2025); Yang et al. (2025). Global gridded crop models (GGCMs) are central to assessing these risks, as they simulate the effects of climate and management on crop growth and yield Jones et al. (2003); Bondeau et al. (2007); Von Bloh et al. (2018); Enders et al. (2023); Mialyk et al. (2024). However, projected climate responses differ widely among models owing to uncertainty in process representation and parameterization Müller et al. (2017); Folberth et al. (2019); Franke et al. (2020); Müller et al. (2021); Wang et al. (2024); Li et al. (2025). GGCMs also often underestimate low-yield risks and the magnitude of losses during climatic extremes Kornhuber et al. (2023); Auer et al. (2026). Together, these limitations reduce confidence in assessments of crop production risks and adaptation benefits under climate change. Improving the reliability of crop projections therefore requires progress in calibrating process-based crop models, quantifying parameter uncertainty and better diagnosing yield losses from climate extremes.

Process-based GGCMs link climate to crop growth and yield through coupled physiological and soil processes. The magnitude and timing of simulated responses to temperature, water, radiation and nutrient availability depend on many process parameters Folberth et al. (2019). Poorly constrained parameter values can bias simulated yield responses, making calibration against observations essential for reliable projections. Yet systematic calibration remains a long-standing challenge for GGCMs Maiorano et al. (2017); Xiong et al. (2016); Wallach et al. (2025). Current approaches rely on expert judgement, iterative trial and error and repeated forward searches, which become increasingly impractical as the number of parameters grows Seidel et al. (2018); Gawinowski et al. (2025); Machado et al. (2026). Moreover, these efforts typically target end-of-season yield rather than sub-seasonal processes, thereby leaving the underlying crop dynamics weakly constrained despite the increasing availability of growing-season carbon and water flux observations He et al. (2017); Seidel et al. (2018); Pastorello et al. (2020).

Quantifying parameter uncertainty poses another major challenge Wang et al. (2024). Multiple parameterizations perform comparably against historical observations but may diverge under future climate Xiong et al. (2016); He et al. (2017). Global crop projections from multi-model ensembles often use a single parameter set for each model, although parameter uncertainty within individual models can be substantial Folberth et al. (2019); Wallach et al. (2025). Constructing and evaluating parameter ensembles at the global scale is difficult because each ensemble member requires separate calibration. Given the projected increases in frequency and intensity of extreme events in a changing climate IPCC (2023), identifying the extreme weather drivers of yield losses is crucial for understanding crop vulnerability and informing adaptation. Existing GGCM sensitivity analyses rely on large ensembles of forward simulations, an approach that is both computationally intensive and restricted to predefined weather variables and perturbation ranges Franke et al. (2020). GGCM emulators reduce computational cost but are less reliable outside their training ranges. Emulators trained on growing-season means do not resolve the sub-seasonal weather conditions or within-season timing of extreme events Franke et al. (2020).

(2023); Shen et al. (2023), and has recently been applied in land surface and atmospheric modelling Fang et al. (2026); Kochkov et al. (2024). Its core tool, automatic differentiation (AD), computes the local sensitivities of model outputs or optimization objectives to parameters and inputs Baydin et al. (2018). In reverse mode, a single backward pass yields gradients of the objective with respect to all selected parameters or inputs. Finite-difference methods instead require repeated forward simulations with slightly perturbed parameter values or inputs. Conventional GGCM implementations are not designed to propagate gradients through their complete seasonal simulations. An early proof-of-concept study applied AD to crop model sensitivity analysis Lauvernet et al. (2012). A recent hybrid GGCM used this approach to train embedded neural network components rather than optimize physical process parameters Lin et al. (2025). (2024) (Agrocosm), capable of quantifying the sensitivity of crop growth, soil dynamics and end-of-season yield to process parameters and daily weather inputs.

An early proof-of-concept study applied AD to crop model sensitivity analysis Lauvernet et al. (2012). A recent hybrid GGCM used this approach to train embedded neural network components rather than optimize physical process parameters Lin et al. (2025). To our knowledge, this gradient-based parameter optimization has not previously been demonstrated in a fully process-based GGCM. Here we present a differentiable implementation of the crop and soil formulations of LPJmL Bondeau et al. (2007); Schaphoff et al. (2018); Von Bloh et al. (2018); Lutz et al. (2019); Wirth et al. (2024) (Agrocosm), capable of quantifying the sensitivity of crop growth, soil dynamics and end-of-season yield to process parameters and daily weather inputs.

We use Agrocosm to demonstrate the advances enabled by differentiability in a fully process-based GGCM. We integrate process observations into GGCM calibration using AD to optimize model parameters against site-scale carbon and water fluxes. The resulting parameterizations generalize to held-out sites and strongly improve global simulations of historical yield variability for wheat, rice, maize and soybean, despite being calibrated without yield data. Future simulations under two emission scenarios show how parameter optimization alters projected production responses and yield sensitivities to CO2 and temperature, while revealing substantial projection uncertainty across crops and regions. For rice under SSP5–8.5, parameter uncertainty accounts for about twice as much end-of-century projection variance as climate model uncertainty. We further use derivatives of end-of-season yield with respect to daily weather inputs to identify spring heat and water limitation as contributors to the 2018 European wheat yield loss. We also demonstrate how AD enables more effective irrigation strategies to improve regional yield recovery for the same event. Together, these analyses highlight how differentiability expands the capabilities of fully process-based GGCMs for assessing climate risks to crop production.

papers.title: MVRCap: Towards Comprehensive Video Captioning via Hierarchical Multi-Dimensional Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Despite significant progress, current models struggle to generate comprehensive video captions, constrained primarily by coarse-grained supervision, which often fails to capture spatial-temporal dynamics and the underlying logical intent. To address this issue, we introduce MVRCap, a novel framework that reformulates video captioning as a reinforcement learning task steered by structured verification. Central to our approach is a Fine-Grained Verifiable Reward mechanism, serving as dense supervision to enforce rigorous visual-semantic alignment. Specifically, we construct this reward system anchored by three complementary pillars: a Hierarchical Concept Coverage Reward utilizing our newly constructed MVRCap-QA dataset to ensure multi-dimensional completeness and semantic depth, a Factuality Verification Reward to enhance factual consistency, and a Conciseness Constraint to maximize semantic density. Furthermore, we curate the high-quality MVRCap-SFT dataset, providing structured annotations across six key dimensions, to serve as a robust foundational initialization for the RL policy in this training pipeline. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MVRCap achieves state-of-the-art performance on authoritative benchmarks including VDC, CAPability, and VC4VG.

papers.title: When Black-Box Robot Policies Fail: Online Sensor Diagnosis and Repair with a Transparent Surrogate
papers.abstract: Robot foundation models may generalize across tasks and embodiments, but their actions still depend on sensors that can fail. When the policy is frozen or inaccessible, can an external monitor diagnose and repair corrupted inputs without access to its internals? We test a structured surrogate that separates periodic gait from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair around a frozen locomotion policy. On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis raises walking success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reaches 382/640, with no triggers in 64 held-out fault-free episodes. A matched boosted-tree surrogate predicts clean actions similarly well but yields no detected repair improvement over no repair. Separate fits improve walking on Go1 and ANYmal C, although phase-aware gradients perform better. Evidence remains limited to one policy and a partly screened simulated fault suite; robot foundation model and hardware validation remain open.

papers.title: A microscopic analysis of shear acceleration in the relativistic regime
papers.abstract: Relativistic shear flows, as encountered in jets of powerful astrophysical sources, offer promising sites of particle acceleration up to the highest energies. This stochastic acceleration process is usually described with Fokker-Planck transport equations, which assume small momentum gains per scattering. The present paper introduces a covariant microscopic description of relativistic shear acceleration, building on the formalism of generalized Fermi acceleration and formulating angular scattering in the locally comoving frame in terms of stochastic differential equations. This allows us to model relativistic shear profiles and to study the transition from gradual to non-gradual shear acceleration, where the particle mean free path becomes comparable to the shear length scale. Assuming an infinite shear layer, linear in the flow four-velocity, we observe that the shear rate peaks where the flow is mildly relativistic, whereas Lorentz aberration suppresses the transverse velocity of particles where the flow is relativistic. Consequently, particles that leave the central layer experience long waiting times with a heavy-tailed, power-law distribution. The momentum evolution becomes subdiffusive and the acceleration time can substantially exceed local estimates. We successfully reproduce the Monte Carlo energy distributions using a two-state continuous-time random walk with L\'evy-distributed waiting times. We also show how a momentum-dependent mean-free path can introduce breaks in the spectrum and extend our discussion to finite jet profiles. These effects should be accounted for in models of relativistic jets as sources of high-energy particles.

By tracking the particle momentum in the comoving frame at all times, this formalism provides a direct microscopic description of Fermi-type particle acceleration in structured or random velocity flows. papers.title: TrawMem: Reframing Agent Memory as Task-Oriented Role-Adaptive Workspaces
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on memory systems to leverage long-term interactions, yet existing systems typically retrieve memories based on their relevance to the current query and use them as contextual evidence. However, relevance alone does not characterize how a memory contributes to task solving: the same memory may serve different roles across tasks, such as directly supporting the answer or linking to complementary memories with weaker semantic relevance but necessary information. We therefore reframe agent memory systems as Task-Oriented Role-Adaptive Workspaces, where memories are selected and organized by their task-oriented roles and relations. Based on this view, we propose TrawMem, which organizes interaction histories into local threads and constructs task-oriented workspaces by assigning roles and jointly selecting complementary memories. Experiments on LoCoMo and MemGallery with four open- and closed-source backbones show consistent improvements over representative memory systems, with macro-F1 gains of 2.23-3.14 points. On LoCoMo, TrawMem improves the LLM-Judge score over SimpleMem by 4.07 and 4.31 percentage points on Qwen3.5-9B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, respectively, while requiring approximately 12.8% and 5.1% fewer context tokens, respectively.

In recent years, agents have been widely applied to long-horizon multi-turn dialogue, personalized assistants, and continuous task (Packer et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2025). These tasks require agent systems to maintain conversational memory across evolving interactions to understand user needs and complete subsequent tasks. However, growing interaction histories make limited context windows a key bottleneck for long-horizon tasks (Packer et al., 2023). Although larger context windows (Chen et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2024) can accommodate more history, information in less salient positions remains prone to being overlooked (Liu et al., 2024). Reprocessing full history for each query also incurs substantial inference overhead (Fang et al., 2026).

In recent years, agents have been widely applied to long-horizon multi-turn dialogue, personalized assistants, and continuous task (Packer et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2025). These tasks require agent systems to maintain conversational memory across evolving interactions to understand user needs and complete subsequent tasks. However, growing interaction histories make limited context windows a key bottleneck for long-horizon tasks (Packer et al., 2023). Although larger context windows (Chen et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Ding et al., 2024) can accommodate more history, information in less salient positions remains prone to being overlooked (Liu et al., 2024). Reprocessing full history for each query also incurs substantial inference overhead (Fang et al., 2026).

Agent memory systems have therefore emerged to store information outside the current context and retrieve relevant memories for new queries, mitigating information loss from growing interaction histories. Existing work (Du et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a) advances memory construction, maintenance, and retrieval. For example, Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) integrates long-term memory (LTM), A-MEM (Xu et al., 2026a) organizes related information through memory links, while LightMem (Fang et al., 2026) and SimpleMem (Liu et al., 2026) improve efficiency through offline memory maintenance, and memory compression with dynamic retrieval planning, respectively. Despite these advances, existing agent memory systems typically select memories by their direct relevance to the query and use them as context for task solving. This focuses on whether a memory is relevant to the task, while overlooking the role it plays in solving it.

For example, Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) integrates long-term memory (LTM), A-MEM (Xu et al., 2026a) organizes related information through memory links, while LightMem (Fang et al., 2026) and SimpleMem (Liu et al., 2026) improve efficiency through offline memory maintenance, and memory compression with dynamic retrieval planning, respectively. Despite these advances, existing agent memory systems typically select memories by their direct relevance to the query and use them as context for task solving. This focuses on whether a memory is relevant to the task, while overlooking the role it plays in solving it.

Indeed, a memory’s importance depends not only on its semantic relevance but also on its task-oriented role. As shown in Fig. 1(a), memory unit A is highly relevant to both Task A and Task B, but serves different roles. For Task A, it directly supports the answer; for Task B, it primarily connects to other memories, such as unit B. By recognizing this role, we can identify complementary memories such as B, whose semantic relevance to Task B may be weaker and thus be overlooked by existing methods. This motivates identifying the roles of memories for a given task and organize memories that jointly support task solving. Rather than viewing memory as a collection of records awaiting retrieval, we therefore reframe it as a workspace temporarily formed for the current task, where the system can construct effective combinations of information according to distinct roles and relations of memories in the current task.

papers.title: Local Metrics for Exact Streaming on Curvilinear Lattices: A Curvilinear D3Q27 Cumulant Lattice-Boltzmann Method
papers.abstract:
A three-dimensional curvilinear lattice-Boltzmann method is introduced for simulations on smoothly deformed grids while retaining exact one-to-one streaming on a uniform computational lattice. The coordinate transformation is represented locally through a metric-Gaussian equilibrium and a Christoffel-connection source in moment space. A dynamically reconstructed homogeneous-state perturbation streaming procedure preserves homogeneous physical states on warped meshes without interpolation in the advection step. The method is implemented on a D3Q27 lattice with a cumulant collision operator, while the geometric construction remains compatible with other local collision models.
  The formulation is assessed using two sets of tests. First, static non-orthogonal warped-cube cases validate the bulk curvilinear solver through a convected helical shear wave, the Taylor--Green vortex, and Arnold--Beltrami--Childress flow. These tests verify viscous decay, clean freestream preservation, vortex-breakdown dynamics, and the nonlinear inertial--pressure balance induced by geometric acceleration. Second, wall-bounded and moving-boundary demonstrations assess the boundary-compatible extension through warped plane Poiseuille flow, arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian (ALE) peristaltic pumping, and a two-way fluid--structure interaction (FSI) case with added-mass frequency shift. The results show that the proposed curvilinear LBM avoids interpolation-based transport, reduces geometry-locked numerical modes, preserves global mass and momentum to round-off accuracy in the tested warped periodic cases, and extends to wall-bounded ALE/FSI configurations with conservative treatment of mass and physically consistent momentum exchange.

papers.intro:
The lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) advances discrete populations through local collision and exact streaming along lattice links. This structure is attractive for parallel computation and avoids a separate spatial discretization of the transport step [1]. Its application to curved domains remains less direct because a smooth physical geometry is generally not aligned with a Cartesian lattice. Common treatments include interpolated bounce-back rules, immersed-boundary methods, cut-cell corrections, and local grid refinement [2, 3, 4]. These methods are effective in many settings, but they introduce additional reconstruction operations near the physical boundary.

Several extensions relax the restriction to a uniform Cartesian mesh. Finite-difference formulations in generalized coordinates discretize the discrete-velocity transport equation on body-fitted grids [5]. Adaptive and multi-resolution methods introduce refinement and grid-coupling operations [6, 7], while mesh-less formulations use irregular point distributions [8]. In these approaches, geometric flexibility is obtained by modifying the transport discretization. An alternative objective is to retain exact one-to-one streaming on a uniform computational lattice while representing a smooth deformation of the physical domain.

The same Riemannian framework was also used to study transport in intrinsically curved media [10]. These works established that metric and connection terms can be incorporated directly at the kinetic level.

The volumetric curvilinear formulation of Chen provides another important basis for retaining the on-lattice structure in curvilinear coordinates [11]. Relative to earlier curved-space kinetic formulations, this approach emphasizes a volumetric representation of the populations: the physical mesh is represented through a curvilinear mapping, whereas streaming is performed on a uniform computational lattice. Cell-volume-weighted populations preserve the conservative form of the update, and the variation of the local basis is represented through a geometric source term. In this sense, Chen’s formulation moves curvilinear LBM toward an exactly conservative one-to-one advection structure on the computational lattice. Chekhlov et al. subsequently examined this formulation using analytically solvable two-dimensional flows [12]. Their results showed that the practical implementation depends on the isotropy of the velocity stencil, the evaluation of geometric quantities, and the treatment of the source term.

papers.title: Residual dynamics determine dissipation in strongly coupled linear Langevin systems
papers.abstract: Interactions shape the properties of many physical and biological nonequilibrium systems, but whether collective operation raises or lowers entropy production remains difficult to predict. Here, we show that strong coupling suppresses irreversible circulation associated with the directly coupled degrees of freedom. In identical two-dimensional systems, this suppression is monotonic for nonzero coupling modes and guarantees a monotonic decrease of the entropy production rate (EPR), with the corresponding probability currents vanishing in the strong-coupling limit. In higher dimensions, suppressing the circulation associated with the coupled degrees of freedom does not generally eliminate all irreversible circulation, since the remaining degrees of freedom can still sustain nonequilibrium currents. The EPR of these residual dynamics sets the strong-coupling limit, providing a criterion for whether a given choice of coupled variables leads to lower dissipation than the uncoupled system. The approach to this limit depends on how the finite-coupling current correction aligns with the residual current. Further, we show that convergence to residual dynamics in the strong-coupling limit also applies to coupled non-identical systems. Finally, we demonstrate the predicted EPR reduction in nonlinear models of vertebrate hair-cell bundles and bacterial chemotaxis.

Biological systems continually dissipate energy to sustain their functions [62, 59, 50, 13]. Many operate collectively and far from equilibrium with high functional efficiency [35, 85, 72, 77]. Across scales, a recurring theme is that collective organization can shape the energetics [41, 72, 8, 87, 44, 77]. This raises a general question: when can coupling reduce the thermodynamic cost of nonequilibrium operation, and by what mechanism?

Biological systems continually dissipate energy to sustain their functions [62, 59, 50, 13]. Many operate collectively and far from equilibrium with high functional efficiency [35, 85, 72, 77]. Across scales, a recurring theme is that collective organization can shape the energetics [41, 72, 8, 87, 44, 77]. This raises a general question: when can coupling reduce the thermodynamic cost of nonequilibrium operation, and by what mechanism?

A natural measure of this cost is the steady-state entropy production rate (EPR) [73, 63, 68]. Beyond its foundational role in nonequilibrium thermodynamics [25, 20, 68, 40, 12, 11], the EPR also constrains information processing, control and adaptation in stochastic systems [75, 4, 36, 38, 60, 86, 58, 46, 67]. Understanding how coupling changes the EPR is therefore central to both interpreting biological efficacy and designing low-dissipation synthetic and engineered networks.

Recent work has increasingly addressed how interactions reshape dissipation in collective nonequilibrium systems. In interacting oscillator systems, approaches from stochastic thermodynamics have connected synchronization and collective dynamics to thermodynamic performance and energetic costs [52, 37, 39, 48, 8]. Cooperative effects have also been studied extensively in molecular-motor systems, where interactions between motors can modify collective force generation, transport, and energetic efficiency [41, 42, 77, 43]. For example, interactions between kinesin motors have been shown to enhance their efficiency at maximum power relative to the single-motor case [30]. In chemosensory systems, cooperative interactions have been shown to influence sensing accuracy, sensitivity, and energetic dissipation [44, 33]. Additionally, hydrodynamic coupling has been shown to alter irreversibility in mesoscopic systems [14]. Together, these studies demonstrate that interactions can modify nonequilibrium dissipation across a broad range of systems. However, existing results are often model-specific and can depend sensitively on the coupling architecture or driving protocol [30, 44, 43].

In general, the dynamics of linear Langevin systems are described by Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) processes [80, 83], whose steady-state statistics and stochastic thermodynamics are well established when the dynamics are stable [47, 29, 17]. Recent work has continued to uncover nontrivial connections between entropy production, oscillatory dynamics, spectral properties, and nonnormality [70, 24, 57]. Yet even within this seemingly simple and ubiquitous class, several fundamental questions remain open.

Recent work has continued to uncover nontrivial connections between entropy production, oscillatory dynamics, spectral properties, and nonnormality [70, 24, 57]. Yet even within this seemingly simple and ubiquitous class, several fundamental questions remain open.

One such question concerns the conditions under which coupling between these systems suppresses or enhances dissipation. In particular, it is not immediately clear how coupling reorganizes irreversible probability currents and how these changes affect the EPR. The strong-coupling regime offers a useful setting in which to investigate these questions. At sufficiently large coupling strengths, the relaxation rates of the directly coupled degrees of freedom (DoF) can effectively increase, leading to a separation of timescales between the coupled and uncoupled variables. This separation provides a way to examine how coupling affects the irreversible circulation associated with each set of variables and, consequently, their respective contributions to the EPR of the full system.

In this article, we study linear Langevin subsystems coupled through reciprocal linear interactions. We show that strong coupling suppresses irreversible circulation associated with the directly coupled DoF. In two dimensions, this suppression is monotonic for nonzero coupling modes and guarantees a monotonic decrease of the corresponding EPR contributions, while their probability currents vanish in the strong-coupling limit. In higher dimensions, however, the remaining DoF can sustain residual irreversible circulation. The EPR associated with these residual dynamics determines the strong-coupling limit, thereby providing a criterion for whether a strongly coupled system dissipates less than the corresponding uncoupled system. The approach to this limit depends in part on the alignment between the residual irreversible current and the leading finite-coupling correction induced by the coupled DoF. This picture naturally extends to non-identical subsystems, where parameter heterogeneity modifies the residual dynamics and can alter the limiting EPR. We use nonlinear models of bacterial chemotaxis and vertebrate hair-cell bundles to further illustrate this mechanism beyond the linear setting.

papers.title: GraftRay: Physically Based Mesh Insertion into Gaussian Splatting Scenes via Path Tracing
papers.abstract: Inserting virtual objects into scenes reconstructed via 2D or 3D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS/3DGS) is a key capability for content creation, AR, and synthetic data generation. However, realistic insertion requires the object to be seamlessly lit by the scene and, conversely, to cast physically plausible shadows onto it. Existing approaches either harmonize appearance in image space, sacrificing multi-view consistency, or approximate scene illumination with an environment map at the insertion point, which cannot represent near-field area lights such as windows and lamps that dominate indoor lighting. To address this, we present GraftRay, a unified method for physically consistent insertion of mesh objects into indoor scenes represented by either 2D or 3D Gaussians. We recover scene materials and surface normals with diffusion-based priors, and explicitly model spatially-extended emitters, solving their radiance in closed form. A hybrid renderer then jointly path-traces the scene Gaussians and inserted meshes, producing view-consistent shading, interreflections, and soft shadows. On FIPT, GraftRay sets a new state of the art, outperforming recent baselines such as ComGS and EAG-PT in rendering fidelity and shadow accuracy, while maintaining highly competitive rendering efficiency.

papers.intro:
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [21] and its 2D counterpart [15] enable high-quality, real-time rendering of reconstructed scenes. However, inserting a virtual object into such scenes remains challenging. Beyond matching its appearance to the background, the inserted object must respond to the scene’s illumination, cast geometrically consistent shadows, and contribute indirect light to surrounding surfaces. Achieving these effects requires explicit light transport while preserving the visual fidelity of the original reconstruction.

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [21] and its 2D counterpart [15] enable high-quality, real-time rendering of reconstructed scenes. However, inserting a virtual object into such scenes remains challenging. Beyond matching its appearance to the background, the inserted object must respond to the scene’s illumination, cast geometrically consistent shadows, and contribute indirect light to surrounding surfaces. Achieving these effects requires explicit light transport while preserving the visual fidelity of the original reconstruction.

Existing approaches address this problem from three main directions. Environment-map-based methods estimate local illumination from HDR environment maps [2, 26, 16]. Although effective for approximating incident illumination, environment maps do not explicitly represent the spatial positions of local emitters or their interactions with scene geometry, limiting their ability to reproduce spatially varying illumination and geometrically consistent shadows. Inverse-rendering methods jointly recover scene materials and illumination [28, 8, 13, 47, 29, 37, 3]. While physically grounded, these methods introduce additional unknowns beyond those strictly required for object insertion. Moreover, low-dynamic-range (LDR) observations weaken the photometric constraints needed to distinguish emissive sources from highly reflective surfaces. Finally, image-space harmonization methods use generative models to refine the appearance of composited objects [36, 42, 38, 24]. Despite producing visually plausible results, they do not explicitly model scene-level light transport and therefore cannot guarantee consistent relighting when the object or illumination changes.

We propose GraftRay, a unified framework for physically consistent object insertion into 2D and 3D Gaussian scenes (Fig. 1). Because our pipeline extracts material priors directly from rendered views rather than relying on original capture data, it uniquely supports physically-based insertion even for synthetically generated Gaussian scenes where original training images are unavailable. We first render multi-view images from the Gaussian scene and estimate material properties, including albedo, roughness, metallicity, and normals, using robust 2D estimators such as RGB-X or diffusion-based models. These predictions are then unprojected onto individual 2D/3D Gaussians to provide scene-level material attributes, bypassing the complex joint optimization of traditional inverse rendering. Building on these attributes, we extend an OptiX-accelerated path tracer to support Gaussian primitives with stochastic transparency [9] and 3​σ3\sigma axis-aligned bounding boxes, traced jointly with inserted meshes. The extended path tracer incorporates a Mitsuba-style path integration scheme [17], analytic area emitters, multiple importance sampling (MIS), and explicit shadow rays to enable light transport directly on Gaussian scenes. We further recover scene illumination from LDR observations by treating saturated pixels as lower-bound constraints and using unsaturated surfaces to constrain emitter intensities. Since light transport is linear in emitter intensities with fixed geometry and materials, we precompute unit-radiance basis images and formulate light estimation as a nonnegative least-squares (NNLS) problem. Finally, we use differential rendering [7] to introduce the inserted object’s shadows and indirect illumination while preserving the original background reconstruction.

papers.title: Acoustic Signature Optimisation for Bioinspired Flapping-Wing Micro Aerial Vehicles
papers.abstract: Flapping-wing micro air vehicles are prized for quiet flight, yet the few existing measurements show engineered wings to be 15-30 dB louder than the animals they imitate. This paper investigates two passive geometric approaches to reduce the acoustic signature of a flapping membrane wing, and applies these to an exemplary wing. A significant sound source in flapping wings is the impulsive click radiated at stroke reversal, when a slack membrane snaps between two curvatures. Our first noise-reduction approach optimises the wing's venation layout, based on an analytical model of the reversal click as a dynamic snap-through of the membrane. The optimised venation pattern was manufactured and resulted in a reduction of up to 8 dB during the reversal snap in experiments. During testing, the venation was found to be sensitive to orientation rather than thickness. Secondly, an additive trailing-edge fringe inspired by hummingbird feathers was shown to further reduce the broadband swoosh by 3-4 dB at no lift cost, matching a cut serration wing without removing lifting area.
papers.intro:
Micro aerial vehicles are increasingly deployed in confined, cluttered spaces shared with people and wildlife, where safety and unobtrusiveness matter as much as endurance. Flapping-wing micro aerial vehicles (FWMAVs) suit such settings well, because their wings are light and compliant and the wingtips slow to a stop at each stroke reversal, so a collision carries far less energy than the fast, stiff rotor of a comparable multirotor [1]. This ability to operate safely in tight spaces makes FWMAVs attractive for tasks such as infrastructure inspection, wildlife observation and indoor monitoring. Tasks that operate close to animals or people, in particular, benefit directly from quiet flight and an unobtrusive vehicle. Low acoustic emission is repeatedly cited as a key advantage of flapping over rotary-wing flight, yet the claim is rarely tested. Across the FWMAV literature, only a handful of studies measure noise at all [2, 3, 4, 5], and two recent comprehensive FWMAV reviews compare flight time, mass, mechatronics, control and autonomy, but neither reports the acoustic signature of a single platform [1, 6].

The time derivative of that force radiates to the far field [7]. papers.title: Three quantitative central limit theorems for the unbounded excursion component of a Gaussian field
papers.abstract:
For a class of smooth stationary Gaussian fields, we study the fluctuations of the volume, surface area and Euler characteristic of the unbounded excursion component in growing boxes $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^d$. We establish nondegenerate central limit theorems for all three functionals throughout the supercritical regime in every dimension $d\geq 2$.
  We further quantify these central limit theorems by establishing Berry--Esseen bounds of order $O\bigl(|\Lambda_n|^{-(1-1/s)}\bigr)$ in Kolmogorov distance, where $s\in(1,2]$ depend on the regularity and decay assumptions. Especially for the Bargmann--Fock field, we obtain a Berry--Esseen bound of $O\bigl(|\Lambda_n|^{-1/2}\bigr)$ for all three functionals. A matching lower bound shows that this rate is sharp for the Euler characteristic. For the volume, we improve the previously known rate of $O\bigl(|\Lambda_n|^{-1/2}(\log|\Lambda_n|)^{2d}\bigr)$. We mainly use Stein's method and moment bounds for differences arising from white-noise resampling to finish our proof.

papers.title: GradCO: Behavior-Aware Gradient-Conflict Offloading for Text-Based Person Anomaly Search
papers.abstract: Text-based Person Anomaly Search (TPAS) retrieves a target pedestrian using natural-language descriptions of appearance and normal or anomalous behavior. Unlike conventional text-based person retrieval, TPAS must preserve identity cues while distinguishing fine-grained behaviors. It presents two challenges: same-identity, different-behavior hard negatives cause gradient conflict during granular alignment, while strong appearance cues can obscure weak behavioral evidence during aggregation. We propose GradCO (behavior-aware Gradient-Conflict Offloading), comprising three complementary components. Behavior-Aware Mixture-of-Experts (B-MoE) forms appearance, normal-behavior, and anomalous-behavior streams whose roles are learned from retrieval objectives without expert-specific semantic labels. Conflict Offload Learning (COL) uses pair-conditioned offload anchors in similarity computation to reduce the conflicting-gradient burden on the main text representations. Hierarchical Intent Alignment (HIA) aggregates expert similarities and features using query-conditioned weights. Experiments on five TPAS/TIPR benchmarks show GradCO significantly surpasses SOTA methods and validate our design.

papers.title: Rare Blue-core BCGs as Optical Signatures of ICM Cooling
papers.abstract: Blue cores in brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) trace recent central activity associated with cooling cluster atmospheres. We search for blue cores at $z<0.6$ in five eROSITA all-sky surveys using X-ray data, optical imaging, and optical spectroscopy. We identify 379 blue-core BCGs among 11352 systems (3.3%), although contamination increases toward higher redshift. Of these, 98 (0.86%) are X-ray bright. Their defining signature is a central $g-r$ color at least 0.2 mag bluer than the reference population within $a=20$ kpc before returning to the normal BCG envelope. Ha emission equivalent width correlates strongly with the blue continuum excess, consistent with young stellar components comprising ~0.1-1% of pre-existing stellar mass. Line ratios indicate widespread LINER-like excitation, with a larger star-forming contribution in blue Ha emitters but substantial non-stellar excitation. This activity is closely linked to the thermodynamics of the host-cluster gas. At $0.1R_{500}$, cooling times decrease from BCGs without significant Ha emission to red and then blue Ha emitters. Blue BCGs preferentially occur in clusters with $L_{\rm X,300}>10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$; red Ha emitters also favor higher X-ray luminosities. The blue-core fraction rises with optical richness. For systems with $t_{\rm cool}(0.1R_{500})<20$ Gyr, doubling richness increases the odds of hosting a blue-core BCG by $2.45\pm0.39$. This indicates that cluster scale carries information beyond cooling time, plausibly through the amount of gas available for cooling and condensation. The scarcity of blue BCGs without significant Ha emission disfavors isolated short bursts followed by long Ha-quiet fading phases. It can instead be explained by sustained or closely recurrent star formation over timescales much longer than 100 Myr, or by Ha persisting through additional excitation mechanisms as the young stellar component fades.

The hot intracluster medium (ICM) dominates the baryonic content of galaxy clusters. With typical temperatures of T∼107T\sim 10^{7}–108​K10^{8}\,{\rm K}, the ICM emits primarily in X-rays. In relaxed clusters, the central ICM can form a dense cool core with a radiative cooling time below a gigayear. In the absence of heating, such short cooling times would imply large classical cooling flows, with mass-deposition rates of tens to thousands of solar masses per year (Fabian, 1994). However, high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy shows a strong deficit of emission from gas cooling to the lowest X-ray temperatures, and the observed amounts of cold gas and star formation in brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) are usually much smaller than these classical predictions (Peterson and Fabian, 2006). This discrepancy is the classical cooling-flow problem.

These systems show that some fraction of the cooling ICM can still reach low temperatures and fuel activity in the BCG.

A fundamental open question is therefore what determines whether a favorable cooling atmosphere leaves the BCG largely passive, produces line-emitting multiphase gas, or proceeds far enough to actively form stars. The outcome may depend not only on the current thermodynamic state, but also on the scale of the available gas reservoir and on when the system is observed within the cooling–feedback cycle. The extended ROentgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array (eROSITA; Predehl et al. 2021) on board the Spectrum-Roentgen-Gamma observatory (SRG; Sunyaev et al. 2021) has delivered large samples of X-ray-selected sources in the first and cumulative third eROSITA All-Sky Surveys (eRASS1; Merloni et al. 2024 and eRASS:3; Ramos-Ceja et al. 2026). The corresponding eRASS1 cluster catalog contains 12 247 spatially extended X-ray sources identified as galaxy groups and clusters (Bulbul et al., 2024), with optical identification based on red-sequence galaxy overdensities (Kluge et al., 2024). In this work, we use the deeper eRASS:5 data set, corresponding to an effective depth of 4.4 all-sky surveys, to search for rare BCGs with anomalous central optical colors in X-ray-selected environments.

papers.title: RPSD: Retrieval-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: Sequential recommendation predicts a user's next interaction from historical behavior. Recent LLM-based methods recast this task as generative recommendation and increasingly adopt reinforcement learning such as GRPO for post-training. However, these methods suffer from two limitations, namely credit-blind optimization, where a sequence-level reward is shared across all generated tokens, and collaborative-blind supervision, where each training signal is derived from a single user and ignores behavioral patterns shared across similar users. To address both issues, we propose Retrieval-Privileged on-policy Self-Distillation (RPSD). For credit-blind optimization, we introduce on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), in which a teacher with privileged knowledge re-evaluates the student's on-policy response, and the token-level confidence difference between the student and teacher reshapes the shared sequence-level advantage into token-specific credit. However, the privileged knowledge in vanilla OPSD is still derived from a single user, leaving collaborative-blind supervision unresolved. We therefore ground the teacher in collaborative behavioral evidence from similar users. Specifically, we use temporally aware optimal transport (OT) to compare interaction trajectories across users by jointly considering item similarity and temporal structure, and further apply diversity-aware selection to retain complementary trajectories as privileged evidence. In this way, on-policy self-distillation provides fine-grained token-level credit, while OT enriches the teacher with structured cross-user evidence. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to bring on-policy self-distillation to sequential recommendation and to use cross-user behavior as its privileged signal. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that RPSD achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers.intro:
Sequential recommendation predicts the next item that a user will interact with from the ordered history of past interactions and it is central to content, e-commerce, and media platforms Ma et al. (2026) where user interests change over time (Hidasi et al., 2016; Kang and McAuley, 2018). Traditional methods treat the sequential recommendation problem as next-item prediction over an interaction sequence, evolving from recurrent and self-attention encoders (Hidasi et al., 2016; Kang and McAuley, 2018) to graph-based and contrastive variants, which model higher-order transitions and augment sparse signals (He et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022; Qiu et al., 2022). Although these models are effective and efficient, they represent items as opaque identifier embeddings and reason over co-occurrence statistics rather than the semantics of what a user consumed, which limits generalization when histories are short. An ideal recommender, however, should do more than name which candidate comes next and it should ground that choice in why the recommended item matches the user’s evolving interest.

Although these models are effective and efficient, they represent items as opaque identifier embeddings and reason over co-occurrence statistics rather than the semantics of what a user consumed, which limits generalization when histories are short. An ideal recommender, however, should do more than name which candidate comes next and it should ground that choice in why the recommended item matches the user’s evolving interest.

Large language models (LLMs) address the semantic side of this gap by casting recommendation as language generation, either unifying recommendation tasks in a text-to-text format (Geng et al., 2022; Rajput et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2026; Kong et al., 2025b) or fine-tuning a pretrained LLM to reason over item titles and name the next item directly in text (Bao et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). To align such an LLM with the recommendation objective, reinforcement learning has become a standard post-training recipe. Recent work adapts GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) to LLM-based recommendation, tailoring its reward and credit assignment to the ranking structure of the task. For example, Rank-GRPO (Zhu et al., 2026) moves the reward from the whole sequence to each individual rank, so that later positions in the list get their own credit instead of sharing one signal. RecZero (Kong et al., 2025a) keeps GRPO unchanged but reshapes the rollout into explicit analyze-user, analyze-item, match, and rate steps, replacing exact-match correctness with a reward graded by the predicted rating’s closeness to the true one. However, these adaptations only change which part of a response the reward is applied to. Rank-GRPO gives each rank its own reward and RecZero gives each reasoning step its own, but in both cases a single number is still shared by all the tokens inside that rank or step. The source of the reward is left untouched as well. Whether it is computed over the sequence, the rank, or the step, it always comes from the next item of the user being scored. A reward of this kind can confirm that a recommendation is right, but one user’s interactions are a thin basis for learning why, since a short history reflects accident as much as preference. The same pattern observed across many users with comparable histories is far more dependable, and it is the only evidence available when a single history is too short to be read on its own. Therefore, two problems remain unaddressed, namely credit-blind optimization and collaborative-blind supervision.

Credit-blind optimization concerns how the reward is assigned. Not every token in a response contributes equally to the recommendation. Most tokens provide shared linguistic or formatting structure, while only a small subset determines which item is ultimately selected. GRPO nevertheless assigns the same sequence-level advantage to every generated token, providing no indication of which tokens actually make the recommendation correct. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) (Zhao et al., 2026) provides a promising direction for addressing this limitation. By deriving token-level guidance from a more informed teacher on the same on-policy response, OPSD enables finer-grained credit assignment while preserving the original policy and inference procedure. These properties make it particularly appealing for sequential recommendation. However, the effectiveness of OPSD is ultimately limited by the informativeness of the teacher’s privileged knowledge. If the teacher lacks sufficient behavioral context, the resulting token-level guidance may still be inadequate for capturing the preference signals underlying the target item. Therefore, the second issue collaborative-blind supervision is introduced. Existing generative recommenders derive supervision from the user alone, overlooking regularities shared across similar users.

The teacher then re-evaluates the student’s on-policy response under this privileged view, and the resulting token-level confidence difference is used to reshape the sequence-level advantage into token-specific credit. The privileged knowledge is used only during training, leaving inference unchanged and introducing no additional deployment cost. As shown in Figure 1, the retrieved behavioral evidence further strengthens teacher supervision and leads to improved training dynamics. To the best of our knowledge, RPSD is the first method to introduce OPSD into sequential recommendation and to use cross-user behavior as privileged knowledge. papers.title: The First Deep Learning all-sky List of Fermi-LAT Gamma-ray Sources
papers.abstract:
Aims: We develop a deep-learning-based pipeline to construct a list of {\gamma}-ray sources and to quantitatively assess the impact of background uncertainties on source detection and characterization. This work extends and enhances the existing AutoSource-ID algorithm, previously adopted on optical observations, for applications on {\gamma}-ray data.
  Methods: Source detection was performed through image segmentation using a U-Net architecture, while dedicated deep neural networks (DNNs) were employed for source localization, flux estimation, and the classification of detected sources as either genuine or spurious. The training data were generated from Monte Carlo simulations based on 10 years of Fermi-LAT observations.
  Results: We present the first Fermi-LAT {\gamma}-ray all-sky source list derived using a deep-learning-based method (1FDL), containing more than 3800 sources with estimated positions, fluxes, and probability scores that quantify the likelihood of each detection being genuine or spurious. We further evaluated the robustness of the pipeline against variations in the interstellar emission model (IEM) and compared the resulting source list with the 4FGL-DR2 catalog.
  Conclusion: We find that the our deep-learning-based approach achieves performance comparable to, or better than, the likelihood-based methods employed in the standard Fermi-LAT catalog pipeline when tested against changes in the IEM. The 1FDL source list is broadly consistent with the Fermi-LAT 4FGL-DR2 catalog obtained over the same 10-year observational period, including a few new sources confirmed in the recent Fermi-LAT 16-year source list (FL16Y). These results demonstrate the potential of DNN methods for the detection and characterization of {\gamma}-ray sources and provide a foundation for their application in future high-energy astrophysical analyses.

Recent advances in deep neural networks (DNNs) have transformed many areas of science and engineering, yet their application to the detection and characterization of γ\gamma-ray sources remains scarce (Drozdova et al., 2020; Panes and others, 2021; Eckner et al., 2025). One reason for this is the success of traditional likelihood-based methods. In particular, parameter estimation through maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is statistically well motivated: under the assumption that the adopted model correctly describes the data, MLE provides asymptotically efficient and unbiased estimators. According to the Cramér–Rao bound (Cramér, 1946; Rao, 1992), no unbiased estimator can achieve smaller statistical uncertainties than those obtained with MLE.

According to the Cramér–Rao bound (Cramér, 1946; Rao, 1992), no unbiased estimator can achieve smaller statistical uncertainties than those obtained with MLE.

In practice, however, the performance of MLE strongly depends on the adequacy of the assumed model. In γ\gamma-ray astronomy, one of the major challenges is the imperfect modeling of the diffuse Interstellar Emission Model (Strong et al., 2000; Strong et al., 2007; Vladimirov et al., 2011; Acero and others, 2016, IEM,). The diffuse Galactic γ\gamma-ray background models are affected by substantial uncertainties related to the distribution of interstellar gas, particularly toward the Galactic center, as well as to the spatial distribution of cosmic-ray (CR) sources, CR propagation, and energy losses in Galactic radiation fields. As a consequence, mismodeling of the diffuse emission can produce residual structures that may be incorrectly interpreted as point-like sources, leading both to spurious detections and to biased reconstruction of source properties. This remains one of the major unresolved systematic uncertainties in high-energy astrophysics.

In this work, we i) build a more optimal pipeline that takes into account the energy dependence of the point spread function (PSF); ii) improve the realism of training data by using four different source classes; iii) extend the characterization stage to include dedicated networks for flux estimation and source validation; iv) investigate the robustness of the pipeline against uncertainties in the diffuse background by testing its performance under different IEMs; in order to test the effect of uncertainties in the IEM, we train the DNN with data generated using one model and test it with the data either generated with the same or with a different model, we compare the performance of our pipeline with 4FGL-DR2 catalog (Abdollahi and others, 2020; Ballet and others, 2020); v) apply the pipeline to 10 years of Fermi-LAT observations and construct the first deep-learning-based list of γ\gamma-ray sources, denoted 1FDL, using the same observational period as the 4FGL-DR2. papers.title: Toric Varieties from Multiple Zeta Values
papers.abstract: The linear relations among fixed weight multiple zeta values (MZVs) are a well-studied subject in number theory. Elements of putative linear bases for this fixed-weight space are, however, not algebraically independent; they satisfy non-linear relations. We study these relations by approximating them through motivic MZVs, formal MZVs and numerical computations. We show that motivic MZVs in fixed weight span a projective toric variety and explore its geometry. We define an outer approximation to the variety of formal MZVs in fixed weight by introducing toric varieties coming from shuffle and stuffle relations and taking their intersection. We conjecture that this intersection in fact agrees with the variety of formal MZVs and hence conjecturally also with the variety of motivic MZVs. This leads to a novel conjecture on a generating set for the extended double shuffle relations, which we checked computationally up to weight $23$.
