In other words, we ask for the algebraic variety spanned by weight jj MZVs over the rational numbers. We approach this question by first setting up the conventions to study these relation varieties for MZVs in Section 2. We explain in general how to approximate these varieties via free graded Hopf algebras which surject onto 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. The key point here is that for any such free graded algebra, the associated relation varieties are toric. Our first approximation is the free graded Hopf algebra of motivic MZVs. In Section 3, we study the associated relation varieties in detail. The main results in this section concern their geometric properties: Theorem 3.11 determines the dimension of the motivic MZV variety, Theorem 3.15 the normality properties, and Proposition 3.18 shows that there is no general bound on the degree of the minimal generators of its ideal. Table 1 showcases key properties of these varieties up to weight 2323, obtained by symbolic computations in Macaulay2. In Section 4, we recall the shuffle and stuffle relations satisfied by MZVs, as well as the associated regularizations, and use them to define (regularized) shuffle and stuffle varieties. Our considerations motivate Conjecture 4.14 which posits a small generating set for the ideal of the extended double shuffle relations, which seems to be novel. We have verified this conjecture computationally up to weight 2323. The conjecture would imply that the intersection of regularized shuffle and stuffle varieties yields the relation variety of formal MZV in the given weight. Motivated by this, we study the regularized stuffle variety in Section 5. The main result here is Theorem 5.3 which studies the geometry of such varieties, and Table 5 showcases again central properties of the variety and its ideal up to weight 1414. In Section 6, we compare the intersection of the regularized shuffle and stuffle variety to the double shuffle scheme DM\operatorname{DM} introduced by Racinet [31]. We explain the connection between MZVs and the theory of path signatures. In Section 7, we provide extensive computational and numerical evidence in Pari/GP and SageMath to supplement our main results. We explain our computational workflow in detail. We analyse the existence of what we call exceptional relations (which are relations not predicted by our toric formalism) and provide certifiable results (in a few degrees and weights) for the absence of such relations in accordance with the Grothendieck period conjecture. Details for the GitHub repository hosting code and results is also made available here, including Macaulay2 code for evaluating MZVs for the benefit of readers unfamiliar with Pari/GP or SageMath. The mathematical approach for this evaluation is outlined in Appendix E. Our results provide a novel viewpoint on the algebraic structures governing MZVs. For future work, it would be desirable to connect our findings to the theory of classical modular forms which play an important role in theory of MZVs (cf. [24] and [42, Chapter 5]).

papers.title: Coulomb Crystallization in Free Electron Beams
papers.abstract: Classical Coulomb crystals and quantum Wigner crystals typically arise when repulsive interactions order like-charged particles in spatially confined environments. Here, we show that transient crystallization can also emerge in freely propagating electron pulses without external trapping. Experimentally, we use a transmission electron microscope to measure number-resolved energy correlations in photoemitted pulses containing up to nine electrons, revealing strong correlations at small particle numbers that progressively disappear in the pulse interior as the number increases. To explain these observations, we combine many-body simulations with a one-dimensional statistical-mechanical model, showing that the leading and trailing electrons generate a self-induced longitudinal potential that transiently confines the inner particles, enabling the formation of an ordered chain during propagation. The resulting crystallization phase diagram reveals how many-body ordering dynamics can be understood in terms of evolving macroscopic beam properties, namely its geometry and the ratio of the mean Coulomb interaction energy to the longitudinal thermal energy. Extending this framework, we theoretically demonstrate that weak transverse guiding through electrostatic or optical ponderomotive forces can sustain crystallization at larger particle numbers and predict spontaneous longitudinal periodic bunching in continuous electron beams. Our results identify conditions under which stochastic Coulomb interactions can be harnessed to generate self-structured, strongly correlated electron beams in both pulsed and continuous regimes.

papers.intro:
Long-range interactions can govern the behavior of many-body systems, promoting the spatial stabilization of their components and giving rise to ordered phases in the limit of strong coupling. For like-charged particles, the equilibrium configuration takes the form of a crystalline structure when the average Coulomb energy ECoulE_{\rm Coul}, arising from repulsive inter-particle interactions, dominates over the average kinetic energy EkinE_{\rm kin} [1]. In classical systems, where the kinetic energy is set by thermal motion, this condition can be achieved by increasing the particle density or by lowering the temperature. Due to the repulsive nature of the interaction, Coulomb-induced crystallization generally requires the presence of a confining potential. This has so far been realized through the external confinement of laser-cooled ions in Paul traps [2] or through alternating static electric and magnetic multipoles in storage rings [3, 4, 5, 6], giving rise to so-called Coulomb crystals [7, 8, 1]. In quantum systems, in which the Fermi energy sets the relevant kinetic-energy scale, decreasing the density can instead drive a quantum transition toward spatial ordering [9]. This regime is typically reached in cryogenically cooled solid-state systems, where confinement is naturally provided by the atomic potential landscape, allowing conduction electrons to crystallize. Such ordered structures are known as Wigner crystals [10] and have been observed in carbon nanotubes [11, 12], in twisted transition-metal dichalcogenides [13], and twisted bilayer graphene [14]. Beyond equilibrium crystalline phases, Coulomb-induced correlations have been observed in electron pairs exhibiting interaction-driven antibunching and partitioning when traveling in cryogenic semiconductor nanostructures, including ballistic edge-channel beam splitters [15, 16] and surface-acoustic-wave circuits [17]. Moving few-electron droplets in a GaAs heterostructure have further revealed signatures of a correlated Coulomb liquid [18].

We show that, in one-dimensional beams with high pulse current, the leading and trailing electrons form a self-induced potential that confines the inner particles in free space. papers.title: The CGM in a New Light: Emitted H$\alpha$, [NII], and [OIII] around Simulated Dwarf Galaxies
papers.abstract: Mapping the circumgalactic medium (CGM) in emission is a critical next step in understanding its role in the baryon cycle and galaxy evolution, and dwarf galaxies ($M_{\star}\lesssim 10^9 M_{\odot}$) are essential laboratories to study the effects of feedback on the CGM. Using the Marvelous Massive Dwarfs simulation suite, we model the CGM surface brightness (SB) around dwarf galaxies in H$\alpha$, [NII]$\lambda$6583, and [OIII]$\lambda$5007, lines accessible to current integral-field spectrographs (e.g., MUSE and KCWI) and to narrow-band imaging with the MOTHRA telephoto array. We investigate trends in SB magnitude, extent, and geometry as well as correlations with gas kinematics, recent star formation, and galaxy size. Emission in the three lines typically traces distinct CGM structures and phases. SB and the size of the emitting region can differ significantly at a given galaxy mass, but enhancements or suppression in either brightness or extent correlate well across lines. Typically, emission is preferentially eccentric and oriented along the galaxy's semi-minor axis. While outflows are key drivers in dispersing metals into the CGM and shaping SB, they remain difficult to identify in SB maps and contribute $\sim40\%$ of the total SB across lines and galaxy masses, while inflows contribute $\sim50\%$. Finally, we identify evidence for a positive correlation between SB and recent star formation and weaker but still significant evidence for a negative correlation between SB and HI disk size. These results link CGM emission to both a galaxy's recent star formation and its cumulative evolution, yielding predictions that ongoing surveys can test and further establishing emission mapping as a new window into the baryon cycle.

papers.intro:
The circumgalactic medium (CGM) is the diffuse, multiphase atmosphere within which galaxies reside. The CGM holds the majority of a galaxy’s baryonic budget [59, 44] and mediates galaxy evolution as the interface between the interstellar medium (ISM) and intergalactic medium. Galaxies across the mass spectrum depend on inflows from the CGM to fuel star formation [59], while feedback processes can generate outflows that distribute energy, mass, and metals back into the CGM [25, e.g.,]. Therefore, mapping the CGM is critical to understanding how galaxies grow and in turn shape their environment via feedback processes.

Dwarf galaxies (M⋆≲109​M⊙M_{\star}\lesssim 10^{9}\rm\,M_{\odot}) are essential laboratories for studying feedback due to their shallower gravitational potential wells [52]. Observationally, the imprint of this feedback sensitivity has been noted in the declining metallicities along the mass-metallicity relation [57, 36] and CGM O vi detections extending to twice the size of the halo [27, 54, 38, 21], which suggest that feedback-driven outflows escape dwarfs more readily than higher-mass galaxies, evacuating metals from the disk. As the repository of these outflows, the dwarf CGM is critical to understanding dwarf galaxy evolution and the role of feedback across the mass spectrum.

Up to now, the overwhelming majority of CGM observational programs have used absorption spectroscopy to detect the CGM around a wide range of galaxy masses [7, 62, 11, 14, 64, 38, e.g.,] and derive integrated column densities in a variety of ions. These studies have yielded insights regarding the extent of the metal-enriched CGM and the complex and multiphase nature of the CGM. However, absorption-based CGM measurements face key limitations: (1) the availability of quasars directly constrains the number of galaxies for which the CGM is observed, (2) in most cases, only a single quasar sightline is available for a given halo, limiting insights into the global CGM structure, and (3) column densities integrate over gas at a range of densities and temperatures, obscuring the information on local conditions.

[20] find extended [O ii], [O iii], and H​β\rm H\beta emission and constrain both the ionization parameter and metallicity gradients.

Furthermore, the Aspera smallsat [17] is set to launch in January 2027 and will target O vi emission, and the planned Habitable Worlds Observatory is also poised to target CGM emission [10, HWO;]. Ultimately, emission mapping is the cornerstone of the next phase of CGM observations, and modern simulations are needed to inform observations at this new frontier.

papers.title: Evidence for a nova super-remnant surrounding the recurrent nova V745 Scorpii using eROSITA
papers.abstract: Nova super-remnants (NSRs) are vast shell-like structures encompassing recurrent novae (RNe), created through the excavation of large amounts of local interstellar medium by repeated nova eruptions. Simulations predict that such NSRs should surround all novae. Indeed, NSRs have now been discovered around the Galactic RNe KT Eridani, RS Ophiuchi and T Coronae Borealis, and the Large Magellanic Cloud RN LMCN 1971-08a, to place alongside the prototypical NSR in M31, associated with the extreme RN, M31N 2008-12a. Highly energetic novae ejecta impacting the inner boundary of the NSR shell alongside inter-ejecta shocks are predicted to generate high levels of X-ray emission in the form of an extended shell-like structure. A search for X-ray emission from a present NSR surrounding the Galactic RN, V745 Scorpii, using observations from the extended Roentgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array (eROSITA) on board Spektrum-Roentgen-Gamma (Spektr-RG, SRG) led to the identification of a shell coincident with the nova. Based on (i) the structure being aligned with the location of the central nova; (ii) its size being consistent with the sizes of other known NSRs; (iii) the similarity between the emission radial profiles of the X-ray structure and the confirmed NSR around M31N 2008-12a; (vi) the presence of a corresponding infrared cavity; (v) the resemblance of the radial profile of the synthetic X-ray ring derived from a modelled NSR structure with the radial profile of the observed ring; and (vi) the lack of other sources capable of creating such a large structure, we propose this X-ray structure to be another Galactic NSR to be uncovered, and the first NSR to be captured through its X-ray emission.

papers.intro:
Classical novae (CNe) and recurrent novae (RNe) are luminous transient events arising from the surfaces of accreting white dwarfs (WD; Warner 1995, and see e.g. Darnley and Henze 2020). A thermonuclear runaway triggers at the base of the accreted material once a critical mass is reached (Shara, 1981), resulting in a portion of the accumulated material being ejected in the form of a nova eruption (Starrfield et al., 1972; Prialnik et al., 1978). Observationally, CNe have been observed in eruption once and RNe have exhibited more than one eruption in the last hundred years (Schaefer, 2010; Darnley, 2021). Yet theoretically, all novae are recurrent and can have periods between eruptions ranging from 10−110^{-1} yr (Hillman et al., 2016) to 10610^{6} yr (Hillman et al., 2020). Up to ∼10−4​M⊙{\sim}10^{-4}\ \text{M}_{\odot} of the accreted material is expelled during a nova eruption and can reach velocities of up to 10,000 km s-1 (O’Brien et al., 2001). Such ejecta consequently expands to form a shell around the nova (Cohen 1985; Slavin et al. 1995; Gill and O’Brien 1998; Downes and Duerbeck 2000 and see Santamaría et al. 2025 for a extensive catalogue of known optical nova shells). Though only ∼10%{\sim}10\% of Galactic novae have observed nova remnants, these shells can fade within decades (Tappert et al., 2020) so it is probable that all novae host a nova shell and currently only the brightest examples are detectable. Matter retained on the surface after the nova eruption can grow the WD (Yaron et al., 2005; Hillman et al., 2016) towards the Chandrasekhar (1931) mass and result in a type Ia supernova (Whelan and Iben, 1973).

Nova super-remnants (NSRs) are greatly-extended shells created as a result of the continual sweeping up of up to thousands of solar masses (Darnley et al., 2019; Healy-Kalesh et al., 2023) of local interstellar medium (ISM) by many prior RN eruptions (Darnley et al., 2019; Healy-Kalesh et al., 2023; Healy-Kalesh, 2024). Unlike nova shells observed around CNe (e.g. HR Del: Harman and O’Brien 2003 and V4362 Sgr: Harvey et al. 2020), RNe (e.g. RS Oph: O’Brien et al. 2006; Bode et al. 2007; Ribeiro et al. 2009 and T Pyx: Shara et al. 1997; Shara et al. 2015) and dwarf novae (e.g. Z Cam: Shara et al. 2007; Shara et al. 2024b and AT Cnc: Shara et al. 2012a) which are all less than a parsec across, NSRs are defined as such on account of extending tens of parsecs in diameter (see Healy-Kalesh, 2024, for a review of NSRs): in particular, the most rapidly recurring nova, M31N 2008-12a, hosts the prototypical NSR with dimensions of 90 ×\times 134 pc (Darnley et al., 2019). Crucially, all RNe should host an NSR (Darnley and Henze, 2020; Healy-Kalesh et al., 2023).

The nova system consists of a >>1.3 M⊙\text{M}_{\odot} WD (Page et al., 2015) and a M6 III (Duerbeck, 1989) or M4 III (Harrison et al., 1993) red giant companion and is estimated to be located at a distance of 7.8±1.87.8\pm 1.8 kpc (Schaefer, 2010), though recently Molina et al. (2024) state a revised estimated distance of 8.2−1.0+1.28.2^{+1.2}_{-1.0} kpc. During its 2014 eruption, the nova ejected 10−7​M⊙10^{-7}\ \text{M}_{\odot} (Banerjee et al., 2014; Page et al., 2015; Drake et al., 2016) of material at velocities of ∼4000{\sim}4000 km s-1 (Anupama et al., 2014; Banerjee et al., 2014) and declined from peak by three optical magnitudes in 9 days (Banerjee et al., 2014). Over its multiple eruptions, V745 Sco has been observed across optical (Sekiguchi et al., 1990; Mróz et al., 2014), near-infrared (Harrison et al., 1993; Banerjee et al., 2014; Banerjee et al., 2023), radio (Kantharia et al., 2016; Molina et al., 2024), UV (Page et al., 2015) and X-ray (Orio et al., 2015; Page et al., 2015; Drake et al., 2016) wavelengths as well as being one of the collection of novae to have been detected in γ\gamma-rays (Cheung et al., 2014; Franckowiak et al., 2018). Furthermore, with a WD growing in mass, V745 Sco is proposed to be a SN Ia progenitor (Drake et al., 2016, see e.g.).

papers.title: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents
papers.abstract: Clinical research over electronic health records depends on derived variables whose definitions sit outside the schema, in item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output-grain choices that change cohorts and downstream conclusions. We introduce M4Bench, 28 clinical derivation tasks across 15 task families on MIMIC-IV and eICU, to test whether AI coding agents can reproduce such derivations and how clinician-reviewed agent skills change their results. Its controls decompose the value of skills into specification completeness, delivery format, and schema familiarity. In a Docker-isolated Codex campaign (GPT 5.4 Mini and GPT 5.5), skills raise reward by 0.136 over the no-skill baseline, with 26 of 28 tasks improving. Specification completeness accounts for most of this gain: on an eight-task control subset, an operational spec alone raises reward by 0.162, and skills add only 0.024 on top, indistinguishable from zero. On a ten-task subset, decoy skills score like no skill and raw reference SQL nearly matches targeted skills, arguing against generic context or the skill format as the explanation. Schema obfuscation and restructuring preserve 86% and 70% of the skill gain (GPT 5.4 Mini, 26 MIMIC-IV tasks), a descriptive robustness check rather than a bound on memorization. A descriptive Claude Code replication on all 28 tasks (Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6, 560 runs) is directionally consistent (+0.120, 21 of 28 tasks improving). These gains are partial agreement with the reference, not completed tasks: only 25 of 280 with-skill and 13 of 280 no-skill Codex runs pass every strict check, and skills barely change which rows agents return (key F1 +0.003). Skills are released as a versioned, clinician-reviewable markdown delivery format, with a family-level reference-validity audit. M4Bench releases tasks, skills, evaluation code, and sanitized per-run evidence as an open-source benchmark.

papers.intro:
Observational clinical research using electronic health records (EHRs) commonly relies on derived variables: severity scores such as Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) (Vincent et al., 1996) and Acute Physiology Score III (APS-III) (Knaus et al., 1991), organ-dysfunction measures such as Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) acute kidney injury staging (KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury Work Group, 2012) and Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) (Kamath et al., 2001), and cohort-defining phenotypes such as suspected infection and Sepsis-3 (Singer et al., 2016). These variables are rarely available as simple columns. They are reconstructed from raw tables whose clinical meaning is distributed across item identifiers, units, documentation practices, time windows, and dataset-specific conventions, and the implementation choices behind a single derivation change cohort membership, score distributions, and downstream conclusions in observational studies (Johnson et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2018; Ostropolets et al., 2023).

Yet clinical derivation tasks often require procedural knowledge that is invisible from schema structure alone. A SOFA implementation, for example, needs the score definition plus how vasopressors are encoded, how oxygenation variables are paired, how ventilation status changes respiratory scoring, and how missing components are handled in a specific database release. This procedural knowledge is held by clinicians and embedded in community concept code such as the MIT-LCP MIMIC-Code repository (Johnson et al., 2018), but no benchmark we are aware of represents it as an auditable agent artifact.

M4Bench studies this gap as an evaluation problem. Rather than asking whether an agent can answer clinical questions in free text, M4Bench asks whether a coding agent can reproduce declared EHR research derivations and whether explicit procedural specifications change that behavior. papers.title: How Reliable Is Individualized Functional-Network Attribution in Resting-State fMRI Cognitive Prediction in ADNI?
papers.abstract: Individualized attribution estimates which functional networks drive a model prediction for a given subject and is often proposed as an interpretable resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) biomarker, but its test-retest reliability is rarely quantified. We evaluate per-subject network-ablation attribution for a frozen resting-state functional connectivity (FC) predictor (Schaefer-200 FC predicting MMSE/ADAS-Cog13) trained on N=875 subjects from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), using, and (iii) a subject-level permutation null. Split-half reliability is near-ceiling (Spearman p=0.948/0.950) but drops on scan-rescan (p=0.609/0.616). Under the mismatched-subject null, correlations remain substantial (p~0.46-0.47), indicating strong population-shared structure, yet matched pairs exceed this null (z~6.6-6.9, p<=10-4). Thus, in ADNI, individualized network attribution contains a modest but non-zero person-specific component atop a strong population-shared pattern. We recommend reporting scan-rescan reliability together with a permutation-null control, rather than within-session proxies alone, to avoid overstating individual specificity.

Beyond group-level accuracy, a common objective is individualized attribution: for a given subject, estimating which functional networks drive that subject’s prediction. Such per-subject attribution is only meaningful if it is reproducible.

Reliability is a central constraint. Large-scale analyses suggest that stable brain–behavior effects often require much larger samples than historically used [11], and FC test–retest reliability is frequently modest (pooled mean edge-level Intraclass Correlation Coefficient, ICC ≈0.29\approx 0.29) [13]. The ICC describes how reproducibly a single connectivity edge is measured. Prior work on subject-specific parcellations reports reproducibility across short-interval repeat sessions [17, 10], but does not quantify test–retest reliability of model-derived attribution signatures over the multi-year intervals typical of aging cohorts.

An additional aspect is attribution stability: feature-importance maps can vary substantially under resampling, noise, and other perturbations even when predictive accuracy is similar [1, 7]. In FC prediction, however, attribution work has largely emphasized group-averaged importance. For connectomes rather than attributions, differential identifiability formalizes the person-specific, test–retest-identifiable component [2], and permutation-null models are standard for separating population-shared from person-specific structure [5, 12]. Neither has been applied to per-subject attribution signatures. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work combines per-subject attribution of an FC-based cognitive predictor with a quantitative test–retest evaluation on independent repeat scans of the same individuals.

papers.title: Little Red Dots with Broad H$\beta$ Lines Reveal the Black Hole Mass Function at 7<z<9.5
papers.abstract: We present a systematic search for broad H$\beta$ emission at $7<z<9.5$ in 21,770 JWST/NIRSpec PRISM spectra drawn from four blank fields and six lensing clusters with photometry spanning 1942 arcmin$^2$. We find a sample of 20 sources with statistically significant broad-H$\beta$ emission, including 13 new sources. Our entire sample has colors and morphologies consistent with little red dots (LRDs), compared to only 37\% of broad-line emitters at $3.5<z<6$. Interpreting the broad-lines as indicators of Broad-line Active Galactic Nuclei (BLAGN), we infer black hole masses of $4.2\times10^{6}-2.1\times10^{8}$\,$M_{\odot}$. We calculate completeness corrections and construct the black hole mass function at $z\sim8$. The normalization of the black hole mass function rises by $\approx1.0$~dex from $z\sim8-5$, consistent with average black hole growth at $f_{\textrm{Edd}}\approx0.1$. Comparing with cosmological simulations, the $z\sim8$ black hole mass function requires heavy ($10^5$\,$M_{\odot}$) seeds or super-Eddington accretion onto light or intermediate mass seeds to match its normalization. Finally, we infer bolometric luminosities for the sample and construct a bolometric luminosity function. We integrate over this luminosity function to derive a black hole accretion density (BHAD) of $4.8^{+5.8}_{-2.6}\times10^{-7}~M_{\odot}~\textrm{yr}^{-1}~\textrm{Mpc}^{-3}$, showing broad agreement with previous photometric work, but disagreement with previous X-ray models, reinforcing the idea that BLAGN are more common in the early universe than previously expected.

papers.intro:
Understanding the evolution of Supermassive Black Holes (SMBHs) across cosmic time is a key component in developing a full understanding of both the evolution of the Universe and the formation of galaxies [69, e.g.,]. As most if not all local massive galaxies are known to host SMBHs at their centers, SMBHs and galaxy properties and evolution are intrinsically tied together. This co-evolution is most apparent when SMBHs actively accrete matter as Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN), which strongly radiate across the electromagnetic spectrum. This emission is thought to significantly influence the star formation and gas dynamics of the host galaxy [97]. In broad-line AGN (BLAGN), the emergent radiation from the SMBH’s accretion disk that is processed through the SMBH’s high-density broad-line region is directly visible, and is detectable through Doppler broadening of permitted emission lines (e.g. Mg ii, Lyα\alpha, Hα\alpha, Hβ\beta, Paα\alpha) and a lack of broadening in density-sensitive forbidden lines (e.g. [O iii]λ​λ\lambda\lambda4959,5007). Due to this direct view of the emitting region, BLAGN are among the most luminous known objects in the universe [128, e.g.].

Due primarily to the broad Balmer lines seen in most LRD spectra, BLAGN were obvious initial candidates for these central engines, with the broad Balmer lines attributed to AGN broad-line region kinematics [68, 90, 89, 109, 85, 134, 10, 106, 22, e.g.].

papers.title: Stability of attractive 3D Bose gases with repulsive three-body interactions
papers.abstract: We consider three-dimensional Bose gases with attractive two-body interactions and repulsive three-body interactions. We prove the stability of the second kind of the system for a large class of interaction potentials and scaling regimes, which includes the Gross--Pitaevskii regime for the three-body potential. In addition, we even prove the classical stability of the system for a more restrictive class of interactions and scaling regimes. The main ingredient of the proof is a bound that was derived recently in a study by the authors on the dynamics of Bose gases with three-body interactions in the Gross--Pitaevskii regime (2026).

In the present work, we are interested in the stability of 3D Bose gases with (partially) attractive two-body interactions and repulsive three-body interactions. Such Bose gases have drawn considerable attention in the Physics literature [3, 2, 18, 20, 23, 46] because repulsive three-body interactions can counterbalance the instability induced by attractive two-body interactions. Our main result is a rigorous justification of this fact under very general assumptions on the interaction, and for a wide range of scaling regimes, which includes the Gross–Pitaevskii regime for the three-body interaction potential. Furthermore, we also prove the classical stability of the system for a narrower range of scaling regimes. Notably, both results are true for very large attractive two-body potentials, as long as the three-body potential does not vanish in an arbitrary small region around the origin. This is in stark contrast to the situation without three-body interactions, where the system is unstable even for very small attractive potentials.

papers.title: Timestral
papers.abstract: We introduce Timestral, a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M and Timestral-123M take the top two places on every metric. We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context. This report describes the model design and its benchmark results. Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face and inference code on GitHub.

\Acp tsfm enable forecasting across datasets and domains without retraining. By training on large collections of real and synthetic time series, these models provide a shared alternative to fitting a separate model for each forecasting problem (Ansari et al., 2024; Das et al., 2024). Recent advances have improved forecast accuracy, demonstrated gains from scaling, and extended support to multivariate series and external covariates (Khwaja et al., 2026; Ansari et al., 2025; Podest et al., 2026; Meyer et al., 2026). These developments place increasing importance on how models use the information available at each forecast origin and on the training distributions that support this use.

Bidirectional encoder-only models such as Chronos-2 and Falcon-2.0 (Ansari et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2026) sample a context length and a horizon length for each training example, so each forward pass covers a single combination of the two. Causal decoder-only models instead forecast from every position of a sequence and thus cover many context lengths in one forward pass. To also cover multiple horizon lengths, recent causal models are trained to forecast several patches ahead directly rather than autoregressively. cpm (cpm), used in TiRex, Toto-2.0, and TimesFM-3 (Auer et al., 2025; Khwaja et al., 2026; Jain and Sen, 2026), achieves this by masking spans of the input sequence. The masked observations, however, are then also unavailable as context for later forecasts in the same training sequence, coupling the horizon distribution to full-patch context masking. Known-future covariates pose a second challenge: their future values must be accessible to forecasts, while future target values must remain hidden.

We introduce Timestral, a family of four foundation models for probabilistic univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed time series forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. All four models share the same architecture and training recipe, offering a range of trade-offs between forecast accuracy and inference cost. Timestral addresses the coupling of horizons and context masking through dhf (dhf), which separates causal context representations from learned prediction tokens, and the covariate challenge through a role-aware covariate framework that integrates known-future information while preserving target causality. The models are pretrained on a synthetic corpus of univariate signals and structured multivariate dependencies, then post-trained on a mixture of real and synthetic data with extended context. Timestral-209M sets a new state of the art in forecasting performance on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench. As shown in Figure 1, all four Timestral models lie on the Pareto front for all benchmark metrics. Timestral-123M already outperforms every other model shown, including models with billions of parameters.

This report presents the released Timestral models, their benchmark results, and the main design choices behind them: • dhf. We introduce dhf, a forecasting formulation that separates missing observations from prediction tokens. dhf preserves observed values as context for later forecast origins within the same training sequence, allowing multiple forecast blocks to be supervised while controlling horizon sampling independently of artificial context masking. • Covariate conditioning within dhf. We integrate past-only and known-future covariates through explicit series roles and asymmetric attention. This enables prediction tokens to use known-future information at multiple forecast origins while preserving causality over target values. • A model family spanning accuracy and inference cost. We release four model sizes, from 5M to 209M parameters. The 209M model ranks first on all reported metrics among the models compared on GIFT-Eval (Aksu et al., 2024), TIME (Qiao et al., 2026), and fev-bench (Shchur et al., 2026).

papers.title: Galactic Dynamics Drives Cyclic Star Formation in Dipole Dwarf Galaxies
papers.abstract: Dwarf galaxies are dark matter-dominated systems that are sensitive to feedback and display bursty star formation histories. This makes them ideal probes of the processes that regulate star formation. This work investigates the timescales of star formation rate (SFR) variability in isolated dwarf galaxies using high-resolution cosmological zoom-in simulations of $50$ dwarf galaxies drawn from the Marvelous Massive Dwarfs and Extended Marvelous Dwarfs simulation suites ($7.3 <$ \lmstar $< 9.1$). We measure star formation histories in $10$ Myr bins and characterize their variability with power spectral densities (PSDs). At the population level, the PSDs of both disk and non-disk galaxies follow a broken power-law, with a break timescale near $100$ Myr. Individually, our galaxies show both smooth and bursty star formation. A subset of disk galaxies show quasi-periodic SFR oscillations about their mean, which we refer to as cyclic star formation. The dominant timescale of these oscillations scales linearly with half-light radius and is approximated by the orbital period at that radius. Cyclic galaxies have Magellanic Spiral (Sm) morphologies and host lopsided dipole gas disks. In these systems, the bulk of the gas in the lopsided disk moves between its maximum and minimum distance from the galactic center, compressing the star-forming gas once per radial orbit and driving the SFR cycle. Cyclic star formation adds a narrow Lorentzian component to the PSD, peaked at radial orbital frequency of the disk ($\sim 200-500$ Myr), which is comparable to burst timescales inferred from observations.

These processes operate on different timescales and leave their imprints on the star formation histories (SFH) that dwarf galaxies display. Disentangling the contribution of each process requires constraining the variability in star formation rates (SFR), and the timescales over which they take place.

Observations find that dwarfs form stars in bursts [88, 56, 55, 101, 46, 7, 6, 60], and constrain that variability through tracers averaging over different timescales [102, e.g.,]. Hα\alpha and far ultraviolet (FUV) emission trace star formation over ∼10\sim 10 Myr and 100100 Myr, respectively. [102] and [22] both argue for significant bursts in low-mass galaxies (log⁡(M⋆/M⊙)\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot}) ≲9\lesssim 9), with burst timescales of ∼100\sim 100–300300 Myr that lengthen with stellar mass. With the advent of JWST there is now also evidence for burstiness on ∼100\sim 100 Myr timescales in cosmic-noon dwarfs [62] and in typical galaxies at cosmic dawn [52, 23, 17, 78, e.g.]. At a population level, and at a given epoch, galaxies observed at different phases of a burst cycle scatter about the star forming main sequence (MS, M⋆M_{\star}–SFR relation), with dwarf galaxies occupying a mass regime where the MS scatter grows [43, e.g.,].

With the advent of JWST there is now also evidence for burstiness on ∼100\sim 100 Myr timescales in cosmic-noon dwarfs [62] and in typical galaxies at cosmic dawn [52, 23, 17, 78, e.g.]. At a population level, and at a given epoch, galaxies observed at different phases of a burst cycle scatter about the star forming main sequence (MS, M⋆M_{\star}–SFR relation), with dwarf galaxies occupying a mass regime where the MS scatter grows [43, e.g.,].

On the theoretical side, the extended regulator model provides a physical framework for this variability [15, 87, 39]. In this model the SFR is set by a gas reservoir that is fed by inflow and drained by star formation and outflows [87]. Fluctuations in SFR due to fluctuations in inflow are damped on short timescales because the gas reservoir averages out fluctuations shorter than its depletion time. This leaves the short-timescale burstiness to processes internal to the galaxy, such as feedback cycles, the formation and destruction of individual molecular clouds, and dynamical disturbances. These short-timescale processes all act on roughly a galactic dynamical time and leave the SFR uncorrelated beyond it. The two families of processes result in a SFH power spectral density (PSD) with three power-law regimes separated by breaks around the galactic dynamical time and at the timescale on which the reservoir responds to inflow. The PSD rises at timescale below the galactic dynamical timescale, is flat between the dynamical timescale and the inflow timescale [40], and steeply rises again above it [87]. The flat regime arises because the two timescales are widely separated, leaving a range over which neither process imprints any structure (white noise). [40] measured the PSDs of SFHs across a wide range of simulations, with different galaxy formation or feedback models, and found them to be well described by broken power-laws, with slopes of ∼1\sim 1 to 33 below the dynamical break and a flattening towards longer timescales.

Section III presents the PSDs of our simulated galaxy sample, separates bursty from cyclic SFHs, and examines how the dominant timescale scales with galaxy properties. papers.title: PrivacyEvalClaw: A Tool-Augmented Deliberative Agent for Auditing Privacy Leakage in LLM Jailbreak Responses
papers.abstract: Reliable evaluation is a critical bottleneck in privacy red-teaming of large language models (LLMs): determining whether a jailbreak response actually reveals personal information can be difficult when disclosures are indirect, contextual, partial, or obfuscated. Existing evaluation approaches increasingly rely on guard models and LLM-as-Judges, yet these evaluators may interpret the same response differently. To better characterize this evaluation setting, we conduct a systematic study of privacy evaluators and find substantial disagreement, particularly in ambiguous cases that require additional evidence or targeted analysis to resolve. Motivated by these findings, we introduce \textsc{PrivacyEvalClaw}, a training-free deliberative agent for evaluating privacy leakage in LLM jailbreak responses. Rather than relying on isolated single-pass judgments, PrivacyEvalClaw treats evaluators and analysis modules as tools, adaptively gathers evidence, investigates uncertain disclosures, and reconciles conflicting signals before producing a final judgment. Our primary experiments use pairwise LLM-as-Judge evaluation of complete trajectories, showing that PrivacyEvalClaw achieves favorable win rates against competing baselines across outcome, process, and overall quality, while producing explicit reasoning traces that make the evaluation process more transparent and auditable.

papers.intro:
Red-teaming of large language models (LLMs) increasingly relies on advanced jailbreak attacks to elicit responses that may reveal personal or sensitive information, providing a practical way to study privacy leakage under adversarial prompting. As LLMs are trained on web-scale corpora containing personal information, such attacks have become an important tool for probing memorization and unintended disclosure Li et al. (2023); Wang et al. (2025). The reliability of these audits, however, hinges on evaluators that can accurately determine whether the resulting jailbreak responses constitute privacy leakage. This is often non-trivial because disclosures may be indirect, contextual, partial, transformed, obfuscated, or dependent on external knowledge. Existing evaluation approaches commonly use automated evaluators such as guard models Zhao et al. (2025); Kang et al. (2026) and LLM-as-a-Judge frameworks Li et al. (2024a), despite growing concerns about their reliability in safety Shen et al. (2025); Eiras et al. (2025) and medicine Diekmann et al. (2025); DeLucia et al. (2026).

As a result, some evaluators aggressively flag weak contextual cues or indirect assistance as privacy leakage, while others focus primarily on explicit disclosures and may miss subtle, transformed, or obfuscated leakage patterns. Motivated by this view, we introduce PrivacyEvalClaw, a training-free deliberative agent for evaluating privacy leakage in LLM jailbreak responses. papers.title: The evolutionary history of ultra-compact accreting binaries. II. HST spectroscopy of two eclipsing AM CVn stars
papers.abstract: AM CVn stars are ultra-compact binaries in which a white dwarf (WD) accretes helium-rich material from a hydrogen-deficient donor. They are promising mHz gravitational-wave sources and potential progenitors of Type Ia supernovae. However, their evolutionary pathways remain uncertain. Three formation channels have been proposed: the WD, helium star, and cataclysmic variable channels. We aim to determine the atmospheric chemical composition of the underlying accreting WDs in two eclipsing AM CVn systems, YZ LMi and ZTF J0407-00, in order to constrain their formation channels. Using ultraviolet spectra obtained with the Hubble Space Telescope, we modelled the atmospheres of the accreting WDs, whose surface compositions are enriched by material transferred from the donor and therefore trace the donor's composition. In particular, the nitrogen-to-carbon abundance ratio provides a diagnostic of the donor's nuclear burning history and hence of the system's formation channel. We measure effective temperatures Teff = 24400 $\pm$ 1500 K and surface gravities logg = 8.36 $\pm$ 0.05 for YZ LMi, and Teff = 29900 $\pm$ 2200 K and logg = 8.37 $\pm$ 0.05 for ZTF J0407-00. The inferred masses of the two WDs are 0.84 $\pm$ 0.10 and 0.86 $\pm$ 0.12 solar masses, respectively. Carbon is not detected in either system, yielding lower limits on the nitrogen-to-carbon mass ratio of N/C > 117 and N/C > 185. We increase from one to three the number of AM CVn systems whose accreting WDs and chemical abundances have been analysed using detailed UV atmosphere models. The high N/C ratios rule out the helium star formation channel for both systems. The WD channel is favoured by the absence of detectable hydrogen at all observed wavelengths, although the evolved cataclysmic variable channel cannot be conclusively excluded.

papers.intro:
AM Canum Venaticorum (AM CVn) stars are ultra-compact interacting binaries composed of a white dwarf (WD) accreting matter from a hydrogen-deficient donor. Mass transfer from the Roche-lobe-filling donor forms an accretion disc around the accreting WD. These systems are of fundamental importance for several reasons. First, accreting WDs provide valuable probes for testing models of compact binary evolution (Nelemans et al., 2001; Postnov and Yungelson, 2014). Second, they are potential progenitors of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia), which play a central role in cosmology. One of several proposed pathways to SNe Ia is the double-detonation scenario, in which helium accretion onto a WD leads to the detonation of the accreted helium layer, subsequently triggering the detonation of the carbon–oxygen core and a thermonuclear explosion (Fink et al., 2010; Maoz et al., 2014). Third, they are ideal multi-messenger laboratories. Their short orbital periods (less than 70 min) make them among the brightest persistent Galactic sources of gravitational waves (GW) in the mHz regime (Nelemans et al., 2004; Kupfer et al., 2024). For reviews of AM CVn stars, see, e.g. Nelemans (2005); Solheim (2010).

The prototype AM CVn star was identified in the 1960s (Smak, 1967; Paczyński, 1967). Since the advent of large-scale surveys, the known population has grown to around 150 systems (Roelofs et al., 2007; Ramsay et al., 2018; Burdge et al., 2020; Pichardo Marcano et al., 2021; Green et al., 2025; Rodriguez et al., 2025; Kára et al., 2026; Hernández-Díaz et al., 2026, e.g.). This population is expected to increase substantially with ongoing and forthcoming surveys across the electromagnetic spectrum. These include photometric surveys such as Gaia (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2023), the Gravitational-wave Optical Transient Observer (GOTO; Steeghs et al. 2022), BlackGEM (Groot et al., 2024), and the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST; Ivezić et al. 2019); spectroscopic surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS; Kollmeier et al. 2026), the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI; Schlafly et al. 2023), and the 4-metre Multi-Object Spectroscopic Telescope (4MOST; de Jong et al. 2019); and X-ray surveys such as the extended ROentgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array (eROSITA; Predehl et al. 2021). Moreover, a subset of AM CVn systems is expected to be individually detected by next-generation GW observatories, including TianQin (Luo et al., 2016), Taiji (Luo et al., 2021), the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA; Amaro-Seoane et al. 2023), and the Lunar Gravitational-wave Antenna (LGWA; Ajith et al. 2025). The brightest systems will serve as verification binaries, whose signals are expected to be individually resolved on timescales ranging from ∼3\sim 3 weeks to ∼48\sim 48 months (Roelofs et al., 2006; Kupfer et al., 2015; Chickles et al., 2025; Chickles et al., 2026). The population as a whole will also contribute to the Galactic GW foreground at mHz frequencies (Nelemans et al., 2004; Kupfer et al., 2018; Kupfer et al., 2024). Understanding the formation and evolution of AM CVn systems is therefore essential for constraining their population properties and informing population-synthesis models (Breivik et al., 2020; Korol et al., 2022, e.g.), particularly in the emerging era of multi-messenger astronomy.

Nevertheless, the formation channels of AM CVn stars remain poorly constrained. Current theories suggest that these systems originate from close main-sequence binaries that undergo one or more phases of binary interaction, such as stable mass transfer or common-envelope evolution (Nelemans et al., 2001; Podsiadlowski et al., 2003). Following the first interaction phase, which leads to the formation of a WD, three evolutionary pathways have been proposed. (i) The WD channel, in which a second interaction phase produces a degenerate donor (Paczyński, 1967; Webbink, 1984; Deloye et al., 2007; Wong and Bildsten, 2021; Chen et al., 2022; Munday et al., 2024); (ii) the helium star (He-star) channel, in which a second interaction phase is again required to produce a semi-degenerate, helium-rich donor (Savonije et al., 1986; Iben and Tutukov, 1987; Yungelson, 2008; Bauer and Kupfer, 2021); and (iii) the cataclysmic variable (CV) channel, which involves only a single interaction phase. In the latter case, the donor’s helium core is exposed as its outer layers are stripped through stable mass transfer (Tutukov et al., 1985; Goliasch and Nelson, 2015; Liu et al., 2021; Belloni and Schreiber, 2023; Sarkar et al., 2023a).

One of the most robust methods for identifying the formation channel of an AM CVn system is to determine the donor’s chemical composition (Nelemans et al., 2010). In particular, the nitrogen-to-carbon abundance ratio (N/CN/C) varies significantly with the extent of prior CNO-cycle burning. The accretor’s photospheric N/CN/C ratio traces the transferred material, as ongoing accretion replenishes the layer at the WD surface. The expected values differ by more than an order of magnitude for the different formation channels, with N/C≲10N/C\lesssim 10 for systems formed through the He-star channel and N/C≳100N/C\gtrsim 100 for those formed through either the WD or CV channels. Although previous studies reported an infrared excess that could have potentially been ascribed to the donor (Rivera Sandoval et al., 2021), recent JWST spectroscopy of AM CVns showed that the infrared emission is still significantly affected by the accretion disc (El-Badry et al., 2026). A direct detection of donors therefore remains missing, limiting our ability to model their spectra and determine their chemical abundances. Instead, the atmosphere of the accreting WDs, enriched by material transferred from the donor, provides an indirect probe of the donor’s composition.

papers.title: The inner galaxy as a window on its early assembly: lessons from a cosmological Milky Way analogue
papers.abstract: Characterising the assembly history of the inner Milky Way is a key goal of upcoming spectroscopic surveys, yet disentangling its overlapping stellar components remains challenging. We investigate the chemodynamics of the centre of a Milky Way analogue in the Auriga Superstars cosmological hydrodynamical simulation suite, focusing on a high-resolution halo (~ 800 M_sun star particles) with a realistic galactic bar and accretion history. We classify stars within the inner 4 kpc into proto-galaxy, subsequent in-situ, and accreted components to assess their distinguishability using kinematics, dynamics, ages, and metallicities. Stellar net rotation declines sharply between [Fe/H]=0 and [Fe/H]=-1, marking the transition from disc-like in-situ stars to the proto-galaxy. While significant chemical and dynamical overlaps complicate the search for structures in energy-angular momentum (E-Lz) space, metal-poor stars ([Fe/H]<-1) at low energy form a remarkably pure (>97%) sample of proto-galaxy stars. Conversely, the high-energy, metal-poor tail offers the best chance of detecting accreted debris. However, at high energies the inner accreted halo is dominated by low-mass systems (M_star ~ 10^7 - 10^9 M _sun), not the earliest massive mergers. Dynamically, few clues remain from early mergers, and early enrichment is rapid and similar across progenitors. In-situ contamination is an issue for [Fe/H]>-1 throughout E-Lz space. Overall, while accurate stellar ages and high-precision chemical abundances may help further constrain the Milky Way's history, we should be cautious when associating stars with individual merger events in the inner galaxy.

papers.intro:
One of the key questions in astronomy is how galaxies such as the Milky Way came to be. Observations of external galaxies provide glimpses into galaxies at different evolutionary stages. This can help inform us on the hierarchical assembly of galaxies and the frequency of mergers at a range of redshifts (Conselice et al., 2003; Bluck et al., 2012; Duncan et al., 2019; Dalmasso et al., 2024), as well as the timescales of secular processes (e.g. the formation of galactic bars, see Abraham et al. 1999; Guo et al. 2025; Le Conte et al. 2026). However, the galaxy that provides us with the most detailed view remains our own Milky Way, which allows for observations on a star-by-star basis. While we can only observe it in its current state, we can still infer from the present how it has evolved in the past.

However, the galaxy that provides us with the most detailed view remains our own Milky Way, which allows for observations on a star-by-star basis. While we can only observe it in its current state, we can still infer from the present how it has evolved in the past.

The formation of galaxies, according to the theory of hierarchical structure formation, is shaped by a series of successive mergers (White and Rees, 1978; White and Frenk, 1991). The search for traces of past merger events in the Milky Way constitutes the field of Galactic archaeology. The search for merger remnants is usually done using a combination of stellar chemistry and dynamics. Its premise is the assumption that with knowledge of a star’s current position and velocity, as well as the composition of its atmosphere, we can infer the environment in which the star formed. We can make use of differences in the chemical evolution of stars, which have been found to differ for stars born in the Milky Way and accreted from dwarf satellites (Venn et al., 2004; Nissen and Schuster, 2010; Nissen and Schuster, 2011; Hawkins et al., 2014; Hawkins et al., 2015). This can be combined with dynamical information allowing us to distinguish accreted stars by their current orbits (see reviews by Binney 2013; Hunt and Vasiliev 2025 and references therein).

Since the launch of the Gaia mission (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016; Gaia Collaboration et al., 2018; Gaia Collaboration et al., 2023), the search for past mergers has been revolutionised. In combination with dedicated large spectroscopic surveys such as APOGEE (Majewski et al., 2017), DESI (Cooper et al., 2023), and upcoming surveys on instruments such as 4MOST (de Jong et al., 2019), it is now possible to study the dynamics and chemistry of the stellar halo of the Milky Way on a star-by-star basis for a significant fraction of stars. The number of known stellar streams discovered surged from around 60 before Gaia, to over 100 since Gaia DR2 (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2018; Bonaca and Price-Whelan, 2025). The most significant single discovery of Gaia is arguably the Gaia-Sausage/Enceladus merger (GSE) (Belokurov et al., 2018; Helmi et al., 2018; Haywood et al., 2018). Debris from this progenitor dominates the halo of the Milky Way within 15-20 kpc from the centre. Since the initial successes of finding signatures of past accretion using Gaia data, there have been efforts to supplement Gaia observations with spectroscopic data, in order to get better chemical abundances as well as more accurate radial velocities for distant stars. This is motivated by simulations, which show that the oldest stars in the galaxy are preferentially found either in the outer halo or close to the centre of the galaxy (Starkenburg et al., 2017b). This motivated the Pristine survey (Starkenburg et al., 2017a) to find very metal-poor stars in the halo, as well as its sub-survey PIGS (Arentsen et al., 2020), which searches for metal-poor stars in the bulge of the Milky Way. Additionally, the COMBS survey (Lucey et al., 2019; Lucey et al., 2021; Lucey et al., 2022), has been using high-resolution spectroscopy to get detailed chemical abundances of metal-poor bulge stars, in order to understand the origin of this population. Other surveys such as SDSS-V (Kollmeier et al., 2026) will further improve our understanding of the stars in the bulge.

With these future observations we hope to reconstruct the formation of the Milky Way up to its earliest building blocks, which make up the proto-galaxy. This is thought to be a metal-poor population of stars with little net rotation and is associated with the so-called “Aurora” population in the Milky Way, as postulated by Belokurov and Kravtsov (2022). This may very well be the same population as the metal-poor concentrated spheroid around the centre of the Milky Way identified by Rix et al. (2022). In 13 haloes of the FIRE-2 simulations, Horta et al. (2024) studied the properties of the proto-galaxy and its building blocks. While this study finds that it may be possible to separate out the dominant component of the proto-galaxy, the centre of the galaxy where remnants of the proto-galaxy are predominantly found is a challenging environment for observations.

papers.title: Revealing the companion of NGC 1850-BH1
papers.abstract: The nature of the system NGC 1850-BH1 is discussed controversially in the literature. Located in the young (100 Myr) massive cluster NGC 1850 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, it was initially proposed to consist of a 5 $M_\odot$ main sequence turn-off star orbiting a stellar-mass black hole. However, subsequent analyses of the system have presented an alternative explanation, comprising of a lower mass (1-2 $M_\odot$) puffed-up donor star orbiting a rapidly rotating mass accretor. Efforts to discern the secondary's nature as a luminous star or a compact object in the original spectroscopy have remained inconclusive. In this work, we analyse a set of follow-up multi-epoch FLAMES-ARGUS spectra, which are bluer and of higher spectral resolution than the original data. Exploiting the spectral disentangling technique, we reveal the luminous secondary, and constrain the parameters of both components. We can describe the system self-consistently, adopting a 1.7 $\pm$ 0.4 $M_\odot$ puffed-up mass donor and a rapidly rotating ($v\sin{i} = 275$ km/s) 5.2 $\pm$ 2.6 $M_\odot$ luminous companion. While this rules out the black hole hypothesis, tensions with the analysis of the original data remain: Our inferred flux ratio of $\sim$ 35-50% in the red optical wavelength range is higher than the 10% upper limit found in previous work. The origin of this discrepancy remains unclear. Thanks to its location in a cluster of well-known mass and metallicity and its peculiar orbital properties, NGC 1850-BH1 has the potential to serve as a benchmark for mass-transfer efficiency studies.

A significant fraction of high mass O- and B-type stars are born in binaries and higher-order multiples (Sana and Evans, 2011; Moe and Di Stefano, 2017; Offner et al., 2023, e.g.), and interactions between the components are thought to affect a majority of them throughout their lifetime (Sana et al., 2012, e.g.). This can shape the physical and chemical evolution of one or both components, through the exchange of mass and angular momentum (de Mink et al., 2013, e.g.).

The most massive among these stars are likely to end their lives as black holes (BHs) or neutron stars (NSs) following core-collapse supernovae. If the binary survives the explosion, the compact object may remain in a bound system with a stellar companion. If the compact object is a BH and X-ray quiet, it is commonly referred to as a “dormant Black Hole” (dBH). Further evolution of the system may lead to an X-ray binary, a second detonation, and/or a binary compact merger (Abbott et al., 2016, e.g.).

This intermediate phase when the compact object is bound to a luminous stellar companion is thought to be comparatively long-lasting, and thus models suggest the presence of O(10510^{5}) of such systems in the Milky Way Galaxy (Breivik et al., 2017; Langer et al., 2020; Nagarajan et al., 2025; Wagg et al., 2026, e.g.). Their observational signatures are, however, challenging to detect, since the compact object must be inferred from the motion it induces on the luminous companion, and systems containing two non-compact stars can produce similar observables (Bodensteiner et al., 2020; El-Badry et al., 2022; El-Badry and Quataert, 2020; Shenar et al., 2020, e.g.). These “imposter” systems contain two stellar non-compact objects with one of them evolving though a short-lived bloated phase following substantial mass loss. In this phase, the star appears much brighter than expected given its mass and can outshine its companion, leading to the binary being incorrectly identified as a BH-star or NS-star system.

For the Magellanic Clouds, the smaller overall stellar mass implies a lower total number of dBHs, although their lower metallicity leads to weaker stellar winds and hence favours the formation of more massive BH remnants (Mapelli et al., 2013, e.g.). Additionally, the Magellanic Clouds host a substantial population of young massive clusters, which may provide favourable formation sites for dBHs, e.g. via dynamical interactions. Interestingly, the most massive dBH known in the Milky Way, Gaia-BH3 (Gaia Collaboration, 2024, 33 M⊙\mathrm{M}_{\odot},), likely formed via a dynamical interaction in the low-metallicity (and now dissolved) cluster ED-2 (Marín Pina et al., 2024), and thus poses an example of the massive BH population that can result from dynamical low-metallicity environments. Thus, the presence of young massive clusters, and the lower metallicity in the Clouds make them promising targets for dBH searches.

NGC 1850 - BH1 was initially proposed by Saracino et al. (2022a) as a system containing a main sequence turn-off primary orbiting an unseen secondary. Situated in the LMC cluster NGC 1850, the object’s location in the CMD and the cluster’s well-constrained age placed initial estimates of the primary mass at around 5 M⊙\mathrm{M}_{\odot}, with simultaneous modelling of the radial velocities (RVs) and lightcurve suggesting a secondary mass around 11 M⊙\mathrm{M}_{\odot}. A non-compact object of this mass would be expected to vastly outshine the proposed 5 M⊙\mathrm{M}_{\odot} primary, and due to the cluster’s age, no stars of 11 M⊙\mathrm{M}_{\odot} could be present in NGC 1850. Thus, the companion was labelled a BH.

papers.title: "Helium Enrichment Law": The Relation Between Helium and Metal Enrichment in Stars in FIRE-3 Simulations of Milky Way-mass Galaxies
papers.abstract: Helium abundance is a key input to stellar models that are used to infer accurate ages, masses, and compositions for individually resolved stars in the Milky Way (MW), underpinning Galactic archaeology. Since spectroscopically measuring He abundances is difficult, stellar models often assume a fixed "chemical enrichment law" dY/dZ (the slope linearly relating a star's helium mass fraction Y to its metal mass fraction Z). If incorrect, this assumption can introduce significant systematics in inferring stellar properties. Using the FIRE-3 cosmological baryonic zoom-in simulations, we investigate helium versus metal enrichment in the stars of MW-mass galaxies. Given the nucleosynthetic yields in FIRE-3, overall metal production is dominated by core-collapse supernovae (CCSN) at all progenitor metallicities. He production is dominated by CCSN for progenitor metallicities of Z <= 0.1 Zsun, but by stellar winds for progenitors near Zsun. Our simulations produce a range of dY/dZ slopes slopes with best-fit values of ~0.75-2.1 depending on the age of the stars considered at present day; on average consistent with the range of values from MW observations but with no single "universal" enrichment law. The dY/dZ slope also shows galaxy-to-galaxy variance in our simulations, and to leading order increases over cosmic time within the same galaxy, based on the peculiarities of the formation histories of each MW-mass system. Despite choosing a fixed set of nucleosynthetic yields for stellar feedback processes in FIRE-3, we predict variance in dY/dZ for stars in MW-mass galaxies, and observations of MW stars must be interpreted in this context.

papers.intro:
After the Big Bang and before the formation of the first stars, the elemental composition of the Universe was primarily hydrogen (H) and helium (He), with very trace amounts of Lithium (Li) and Beryllium (Be) as per Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) models [108, e.g.,]. Heavier elements were produced via stellar processes, and the cosmos was enriched in metals over time as the result of stellar feedback; see Kobayashi et al. [67] for a comprehensive review on the origins of various heavy elements. The elemental abundances of stars thus encode a wealth of information about the formation and evolution of their host galaxies, and the conditions in the interstellar medium (ISM) at various points in cosmic time. The modelling of the elemental evolution of galaxies and in particular, the Milky Way (MW), is the subject of a rich field; see for example Tinsley [113], Matteucci [78], and Somerville and Davé [105].

The modelling of the elemental evolution of galaxies and in particular, the Milky Way (MW), is the subject of a rich field; see for example Tinsley [113], Matteucci [78], and Somerville and Davé [105].

The MW is the best studied galaxy [see 14, for an excellent review] thanks to our ability to individually measure the properties of millions-to-billions of its constituent stars at present day. A key goal of “Galactic Archaeology” of the MW is is to use the observed dynamics, ages, and elemental abundances of its stars at present day to uncover the Galaxy’s formation history, accretion or assembly history, and shed light on the astrophysical processes governing galaxy formation [35, 36, 97, 13, 95, 21, 50, 124, 29, 62, as in]. Galactic archaeology has been revolutionized by recent large-scale astrometric, spectroscopic, and asteroseismic surveys like Gaia [37], APOGEE [75], LAMOST [27], GALAH [28], SDSS-V Milky Way Mapper [100], Kepler [15], and TESS [94]; in particular via measurements of the ages, elemental abundances, and distances of red giant branch (RGB) stars that are bright enough to be observed across the entire Galaxy.

Some studies have inferred He abundances in star clusters or stellar populations using isochrone fitting [20, for example,]. However, for Galactic archaeology we often want to know the ages of field stars, requiring their He abundances as inputs to stellar models. Asteroseismology offers a way to measure the ages of field stars, but even state-of-the-art seismic models still depend on an assumed linear scaling between He and heavy element/metal abundances, anchored to Big BBN and Solar calibrations [22, 49, see reviews by]. The standard approach is to apply a transformation from the observed metallicity [Fe/H] to fractional abundances of heavy elements ZZ based on Solar abundance ratios, and then on to fractional helium abundance YY by assuming a relation between metal and helium content known as the “chemical enrichment law” Δ​Y\Delta Y/Δ​Z\Delta Z, anchored to YY and ZZ values obtained from BBN [108, 89]. Thus if the assumption of a fixed scaling between He and metal content for all stars in the MW is inaccurate, it can introduce systematics when inferring stellar properties (especially age) using standard stellar evolution or asteroseismic models. The existence and value of such a “chemical enrichment law” have long been debated, and current observations favor values in the range 0.8≲Δ​Y0.8\lesssim\Delta Y/Δ​Z≲3\Delta Z\lesssim 3 as obtained from different measurements of individual MW stars [46, 23, 71, 66, 7, 20, 103, 104, 115, and references therein]. Since accurately measuring stellar ages is key for Galactic archaeology, assuming such an enrichment law Δ​Y\Delta Y/Δ​Z\Delta Z can significantly impact the inferences for MW science when applying stellar models to asteroseismic observations of RGB stars.

It is important to note that the assumption of a fixed slope Δ​Y\Delta Y/Δ​Z\Delta Z implies that over the course of the a galaxy’s formation history, helium is created (or destroyed) in lock-step with metals. Given that helium has at least two primary modes of production — core-collapse supernovae (CCSN) and stellar winds from asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars — with different yields [68], there is no particular a priori reason that this should hold. Additionally, many stars in the MW do not have scaled version of Solar abundances [14, 63], which is another reason to not expect all elements to scale in lock-step over the course of the Galaxy’s formation history.

papers.title: Resolvent Components of Completely Normal Elements and the Morgan-Mullen Conjecture
papers.abstract: We study completely normal elements of $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, that is, elements that are normal over every intermediate field, through partial Lagrange resolvents. In these coordinates, complete normality splits into independent components, in a way closely related to Hachenberger's decomposition theory. Our main tool is a structure theorem for the components; together with a finite computation, it shows that every component has weight (the sum of the probabilities that its conditions fail) at most $3/4$, uniformly in $n$. Combined with the classical character-sum method, this gives an explicit sufficient criterion for the existence of a primitive completely normal element. We verify the criterion for all $n>q$ except $70$ pairs $(q,n)$, which we settle with explicit elements found by computer. Since the case $n\le q$ is due to Garefalakis and Kapetanakis, this confirms the conjecture of Morgan and Mullen (1996) that every $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ contains a primitive element that is completely normal over $\mathbb{F}_q$. The same estimates give two further results. First, Hachenberger's conjectured lower bound $(q-1)^{n'}q^{(p^a-1)n'}$ for the number of completely normal elements, where $p$ is the characteristic and $n=p^an'$ with $p\nmid n'$, holds for all pairs $(q,n)$; it was known for regular pairs. Second, primitivity and complete normality are asymptotically independent: as $q^n\to\infty$, the number of primitive completely normal elements is $(1+o(1))\,\varphi(q^n-1)/(q^n-1)$ times the number of completely normal elements (for fixed $n$ this was known). Our arguments for $n>q$ and for both further results, including every computer-assisted step, are formalised in Lean 4 with Mathlib; the formalisation takes the case $n\le q$ and an explicit bound of Rosser and Schoenfeld as axioms and relies on Lean's compiler and interpreter for the large computations.

papers.title: On families of copulas and quasi-copulas homeomorphic to the Hilbert cube and related results
papers.abstract: Working with tools from infinite-dimensional topology and using measure-theoretic ideas we analyze numerous well-known fami\-lies of copu\-las and quasi-copulas from a topological perspective, prove that most of them are homeomorphic to the Hilbert cube $\mathcal{H}$ and hence have the Fixed Point as well as the Disjoint Cells property. Working with so-called $Z$-sets, we then study how large one set is within another. Doing so, in order to show that a set $A$ is small/topologically negligible within a compact metric space $(\Omega,m)$, we construct a homeomorphism $h: [0,1] \times \mathcal{H} \to \Omega$ mapping $\{0\} \times \mathcal{H}$ to $A$. The obtained results are to a certain extent surprising since various supposedly small families are topologically large.

papers.title: Prussian blue and Prussian white thin-film electrodes: Single-step electrodeposition for anode and cathode applications
papers.abstract: This study examines how deposition potential influences the composition and nanoscale structure of Prussian Blue (PB)/Prussian White (PW)-family films, providing an experimental basis for assessing their proposed functions. Films were grown directly on Au/Cr/Si in a single potentiostatic step from a common aqueous bath at $-0.20$ to $+0.40$\,V versus a saturated calomel electrode, with a fixed deposition charge of 10\,mC. Electron microscopy, elemental analysis, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and Raman spectroscopy revealed potential-dependent chemistry and nonmonotonic morphology. EDS indicated greater K incorporation in lower-potential deposits, whose Fe~2p and Raman features were consistent with more reduced, PW-like environments. Surface K/Fe ratios varied nonmonotonically from 1.129 to 1.322 across the series, corresponding to 52.95--56.94\% K within the detected K+Fe population. Larger faceted crystallites at $+0.30$\,V contrasted with finer pyramids and cracks at $+0.40$\,V. Selected PB-like and PW-like regions had local cubic lattice parameters of $(10.31\pm0.10)$\,\AA\ and $(10.36\pm0.10)$\,\AA, respectively; their overlapping uncertainties prevent discrimination by lattice spacing alone. Cross-sectional maps showed broadly uniform framework-element distributions within locally continuous coatings. Together, these observations relate deposition conditions to contrasting chemical and morphological starting states without establishing bulk stoichiometry or phase purity. A literature-grounded outlook identifies ion storage, sensing, electrochromism, resistive switching, and ion handling as research opportunities requiring functional validation in these films.

papers.title: VISTA: Differentiable Viewpoint Planning for Long-Horizon Task Visualization
papers.abstract: Long-horizon object-centered tasks in interactive 3D environments involve heterogeneous events that unfold across time and space, including fine-grained manipulations, larger structural motions, and subtle state transitions. Effectively visualizing such processes is essential for helping users understand how actions lead to outcomes over time. However, existing camera control methods in 3D systems are commonly designed for static objects, and often fail to maintain the legibility of task-relevant components and their evolving relationships throughout long-horizon executions. We present VISTA, a differentiable viewpoint planning framework for long-horizon task visualization. We formulate camera control as a visualization policy that optimizes camera parameters under a unified rendering-based quality objective and we propose five quality metrics to satisfy our five design goals. To support both local part inspection and interaction-centric visualization centered on a primary object, our formulation handles targets defined either as object--part pairs or as relational tuples involving another interacting object. This allows the planner to reveal not only what part is important, but also how it functionally relates to surrounding structures during task execution. We demonstrate that the same planner supports two complementary use cases: presentation-driven narrative visualization for communicating how long-horizon tasks unfold to human viewers, and agent-driven active observation within an observe-act loop. Together, these results position differentiable viewpoint planning as a general mechanism for ``how-things-work'' visualization of long-horizon object-centered interactions in 3D environments.

papers.title: Efficient Remote Sensing Image-Text Retrieval via Interaction-Free Recall and Text-Guided Reranking
papers.abstract: Remote sensing (RS) image-text retrieval plays a critical role in understanding massive RS imagery. However, the dense multi-object distribution and complex backgrounds in RS imagery make it difficult to simultaneously achieve fine-grained cross-modal alignment and efficient retrieval. Existing methods either rely on complex cross-modal interactions that lead to low retrieval efficiency, or depend on large-scale vision-language adaptation, which requires massive data and computational resources. To address these issues, we develop a fast-then-fine (FTF) retrieval framework centered on interaction-free multi-granular recall and parameter-free text-guided cross-modal reranking with the Balanced Text-guided Interaction Block (BTIB). Specifically, interaction-free multi-granular recall pre-computes gallery embeddings and matches them with the corresponding query embedding without full-gallery token-level text-image interaction, while text-guided cross-modal reranking with BTIB refines local semantic correspondence within the top-K candidate set. Furthermore, an inter- and intra-modal loss is designed to jointly optimize cross-modal alignment across multi-granular representations. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate that the FTF achieves competitive retrieval accuracy while significantly improving retrieval efficiency compared with existing methods.

papers.title: PailitaoMMSearch2.0 Technical Report: Scaling Generative Retrieval to Unified End-to-End Multimodal Search
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval models have been increasingly adopted in search and recommendation systems. However, industrial generative retrieval models are commonly specialized to a fixed online scenario: they learn from scenario-specific interactions, support a narrow set of query forms and retrieval objectives. We study how to remove these couplings and build a unified end-to-end multimodal search system for open-ended image--text queries, heterogeneous shopping intents, and online scenarios with different resource constraints. We present \textbf{PailitaoMMSearch}, which directly generates product Semantic IDs from a raw query image and free-form instruction and scales along three dimensions. \textbf{Data scaling} uses a reusable toolset that can be composed into intent- and lifecycle-specific workflows for cold-start synthesis, quality control, real-traffic refinement, and continuous data production. \textbf{Intent scaling} progressively equips one model with e-commerce product knowledge, multiple retrieval relations, and adjustable reasoning budgets through continual pre-training (CPT), mixed-budget supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and unified reinforcement learning (RL). The RL stage combines intent-balanced optimization and Sample--Beam rollouts aligned with multi-candidate serving. \textbf{Scenario scaling} exposes quality--cost operating points across model capacity and reasoning budget. The system is deployed in multimodal search applications on Taobao Pailitao. A controlled online A/B test reports statistically significant improvements, including item page views $\textbf{+17.90\%}$, transactions $\textbf{+27.04\%}$, and gross merchandise value $\textbf{+8.94\%}$.
