papers.title: Cost-based variable selection for prediction models
papers.abstract: Objective: Variable selection for clinical prediction models is commonly done on statistical grounds related to model fit. Statistical approaches ignore the cost of misclassifications and the harm of measuring a variable. We aim to develop a decision-analytic variable selection algorithm based on net benefit. Materials and Methods: The proposed algorithm selects the set of predictors by exhaustively comparing the net benefit of all combinations using cross validation, with an extension based on backward elimination for settings with many predictors. Variables are selected if the increased net benefit from better predictiveness exceeds the net benefit reduction from the harm of variable measurement. Harm includes financial expense, time, resource allocation, and patient burden. We illustrate the algorithm through a simulated example and three real case studies. We compare its performance to traditional backward elimination and LASSO. Results: Across the case studies, parsimonious models were generated that optimized clinical utility with minimal impact on discrimination and calibration. Penalizing predictors based on their cost ensured that expensive or burdensome variables were only selected if they offer sufficient clinical utility. The algorithm was implemented in the R package NBvarsel. Discussion: Decision-analytic variable selection allows prediction models to maximize patient benefit while minimizing unnecessary clinical burden and costs. Conclusion: Clinical utility should not be an afterthought reserved only for implementation. By integrating a harm-adjusted net benefit metric directly into the variable selection process, NBvarsel allows researchers to select only the variables that sufficiently improve clinical utility.

papers.title: GNBG-C: A Unified and Configurable Benchmark Generator for Constrained Continuous Optimization
papers.abstract: Many real-world optimization tasks are governed not only by what should be optimized, but also by what is allowed: a solution must first satisfy physical, operational, safety, budgetary, or structural requirements before its objective value becomes meaningful. Yet benchmark design for constrained continuous optimization often treats these restrictions as fixed properties of predefined test instances. Existing generators and benchmark suites provide essential foundations for reproducible comparison, but they either focus primarily on configurable objective landscapes or expose constraint properties within limited, predefined regimes, making it difficult to ask targeted questions about constraint-induced difficulty: whether an optimizer struggles because feasible regions are small, boundaries are restrictive, variables are tightly coupled, or constraint information is poorly scaled. We introduce GNBG-C, a Generalized Numerical Benchmark Generator for Constrained Continuous Optimization. The central idea is to treat the feasible region itself as a configurable object rather than as an inseparable attachment to a fixed test function. By generating controlled constraint regimes around the known GNBG global minimizer, the generator enables systematic studies in which feasibility pressure can be varied while preserving that point as a global minimizer of the constrained problem. This allows researchers to examine how optimizers discover feasibility, handle constraint pressure, and improve objective quality under diverse and controllable feasibility conditions. GNBG-C therefore provides a flexible and auditable framework for probing the strengths and weaknesses of constrained continuous optimizers under targeted forms of feasibility-side difficulty.

papers.title: Gradient flow of magnetic inclination and intensity as a GPS-free guidance mechanism
papers.abstract: It is well established that some animals, such as sea turtles, sense the Earth's magnetic field and use it as a primary cue for long-distance navigation across the vast and featureless ocean. This remarkable ability has inspired the development of bio-inspired magnetic navigation (BIMN), which seeks to mimic these animals to develop robust and frugal navigation methods. BIMN exploits the Earth's magnetic field, sometimes described as ''Nature's GPS'', as a natural navigation infrastructure, providing a potential alternative to vulnerable satellite navigation systems. However, unlike geographic coordinates, magnetic coordinates extracted from the Earth's magnetic field do not provide a one-to-one mapping to geographic locations. Different locations can exhibit similar magnetic signatures, creating ambiguity and making BIMN inherently more challenging. Despite this fundamental challenge, we demonstrate that, within predefined regions of the Earth, magnetic inclination and intensity provide sufficient information to navigate to any destination. By formulating BIMN as a gradient flow control and guidance problem, we show that the resulting gradient flow act as current that carries the system and can be controlled to guide it through intermediate waypoints toward the desired destination. The resulting framework provides a GPS-free navigation mechanism with potential applications in both engineering and biology. In engineering, it can be used to establish a geomagnetic navigation infrastructure through which prescribed routes can be defined and followed, while in biology, it can be used to analyse the migration routes of animals known to rely on magnetoreception.

papers.title: Bounds for B-coloring planar and outerplanar graphs
papers.abstract:
A proper coloring of the edges of a graph is one in which every $K_{1,2}$ is totally multicolored. A B-coloring is a coloring of the edges of $G$ in which every $K_{1,2}$ and every $K_{2,2}$ is totally multicolored.
  In this paper, we improve two results by the authors and Gy\'arf\'as. The first shows that an outerplanar graph with maximum degree $\Delta$ can be B-colored with $\max\{\Delta,9\}$ colors, improving a bound of $\Delta+1$ and this is best possible up to the constant 9.
  The second shows that a planar graph with maximum degree $\Delta$ can be B-colored with $\max\{2\Delta+4,22\}$, improving a bound of $2\Delta+8$.

authors.name: G\'abor N. S\'ark\"ozy
authors.institution: HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics

papers.title: Mining the Nineteenth Century for the Thirteenth: Register-Scale Forced Alignment and HTR Bootstrapping via Legacy Regesta and Antiquarian Editions
papers.abstract: Handwritten text recognition (HTR) for the registers of Pope Honorius III depends on modern expert transcriptions, which exist only for regnal years 1-2 of Reg. Vat. 9. For the remaining registers, nineteenth-century scholarship offers Pressutti's regesta and partial editions. On fol. 1-203, where both layers exist, we measure what this legacy layer can contribute, on transcriptions that we first audit against it, and find a division of labor across three tiers. At the orthographic tier, raw editions are at best neutral for adapting a recognizer to the second regnal year and harmful without replay, whereas projection onto curial spelling with replay of modern source lines turns them into zero-label adaptation targets: pooled over all 134 year-2 sides, the WER falls by 1.50 points (95% CI -1.84 to -1.15), closing 33% of the gap to an oracle; the spelling changes at the year split, through the scribe or the transcriber, whereas the hand changes visibly only at fol. 191r. At the lexical tier, the corpus-wide legacy lexicon contains 82.2% of the out-of-vocabulary words of unedited entries and flags recognition errors with 66.7% precision, and labels from pre-trained medieval NER models, distilled into the recognizer's NER head, reach F1 82.1% on an expert validated benchmark, level with the best tagger applied after recognition. At the topological tier, Pressutti's regests, the closing datum clauses, and the regests' dates converted to the chancery's Roman form find 73.9% of entry starts in the recognized line stream, and edition agreement estimates a CER of 7.80% beyond fol. 203. Antiquarian scholarship thus cannot replace modern transcription, but it can steer, check, and segment HTR across the untranscribed registers.

papers.title: A Comparison of Electric-Field Profile Reconstruction Methods based on the E-FISH Diagnostic
papers.abstract: Electric-field-induced second harmonic generation (EFISH) is a non-intrusive, non-resonant technique for measuring electric fields in moderate-to-atmospheric pressure plasmas. However, its nonlinear, path-integrated nature introduces measurement uncertainty, preventing a unique relationship between the measured signal and local electric field. One approach to overcome this limitation is to acquire spatial EFISH profiles and invert them to reconstruct the underlying electric-field distribution. Although several inversion methods have been employed, their reconstruction accuracy and overall performance have yet to be systematically evaluated. This study compares three methods: machine learning, linear inversion, and Abel inversion, using EFISH measurements from four electrode geometries with distinct electric-field distributions. Their performance is evaluated in terms of reconstruction accuracy, robustness to sparse data and noise, and ability to reconstruct asymmetric profiles. All three methods successfully reconstruct electric-field profiles, but exhibit distinct advantages and limitations. Machine learning provides high accuracy, computational speed, and noise resilience, but performs poorly on profiles that differ substantially from its training data, particularly asymmetric profiles. Linear inversion accommodates a broader range of field distributions but is sensitive to the initial profile. Abel inversion is limited to axisymmetric fields but performs well for horizontal field polarization. The complementary limitations of machine learning and linear inversion motivate a potential hybrid approach for reconstructing electric fields with unknown spatial distributions. Overall, this study identifies key trade-offs among the methods and provides guidance for selecting suitable reconstruction strategies under different measurement conditions.

authors.name: T. L. Chng
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Detection and characterisation of Starlink VHF TT&C emissions at 137.055 MHz with the 21 CentiMeter Array
papers.abstract: Satellite emissions at low frequencies can interfere with astronomical observations. Observations with the EDA2 have revealed recurrent Starlink emissions near 137~MHz, attributed to very high frequency (VHF) telemetry, tracking, and command (TT\&C) transmissions. We aim to characterise Starlink VHF emissions detected with the 21 CentiMeter Array (21CMA) to better assess their potential impact on future low-frequency radio astronomical observations and inform the development of methods to mitigate the resulting interference. We searched five coordinated VHF channels in observations obtained on 15 April 2025 (UTC) and demodulated and decoded candidate signals. Two valid packets are detected at 137.055~MHz, each lasting 1.027584~s and separated by 99.987~s. A blind comparison with 11\,305 active satellites identifies STARLINK-32838 (NORAD ID 62827) as the transmitter, with differential Doppler measurements linking both events to the same spacecraft. Orbital analysis shows that the satellite was undergoing orbit raising and that the limited number of detections was partly attributable to its being below the horizon for most of the observing time. Re-analysis of EDA2 detections indicates that such emissions are not confined to orbit raising. The stronger event's estimated flux density is 9.23~MJy at 1000~km, consistent with previous measurements at the order-of-magnitude level. Signal demodulation and decoding, combined with orbital analysis, can improve the identification and characterisation of satellite-related radio frequency interference. The detection of similar VHF emissions across different orbital phases indicates that their potential interference with low-frequency radio astronomy should not be considered solely in the context of orbit raising.

authors.name: Feiyu Zhao
authors.institution: First Affiliated Hospital of Chinese PLA General Hospital

papers.title: The maximum size of intersecting $k$-graphs with covering number $k$
papers.abstract:
Let $m(k)$ be the maximum size of an intersecting $k$-graph with covering number $k$. In the present paper, it is proved that for all $k>e^{32}$, \[
  m(k)\ge k^k\exp\bigl(-50\sqrt{k\log k}\bigr). \] Together with Zakharov's upper bound \cite{Z}, this implies $m(k)=k^k\exp\bigl(-k^{1/2+o(1)}\bigr)$.

authors.name: Peter Frankl
authors.institution: HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics

authors.name: Jian Wang
authors.institution: Harbin University of Science and Technology

papers.title: The window process of slightly subcritical frozen percolation
papers.abstract: We study the frozen percolation model on the complete graph $K_n$, where each edge appears at rate~$1/n$ and connected components are destroyed by lightning strikes hitting vertices at rate $\lambda_n$ (thus the rate at which a connected component is destroyed is linear in its size). We focus on the slightly subcritical sub-regime of the self-organized critical (SOC) regime, assuming $(\ln n)^{4/3}n^{-1/3} \ll \lambda_n \ll 1$. Our main object of study is the so-called window process, which allows us to study the fine details of the mechanism that drives the SOC behavior of this dynamic random graph. We prove two scaling limit theorems. First, we show that the fluctuations of the window process around its deterministic fluid limit converge to a stationary Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process, whose mean-reverting property captures the SOC nature of the model. Second, by zooming in on a finer space-time scale, we prove that the scaled increments of the window process converge to a tempered stable L\'evy process.

authors.name: Bal\'azs R\'ath
authors.institution: HUN-REN Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics

papers.title: A Point-source Catalogue from Direction-dependent Calibrated 21CMA Images
papers.abstract: We present a deep low-frequency radio point-source catalogue centred on the North Celestial Pole (NCP) and extending $5^\circ$ in radius, derived from a single 24-h observation with the 21 CentiMeter Array (21CMA). Covering 75-175 MHz, the catalogue characterises extragalactic foreground point sources for Epoch of Reionization (EoR) studies. Previous 21CMA imaging has been limited by reduced dynamic range caused by direction-dependent effects, particularly the severe grating lobes of ultra-bright sources such as 3C 61.1 and ionospheric phase distortions. Here we apply 21CMAcali, a direction-dependent calibration and imaging pipeline, to mitigate these effects. The angular resolution ranges from 2.3 arcmin at 100 MHz to 1.4 arcmin at 168.75 MHz. The resulting maps show reduced artefacts and background noise, enabling more reliable recovery of faint sources. We construct a catalogue of 1246 radio point sources. Cross-matching with LoTSS-DR3, WENSS, and NVSS enables broad-band spectral fitting, while an independent in-band analysis yields a median spectral index of $\alpha=-0.825$ (where $S \propto \nu^{\alpha}$). The Euclidean-normalised differential source counts at 150 MHz, derived from a dedicated 50-MHz-wide multi-frequency synthesis (MFS) image, are broadly consistent with existing measurements and semi-empirical models at the bright end, whereas the deficit at lower flux densities ($S \lesssim 0.04$ Jy) mainly reflects limited sensitivity and incompleteness. This catalogue improves foreground point-source characterisation in the 21CMA NCP field, demonstrates the value of direction-dependent calibration, and provides a reference for deeper catalogues based on multi-day observations.

papers.title: Linear-Time FPT Rectilinear Planarity Testing of Series-Parallel Graphs
papers.abstract: A planar graph is rectilinear planar if it admits a planar orthogonal drawing without bends. For series-parallel graphs in the variable embedding setting the best known testing algorithm takes $O(n^2)$ time. We show that rectilinear planarity of a series-parallel graph with maximum degree four can be tested in $2^{O(k)}\cdot n$ time, where $k$ is the number of degree-4 vertices; the planar embedding is not fixed. In particular, the running time is subquadratic when $k=o(\log n)$. Each node of the SPQ$^*$-tree stores the set of its admissible spiralities; we show that this set is a union of $2^{O(k)}$ arithmetic progressions of step two. All proofs are in the paper and are additionally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

papers.title: MCP-Net: Real-Time Coronary Perception Network and Topological Analysis for Robotic Guidewire Navigation
papers.abstract: Coronary guidewire navigation during percutaneous coronary intervention requires continuous interpretation of vessel anatomy, guidewire position, and target stenosis under two-dimensional X-ray fluoroscopy. While existing approaches commonly address vessel segmentation or device localization as separate tasks, a robotic system requires a more structured perception of the coronary scene to support downstream navigation. In this work, we present a simulation-driven framework centered on a Multi-Task Coronary Perception Network (MCP-Net) for robotic guidewire navigation, integrating coronary vessel segmentation, vascular topology extraction, and roadmap generation. Starting from three-dimensional coronary CT angiography, we generate simulated fluoroscopy images containing vascular structures, simulated guidewires, stenotic lesions with varying severity, and diverse vascular geometries, together with simulation-derived ground truth. MCP-Net jointly performs coronary vessel segmentation, guidewire-tip localization, and stenosis localization from a single fluoroscopic frame. These predictions are subsequently converted into a structured vascular graph containing centerlines, bifurcations, endpoints, branch directions, and branch angles. By associating the predicted stenosis with this graph, the framework generates a roadmap from the automatically selected graph root toward the target lesion. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework can jointly recover coronary perception targets and transform them into an interpretable vascular representation suitable for downstream robotic navigation.

papers.title: Laser-Induced 90-Degree Magnetization Switching for Single-Element 2D Sensing
papers.abstract: Magnetoresistive sensors with multiaxial sensitivity are interesting for field mapping applications where local measurement of multiple magnetic field components is needed. Existing device designs are often discretized with separate sensing elements for each vector component, or they require complex detection schemes to distinguish the different components. In this work, we showcase a single-element two-dimensional vector sensor with on-demand reprogrammable sensing axis using light and optically switchable materials. Our device is an anisotropic magnetoresistive sensor with $90^\circ$ togglable sensitivity upon excitation with ultrashort laser pulses. The sensor consists of an optically switchable Co/Gd thin-film bilayer, patterned into a cross shape that stabilizes two orthogonal in-plane magnetization directions. By selectively addressing one diagonal of the cross, a single laser pulses toggle switches the magnetization direction in the center of the cross by $90^\circ$. Moreover, the field sensitivity of the device is toggled between the $x$- and $y$-axes, which we detected electrically with the planar Hall effect. Our results form a milestone towards optically reprogrammable integrated magnetic vector sensors.

papers.title: SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models
papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) enable world models to plan from images by predicting future embeddings. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly incorporate task-relevant state information, so the physical state that determines task progress may not be reliably captured in the latent space. Supervising world models with simulator state can make planning more informative, but it requires deciding which state features matter. Features are typically selected by hand or weighted uniformly, and a uniform weighting gives every standardized state feature equal influence, so redundant coordinates can overcount the same variation, while irrelevant ones can obscure task-relevant differences. To address this limitation, we propose SWIM (State Weighting with Inverse-Dynamics Model), which learns state weights from offline trajectories by predicting recorded actions from current states and observed future displacements. The learned weights quantify each feature's contribution to action prediction and define a weighted state metric for state-supervised training, which we demonstrate by aligning latent and state distances. The inverse-dynamics model is used only during training, so the resulting world model plans from images with no additional planning-time computation. Across five simulated robotic manipulation tasks, SWIM consistently improves planning success over uniform state weighting.

papers.title: Learning to Formalize: Bridging Open-Ended Workloads and Fast Decision Models
papers.abstract: Decision models offer fast choices over sup- plied alternatives, while general-purpose large language models interpret open-ended tasks through flexible generation and reasoning at the cost of sequential decoding. Many work- loads expect a generative backend to determine what can be done and therefore provide no well-defined candidate list. We bridge this in- terface gap with a small candidate formalizer trained on offline teacher-generated lists. The formalizer constructs explicit, validated alter- natives from task context, and a frozen deci- sion model selects an entry. A motivating com- parison with official TypeSafe Jev-1.13.0 on 200 CALVIN-D test episodes reports 11% suc- cess with generic motions versus 46.5% with DeepSeek V4 Flash pose candidates. Sepa- rately, a six-arm privileged-state evaluation on 1,011 CALVIN-D validation annotations finds that a locally deployed decision model can achieve at most 52.6% task success rate with the fine-tuned formalizer, compared with 11.8% without it, and the end-to-end latency is kept to 2.09 s, whereas Qwen3.5-27B is 3.67 s with the exact experiment setting.

authors.name: Chengxuan Pei
authors.institution: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

papers.title: Right Click, Wrong Box: Grading GUI Grounding by What a Click Does
papers.abstract: Leading GUI grounders score 93 to 96% on ScreenSpot-v2, and reported gaps between new and prior models are about a point. At this level the useful question is what the remaining errors are. Benchmarks count a click as correct only inside one annotated box, but interfaces often expose one action through several elements: a duplicated link, the label of a checkbox, the title next to a logo. The box is not wrong. The rule is incomplete. We call a click correct when executing it produces the same outcome as clicking the annotated target. A probe that executes and fingerprints about a thousand clicks per page turns this definition into outcome maps and an execution judge for live web applications, with no new annotation. We execute the predictions of three strong 7--8B grounders on a code forge and an online shop. About one in five and one in three of the clicks that box scoring rejects reach the intended outcome, and the shares remain one in seven and one in three when the instructions are rewritten as natural tasks. A blind audit of 11 models on ScreenSpot-v2 (three 7--8B grounders and eight 3B variants) finds the same effect on web screenshots, with two independent reviewers on a 60-unit subset. The share is highest for the strongest grounders. Training seeds and test-set sampling add noise that more runs and paired intervals control. Box scoring instead under-counts correct clicks, which repetition does not remove, and the audit-based correction of 0.2 to 1.8 points on ScreenSpot-v2 is as large as the gaps the field reports. The correction is needed in evaluation. In our 3B GRPO study, crediting equivalent clicks in the reward gives no stable gain over box rewards across three seeds and four test sets. We release the probe, the outcome maps, the audit and every prediction.

papers.title: When All Rollouts Fail: Policy-Compatible Joint Decoding for Hard-Problem Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) derives its learning signal from binary rewards via on-policy exploration and becomes a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning of large language models. Yet it faces a learning cliff on problems beyond model's current ability: when every rollout fails, the samples reveal nothing about a correct solution, and group-relative estimators (e.g., GRPO, RLOO) collapse the update to zero advantage. Expert trajectories offer a remedy, but they are incompatible with the current policy and often lie in the student's low-probability regions, so the surviving updates demand large parameter shifts and decay into surface-level imitation rather than transferable reasoning. We argue that a useful learning signal on hard problems must be both verifiably correct and sufficiently compatible with the current policy. We propose Policy-Compatible Reinforcement Learning (PICO), which performs distribution-constrained joint decoding: expert data guides decoding at the token level while preserving the student's relative token probabilities, and a dynamic top-k mechanism confines the sampling distribution under a finite divergence budget, yielding trajectories that are verified and policy-compatible by construction. These trajectories are optimized jointly with on-policy rollouts under a mixed-behavior objective that mitigates their distribution mismatch via importance sampling. Experiments across reasoning diverse datasets and agentic benchmarks demonstrate that PICO consistently outperforms standard RLVR and prior off-policy baselines.

authors.name: Hanzhu Chen
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology of China

authors.name: Runquan Gui
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology of China

papers.title: UniPCH: A Unified Framework for Cross-Chain Payments via Payment Channel Hubs
papers.abstract: Payment channel hubs (PCHs) enable private cross-chain payments, but existing protocols remain difficult to extend across heterogeneous blockchains. Their payment flows often depend on how particular blockchains represent transactions, authorize channel updates, and settle balances. Some protocols do not explain how their channels are implemented on actual blockchains. Supporting a new ledger or execution model requires a corresponding channel realization and may also require protocol adaptation and security analysis. We present UniPCH, a framework with two layers that separates native channel execution from private cross-chain payment logic. The lower UniPC layer defines common state transitions and security requirements. It separates task authorization from confirmation of the complete channel state. We provide realizations for UTXO ledgers and account ledgers that support smart contracts. At the upper layer, we develop selective re-signing blind conditional signatures (S-RBCS) to coordinate conditional authorization across hubs. Using S-RBCS, we construct a payment protocol that coordinates different channels in four phases. Our analysis establishes local UniPC security, griefing resistance, economic atomicity, and session unlinkability. We implement a Go prototype and evaluate the running time and bandwidth of each phase under different network conditions and system parameters. Results show modest computational overhead from the common interfaces. Most evaluated configurations run faster than comparable schemes under network delay. A full refresh ablation shows that reusing valid task evidence reduces computation and communication costs in the account realization.

papers.title: High-dimensional critical percolation and critical Branching random walks are intersection equivalent
papers.abstract: We prove that on $\mathbb Z^d$, with $d>6$, and under the usual assumption that the two-point function and the Green's function are of the same order, the probabilities to hit any finite set for a critical Branching random walk starting from the origin and the critical percolation cluster of the origin are within a positive multiplicative constant one from each other, as long as the set is sufficiently far away from the origin comparatively to its diameter. The proof relies on the introduction of a truncated equilibrium measure in percolation and the derivation of an approximate last passage formula.

papers.title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

authors.name: Haoyuan Chen
authors.institution: Tianjin University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Zichen Jiang
authors.institution: Centre international de recherche sur le cancer

authors.name: Ziyu Guo
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: The geometry of cognition: from neural populations to neurotechnology
papers.abstract: Cognition is implemented by distributed neural populations whose collective activity evolves through structured, low-dimensional state spaces. In this review, we survey the analytical and conceptual tools used to study latent population dynamics in biological neural networks. We begin with single-unit coding, which remains essential for interpreting neuronal selectivity, and then review population-level approaches, including population vectors, cosine similarity, principal component analysis and its mnemonic variants, multivariable linear regression axes, demixed principal component analysis, and single-trial latent-variable models, and distinguish operationally defined population subspaces from neural manifolds with reproducible geometry or topology. We use these methods to discuss sensory coding, working memory, decision-making, temporal processing, and sensorimotor transformations. Two organizing principles are emphasized throughout. First, cognitive variables can be expressed in separable or near-orthogonal population dimensions, reducing interference between sensory, mnemonic, decision-related, and motor signals. Second, such geometric separation does not require anatomically or functionally discrete cell classes; separable population readouts can coexist with a continuum of mixed-selective single-neuron responses within a shared biological substrate. We then consider recurrent neural networks as testbeds for generating and evaluating mechanistic hypotheses about how circuits produce low-dimensional dynamics, and intracortical brain-computer interfaces as a translational domain in which population geometry becomes an operational control signal. Overall, this review argues that population dynamics now provide a common language for linking neurophysiology, computational modelling, and neurotechnology.

papers.title: Replica Analysis of Overfitting in Vector Generalized Linear Models
papers.abstract: We show how the successful recent statistical physics based theory of overfitting in Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) can be generalized to a much larger family of regression models: the so-called Vector Generalized Linear Models (VGLMs), in which not a single linear combination of covariates drives the outcome, but where one has an arbitrary finite number of such linear combinations. The latter more general and complex models can describe more sophisticated statistical patterns in data, but are even more prone to overfitting than GLMs due to their significantly larger number of parameters; this often limits their use. We show that the generalization of the overfitting theory from GLMs to VGLMs causes many mathematical challenges that were absent from the earlier work, mostly related to the increased dimensional complexity of all order parameters in the theory, but that the new problem is once more solvable using the replica method. This opens up the field to many novel and welcome applications, especially in post-genome medical inference and data analysis, where overfitting is and remains a major barrier to progress. After developing the general VGLM overfitting theory, within the replica symmetric (RS) ansatz, we illustrate its merits and its correctness via application to several relevant VGLM regression models.

papers.title: Two-sample inference for sequence-derived feature distributions from deep sequencing data
papers.abstract: Many biological contexts involve heterogeneous populations of related molecular variants within a single individual. For example, some viral infections such as HIV-1 exhibit substantial diversity within a single host. Advances in sequencing technology now make it possible to characterize such populations by generating up to thousands of genetic sequences from a biological sample. In many settings, each sequence can be mapped to a numeric feature, such as Hamming distance to a reference sequence. This collection of feature values defines a one-dimensional distribution that characterizes individual-level viral diversity. When comparing these features across independent groups, past analyses have typically reduced each individual's data to a single summary value, such as the mean or mode. We propose a framework that retains the full individual-level distribution as the object of analysis. Drawing on existing tools from distributional data analysis, our framework uses Wasserstein barycenters to summarize the observed individual-level distributions within groups into a single representative distribution. These group barycenters are then compared using differences in quantiles and tested for equality. A practical challenge is that the number of sequences obtained, known as sequencing depth, can vary across biological samples. Through simulation studies, we examine when low sequencing depth can distort inference and present practical strategies for addressing these issues. We then illustrate the framework using data from the HIV-1 Antibody Mediated Prevention efficacy trials and a human B cell receptor sequencing study of vaccine-elicited immune responses. By using the entire collection of sequences for each individual, our approach can reveal group differences that may be obscured by single-number summary analyses.

authors.name: Linbo Wang
authors.institution: Harbin University of Science and Technology

papers.title: ATEMPO: Amortized Transfer Entropy Model Per-lag Over-Time
papers.abstract: When one time series informs another, the delay at which that information arrives determines if models can utilize this relationship effectively. A source may be strongly predictive at one delay but uninformative at neighboring lags. Therefore, fixed input windows may obscure this structure by bundling informative and irrelevant history together. Transfer entropy (TE) can recover these delays by measuring how much a source's past tells us about a target beyond the target's own history. However, existing TE estimators require separate fits across source and conditioning depths, with further estimation on local windows to track delays over time. We introduce ATEMPO, a diffusion-based transfer entropy estimator amortized over lags and time. ATEMPO samples source and conditioning depths during training and conditions explicitly on temporal position, allowing a single score network to estimate the full TE surface without refitting. Differencing this surface recovers when information arrives. Across synthetic datasets with ground-truth TE, ATEMPO achieves the lowest mean relative error among baselines, and on datasets with known lags, ATEMPO achieves $0.98\pm0.04$ lag-detection accuracy. ATEMPO requires a single fit across source depths $K=6$ and target depths $L=3$, whereas existing estimators require 18 separate fits to evaluate the same $K \times L$ grid. On three systems with time-varying lag, ATEMPO is the only estimator to maintain perfect lag-detection accuracy across all evaluated window lengths. These recovered delays improve downstream forecasting: ATEMPO-selected inputs reduce MSE on WEATHER-5K by 7.25%, while 120 selected inputs outperform the benchmark's 240-feature default by 4.6%. Across three brain-computer interface tasks, using ATEMPO-selected lags achieves the highest or equal-best $R^2$, improving mean $R^2$ by 4.1% relative to the strongest competing baseline.

papers.title: Expressive Guitar Synthesis via Controllable Latent Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Realistic guitar synthesis requires both audio fidelity and interpretable control over how notes are performed. The input timed MIDI events decide what is played but not how, leaving the continuous within-note decisions of guitar performance--such as pitch inflection and per-string articulation--unspecified. A model that directly maps MIDI to audio must therefore realize the performance implicitly, and users are left with limited control over the synthesized performance. We therefore propose a two-stage guitar synthesis pipeline that predicts editable, per-string $f_0$ and amplitude trajectories from timed note events and note-level dynamics, and renders them into audio using latent flow matching. Experimental results show that the proposed system outperforms a matched single-stage counterpart and DDSP-Guitar in control fidelity and perceived quality, while keeping the controls editable. Sound examples can be found online.

papers.title: An Application of Geometric Riemannian Pricing Algorithm for Valuing Catastrophe Bonds in Incomplete Markets: Market-Consistent Financial Entropy and the Split of Frequency and Severity Risk Premia
papers.abstract: This paper presents a framework for pricing catastrophe (CAT) bonds in incomplete markets through Riemannian geometric optimization of financial entropy. We formulate pricing-measure selection as a maximum financial entropy problem on a finite-dimensional manifold of equivalent measures, parameterized by the non-hedgeable market prices of catastrophe frequency and severity risk, with discounting fixed by the default-free term structure. Since unconstrained entropy maximization recovers the physical measure, we incorporate observed secondary-market spreads, both pooled and date by date. For a compound Poisson-generalized Pareto loss model with Wang distortion, we derive closed-form expressions for financial entropy and the Riemannian metric. We show that CAT bond prices depend on frequency and severity premia primarily through the risk-neutral trigger intensity, making the two premia unidentifiable from market data alone; the entropy criterion resolves this ambiguity. Using a hypothetical earthquake CAT bond calibrated to quarterly spreads of Golden State Re II Ltd. (Series 2014-1), we obtain risk-neutral trigger intensities of 6.58 to 10.45 times the physical intensity (9.20 pooled and 18.26 at the end of 2015). The model-implied risk multiple aligns with the market spread-to-expected-loss ratio (8.87 versus 8.81 at issuance). The minimal-entropy measure attributes 53.5% to 63.7% of the log risk multiple to frequency risk, reflecting the selection principle rather than market identification. Finally, equating the coupon with the quoted spread understates the risk multiple by approximately half.

papers.title: Irrationality of the conjugacy growth on Heisenberg groups
papers.abstract: We demonstrate that the conjugacy growth series for the Heisenberg groups $H_n(\mathbb{Z})$ is never algebraic, irrespective of the generating set. This makes progress towards the conjecture that all finitely presented groups that are not virtually abelian have irrational conjugacy growth series. Contrary to the group $H_3(\mathbb{Z})$, where the conjugacy growth is $n^2\log(n)$, the conjugacy growth of the other Heisenberg groups is polynomial, making these groups the first known nilpotent groups where the irrationality does not follow from the asymptotic growth.

papers.title: SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching (Extended Version)
papers.abstract:
Data memory-dependent prefetchers (DMPs) are a microarchitectural optimization recently introduced in mainstream desktop and server CPUs. Although DMPs offer performance improvements, they have been shown to enable side-channel leakage of secrets, even from constant-time code that has been hardened against Spectre attacks. Unfortunately, existing defenses either incur significant performance overhead or, as we show, fail to prevent all DMP leakage.
  In this work, we address this gap by designing a defense that is both secure and efficient. First, we propose a classification of DMP leakage, categorize existing and novel attacks, and analyze which leakage classes are mitigated by existing defenses. We validate this analysis empirically by implementing the first open-source DMPs on a RISC-V processor, showing that the only existing defense that aims to preserve DMP performance fails to protect against entire leakage classes. Next, we propose SecDMP, a provably secure and efficient hardware-based defense. SecDMP requires secrets to be marked in memory and ensures that DMPs never encode these secrets in the microarchitecture---without compromising performance for public data. We formally prove that SecDMP introduces no leakage beyond a baseline semantics without DMPs. Notably, when combined with speculative-execution defenses, SecDMP restores complete microarchitectural security for constant-time code. Finally, our empirical evaluation shows that SecDMP prevents all DMP leakage while incurring minimal performance overhead and hardware cost.

papers.title: ALADDIN: Adversarial Latent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity Swapping
papers.abstract: Face swapping transfers a source identity onto a target image while preserving the target's pose, expression, hair, and lighting. The most realistic current methods are diffusion-based, but they need many network evaluations per image. GAN-based methods are fast, yet trained from scratch they must learn realism from the adversarial signal alone and produce visibly weaker results. We present ALADDIN (Adversarial Latent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity Swapping), a one-step face swapper obtained by initialising the generator from a pre-trained multi-step flow-matching model and training it adversarially under identity and target-preservation constraints. We expose a controllable trade-off between identity transfer and target-attribute preservation by training a student model with triplet pseudo-label supervision. We additionally identify a bias in the standard evaluation protocol, which favours methods trained against the same identity encoder used to score them, and re-evaluate all baselines with an independent one. ALADDIN is state-of-the-art among one-step methods in realism and target preservation at comparable identity transfer, and matches the best multi-step model with 28 times fewer network evaluations and an order of magnitude fewer training pairs.

papers.title: Combinatorial description of the mirabolic quantum Schur-Weyl duality
papers.abstract: We prove an explicit correspondence between the irreducible finite dimensional representations of the mirabolic quantum group $MU(n)$ and those of the mirabolic Hecke algebra $MH_d$ given by the mirabolic quantum Schur-Weyl duality. In particular, this resolves a generalization of a conjecture by the second author. The proof is via a careful analysis of the $MU(n)$-weight spaces and the eigenvalues of the Jucys Murphy elements of $MH_d$ on the mirabolic tensor space.

papers.title: Development and assessment of a target-$\omega$ interfacial turbulence-damping model for stratified gas--liquid flow
papers.abstract: Interfacial turbulence damping is required in Reynolds-averaged simulations of stratified gas--liquid flows when strong interfacial velocity gradients are present. In this work, we develop a target-$\omega$ interfacial damping formulation for the low-Reynolds-number Wilcox-type $k$--$\omega$ model in a one-field RANS/VOF framework. A gas-side target value of the specific dissipation rate $\omega$ is constructed from an effective interfacial wall coordinate determined from the local resolved flow. The constructed target-$\omega$ provides a smooth transition between the viscous and logarithmic limits through power-law blending and requires no calibration of model constants against target data. \textcolor{black}{The formulation is first assessed against three gas-layer DNS cases at $Re_\tau\simeq180$ with different interface velocities. The model reproduces the principal features of the mean velocity, turbulent kinetic energy and Reynolds shear-stress distributions, while showing substantially weaker sensitivity to the near-interface grid resolution than the Egorov-type formulation, although some grid dependence remains on the coarsest mesh. The assessment is then extended to the co-current Fabre stratified-flow experiment at a higher Reynolds number and to the counter-current St\"abler experiment}. In both cases, the present formulation provides generally good predictions of the gas-side mean flow and turbulence statistics without case-specific adjustment. For the St\"abler case, in which the liquid level develops as part of the coupled two-phase solution, the predicted mean liquid depth agrees closely with the measured value. These results indicate that the target-$\omega$ formulation provides a consistent interfacial turbulence-damping treatment for resolved large gas--liquid interfaces over the range of conditions considered.

authors.institution: Lanzhou Institute of Husbandry and Pharmaceutical Sciences
